**Sūrat al-Mu'minūn (23)**

It is Meccan, as Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), it is said to be Meccan without disagreement. As al-Suyuti says in al-Itqan (*al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an*), an exception is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Until, when We seize their affluent ones with punishment﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 64], up to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿they will be in despair﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 77]. The ruling that the rest of it is Meccan raises a difficulty, because it mentions zakat, and zakat was only made obligatory in Medina. It is answered that, even after granting that what is mentioned in it indicates its obligation, it is said that zakat was obligatory in Mecca, while what was made obligatory in Medina was the specified amount (*dhat al-nasb*). You will hear the full discussion of this, God willing. It has, as in Kitab al-'Adad by al-Dani and Majma' al-Bayan by al-Tabarsi, one hundred and eighteen verses according to the Kufan count, and one hundred and seventeen verses according to the rest.

The Prophet (ﷺ) praised the first ten of its verses. Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara, and others reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When revelation came down upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), we would hear beside his face a sound like the humming of bees. One day revelation came down to him, and we waited a while. Then it lifted from him, and he faced the qiblah, raised his hands, and said: 'O Allah, increase us and do not diminish us; honour us and do not humiliate us; give us and do not deprive us; prefer us and do not prefer others over us; be pleased with us and make us pleased.' Then he said: 'Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever observes them will enter Paradise.' Then he recited ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] until he completed the ten."

Its connection with the end of the surah before it is evident, because He, may He be exalted, addressed the believers with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿O you who have believed, bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj: 77] (and) ﴿so that you may be successful﴾ [al-Hajj: 77]. So it was fitting that He confirm that, and He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾.

*Al-falah* means attaining one's aim. It is also said to mean remaining in good, and *al-ifläh* means entering into that, like *al-ibshar*, which means entering into good news (*al-bishara*). It may also be transitive, and on this basis is the reading of Talha ibn Musarrif and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd: *afliha* (in the passive voice). The particle ﴿قَدْ﴾ (*qad*) is for the confirmation of a matter that is expected and certain. The apparent meaning here is that it refers to *al-falah* (success) because ﴿قَدْ﴾ entered upon its verb, and its occurrence is expected from the state of the believers. Al-Zamakhshari took it as an announcement of its establishment, because *al-falah* is a future matter that has been presented in the form of the past, emphasised by ﴿قَدْ﴾ to indicate its certainty. So it conveys the certainty and firmness of the good news, as if it were said: "It has been established that the believers are among the people of success in the Hereafter." It is also permitted that the clause ﴿قَدْ أفْلَحَ﴾ be the answer to an implied oath, and al-Zajjaj mentioned, regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ [al-Shams: 9], that it is the answer to the oath mentioned before it, with the *lam* of emphasis implied.

Warsh, on the authority of Nafi', read ﴿قَدْ أفْلَحَ﴾ by transferring the vowel of the hamza onto the *dal* and dropping the hamza in pronunciation, because two consonants met, as Abu al-Baqa' said. These are the hamza, which is quiescent after its vowel was moved, and the *dal*, which is quiescent by original rule, since its vowel is incidental and is not taken into account.

Talha also read ﴿وَقَدْ أفْلَحُوا﴾ with a *damma* on the hamza and the *ha'* and with the plural *wa'w* dropped. It is explained according to the dialect of "*akaluni al-baraghith*" (the fleas ate me). Ibn 'Atiyya's statement that it is a rejected reading is itself rejected. It is reported from 'Isa ibn 'Umar that he said: "I heard Talha reading ﴿قَدْ أفْلَحُوا المُؤْمِنُونَ﴾, so I said to him: 'Are you committing a grammatical error?' He said: 'Yes, just as my companions committed it.'" Perhaps his meaning is that the basis of my reading is transmission, and whenever it is sound in something, it is not an error in reality, even if it appears to be so. The writing of the *wa'w* in the script is related from the book of Ibn Khalawayh.

In al-Lawami' it is said that it was dropped in continuous speech because two consonants met, and the writing followed that, so it is also omitted in the script. A parallel to this is ﴿wayamhu Allahu al-batil﴾ [al-Shura: 24]. The dropping of the *wa'w* both in pronunciation and in writing has also come, with the *damma* indicating it being sufficient, as in the saying:

"Even if the physicians were around me, and the healers were with the physicians..."

This is a poetic necessity according to some grammarians.

As for "the believers" (*al-mu'minun*), it has been said that they are either those who affirm what is known by necessity to be from the religion of our Prophet (ﷺ), such as monotheism, prophethood, bodily resurrection, recompense, and the like.

Then His saying, ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾, and what is joined to it, are qualifying attributes that specify them. Or they are those who also perform its obligations, as the attribution of the prayer to them indicates, so they are clarifying or praising attributes. Some reports support their being specifying attributes. Al-Zamakhshari made the attribution (of the prayer to them) an indication that they are the ones who benefit from the prayer, not the One to whom it is offered, may He be exalted and glorified. Khushu' (humble submission, lowliness) is humbling oneself together with fear and stillness of the limbs. Accordingly, Ibn 'Abbas said, in what Ibn Jarir and others narrated from him, "khashi'un means fearful and still." From Mujahid: it is lowering the gaze and lowering the wing (of humility). Muslim ibn Yasar and Qatadah said: it is lowering the head.

From 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, it is abandoning turning the head about (ilitifat). Al-Dahhak said: it is placing the right hand on the left.

From Abu al-Darda': it is magnifying the station, sincerity of speech, complete certainty, and gathering one's full attention. Following from this is abandoning turning the head about, and it is from Satan.

Al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about turning the head about in prayer, and he said: 'It is a snatching that Satan snatches from the prayer of the servant.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said during his illness: "Sit me up, sit me up, for I have a trust that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entrusted to me. He said: 'None of you should turn his head in his prayer. If he must do so, then let it be in what Allah the Exalted has not made obligatory upon him.'"

Among what is required is abstaining from fiddling with one's clothing or any part of one's body. Denying that this contradicts khushu' is stubborn obstinacy. Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi included in Nawadir al-Usul, but with a weak chain, a report from Abu Hurayrah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he saw a man fiddling with his beard in his prayer and said: "If this one's heart were humble, his limbs would be humble."

Also required is not raising the gaze to the sky, even if the worshipper is blind, and the prohibition of this has come. Muslim, Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah narrated from Jabir ibn Samurah who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Let people stop raising their gazes to the sky in prayer, or their gazes will not return to them.'"

Before the revelation of the verse, it was not prohibited.

Al-Hakim narrated it and declared it sound, as did Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayrah, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to raise his gaze to the sky when he prayed, then ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾ was revealed, and he lowered his head."

Also required is not adopting the ikhtisar (placing the hand on the hip) in prayer, and they have mentioned that it is disliked.

It has come from him (ﷺ): "Ikhtisar in prayer is the remnant of Hellfire."

That is, this is the practice of the Jews in their prayer, a rest for them, and they are the people of the Fire, not that there is any rest in it. How could there be, when Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It will not be lightened for them, and they will be despairing therein﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 75]. Among their practices in it is also swaying, and the prohibition of this has come.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated through the route of al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, from Umm Ruman, the mother of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, saw me swaying in my prayer, so he rebuked me with a rebuke that nearly made me withdraw from my prayer. Then he said: 'I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "When one of you stands in prayer, let his limbs be still, and let him not sway as the Jews sway, for stillness of the limbs in prayer is part of the completeness of the prayer."'"

In al-Kashshaf he said: "Among khushu' is that one observes the etiquette (of prayer)," and he mentioned among this: avoiding folding up one's garment, stretching, yawning, closing the eyes, covering the mouth, sadl (letting the garment hang over the shoulders), cracking the knuckles, interlacing the fingers, and playing with pebbles. In al-Bahr, quoting from al-Tahrir, it is said that there is disagreement as to whether khushu' is among the obligations of the prayer or among its virtues and completions, on two views, the correct one being the first, and its locus is the heart. End quote. Our own view is the opposite. The truth, indeed, is that it is a condition for acceptance, not for validity.

In al-Minhaj and its commentary by Ibn Hajar: "Khushu' is recommended in the whole of one's prayer, in the heart, by not allowing into it anything other than what one is engaged in, even if it relates to the Hereafter, and in the limbs, by not fiddling with any of them." It is evident that this is what al-Nawawi meant by khushu', because he will mention the first later in saying: "It is recommended to enter the prayer with energy and emptiness of heart, unless one makes that a means to it," and therefore he specified it to the state of entering.

In the verse, both of them are meant, as is evident too. It was a sunnah because Allah the Exalted praised its practitioners in His Mighty Book, and because the reward of the prayer is negated by its absence, as the sound hadiths indicate. Also, we have an opinion adopted by a group that it is a condition for validity. However, in some cases, it is disliked to become absorbed (in thoughts) together with inner speech and fiddling, such as adjusting one's cloak or turban without necessity, such as to achieve a sunnah or to repel harm. It is said that it is forbidden. End quote. Al-Imam (al-Razi) has a lengthy discussion on this matter; whoever wishes it should refer to it.

The fronting of the adverbial phrase (fi salatihim) is said to be for the sake of observing the verse-endings (fawasil). It is also said to bring the mention of the prayer closer to the mention of faith, for they are brothers. The application of the term "faith" to it has come in His saying, ﴿And Allah would not waste your faith﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. It is also said to be for restriction, in the sense that ﴿those who are humble in all their prayer, not just some of it﴾. In placing their description of humility in prayer before everything mentioned after it, there is an unmistakable emphasis on the importance of khushu'. It has also been reported that khushu' is the first thing to be lifted from people. In a report narrated by al-Hakim, who declared it sound, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit said: "It will soon come to pass that you enter the mosque and do not see in it a single humble man."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ahmad in al-Zuhd, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, narrated from Hudhayfah who said: "The first thing you lose of your religion is khushu', and the last thing you lose of your religion is the prayer, and the bonds of Islam will be broken one bond at a time." The report.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 3:

﴿And those who turn away from idle talk﴾ (al-laghw), which is that which is not regarded as worthwhile of statements and actions. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that its interpretation is falsehood (al-batil). It has become common that the term applies to speech that is uttered without deliberation and reflection, so it takes the place of al-ligha', which is the sound of sparrows and similar birds. Every ugly speech may also be called laghw, and one may say of it, as Abu 'Ubayda said: laghw and lagha, like 'ayb and 'aba (to find fault). And he recited: "from idle talk and obscene speech."

﴿are averse﴾ (mu'ridun) at all times, because of the state in them that calls to turning away from it, together with their being occupied with what concerns them. This is more eloquent than saying "they do not indulge in vain things in any way." The sentence is made a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya), indicating permanence and continuity; the pronoun is placed first, which serves to strengthen the judgment through its repetition; the predicate is expressed by the noun form, which, as is common, indicates permanence; the adverbial phrase is placed before it, which conveys restriction (hasr); and aversion is put in place of abandonment, to show that they are distant from it entirely, directly and indirectly, in inclination and in presence, for its original sense is to be on the side of one direction other than the side of it.

The apparent meaning is that by *zakat* is intended the verbal noun (*al-ma'na al-masdari*, the act itself), namely *tazkiyah* (purification), since it is this that their action is related to. As for the second meaning, the amount that the one paying zakat gives out, that cannot itself be the object of their action. So if this meaning is intended, one must posit an elided noun, meaning "they are doers *for* the payment of zakat," or else take ﴿fa'iluna﴾ (doers) in the sense of ﴿mu'addun﴾ (payers). Al-Tibrizi interpreted it this way, but he objected that one does not say "I did the zakat" meaning "I paid it." If the first meaning is intended, then describing them with the act of purification leads to the expression of the act of paying the property through *kinaya* (metonymy, indirect expression), which is more eloquent. This is one of the reasons for departing from "those who give zakat" to the wording of the noble text.

All that was mentioned just now in explaining the eloquence of ﴿And those who turn away from vain talk﴾ applies here as well, with the exception of the fifth aspect, which is agreed upon as not applying, and the fourth aspect according to some, because the fronted element is related to what follows in the manner of a prepositional phrase. Moreover, the *lam* is extra, serving to strengthen the government of the verb in two ways: the fronting of the complement, and the governing element being a noun.

Another scholar said: such a construction may also apply where the complement is fronted despite the weakness of its governing element, not for specification (*takhsis*, restriction) but because it is the place where the benefit lies. It is also permissible to consider relative specification (*takhsis idafi*) in relation to spending on what is not fitting. Describing them with this after describing them with humility in prayer serves to indicate that they spared no effort in worship, both bodily and financial. And placing the topic of turning away between the two is for the full connection of that to humility in prayer; otherwise, these two acts of worship are mostly mentioned together in the Qur'an without any separation.

It is reported from Abu Muslim that *zakat* here means righteous deeds, as in His saying: ﴿better than it in purity﴾ [al-Kahf: 81]. Al-Raghib chose that *zakat* means purity, and the *lam* is for causation. The meaning is: "those who do what they do of worship in order that God, Exalted is He, may purify them, or in order that they may purify themselves." Al-Tibi transmitted something similar from the author of *al-Kashf*, who said: "The meaning of the verse is: those who, for the sake of purity and the purification of the soul, are doers of good." What guides to this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself, and remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾ [al-A'la: 14-15], and ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ [ash-Shams: 9]. Indeed the Qur'an explains part of itself by part, and one should not turn away from explaining one part by another where this is possible. Some eminent scholars said: the juxtaposition of this with prayer calls out that what is meant is describing them with the payment of zakat, which is a financial act of worship. Comparing what we are discussing with the two verses is far-fetched, because these two are not of this category at all. It may be said: the separation between them suggests what al-Raghib chose and those who followed his path. Also, the fact that the sura is Meccan while zakat was prescribed in Medina supports it, so that it does not need the interpretation mentioned above. So reflect.

Whatever the case, the verse is at the highest levels of eloquence and rhetoric. As for the saying of some heretics among the non-Arabs, who have been deprived of the taste of Arabic, that it should have said *mu'addun* (payers) instead of *fa'iluna* (doers), it arises from sheer ignorance and foolishness, which has defeated whoever would treat it. For even if it were supposed that the Qur'an, and God forbid, is the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ), then he, upon him be prayer and peace, is the one for whom eloquence churned its cream and rhetoric gave him its reins. The Prophet (ﷺ) was among the most eloquent critics, who spared no effort in seeking a flaw, so that they might rest from the spears' thrusts by it. A parallel to this has come in the speech of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, who said:

"The feeders of food in the year of drought,
and the doers of the zakat-payments."

No eloquent Arab rejected this or found fault with it. Al-Zamakhshari chose in this matter to take *zakat* as the concrete amount and to posit an elided noun, rather than the verse as it stands. He justified this by its being in the plural, which occurs only for the concrete thing and not for the verbal noun. This was challenged: many verbal nouns have come in the plural, such as *al-zunun* (suspicions), *al-'ulum* (sciences), *al-hulum* (dreams), *al-ashghal* (occupations), and others. Where they differ, most scholars allow their pluralization, and here they differ according to what they relate to, for bringing out money is not bringing out livestock, and bringing out livestock is not bringing out crops. So let this be remembered.

[Page 6]

﴿And those who guard their private parts,﴾ ﴿except from their spouses or what their right hands possess.﴾

This is a description of them with chastity (*'iffah*). Although their description as turning away from idle talk (*al-laghw*) calls for it, it was mentioned for the sake of emphasizing its importance. It may also be said that although what preceded called for describing them with the basic quality of chastity, this was mentioned for what it indicates: that their sexual power impels them toward what is well known, and that they nonetheless guard it against fulfilling its demands, and by this complete chastity is realized. The *lam* is for emphasis, as was explained in its parallel instance. ﴿'Alā⁠﴾ (upon/from) is connected to ﴿ḥāfiẓūna⁠﴾ (guarding), by its being taken to imply the sense of "withholding" (*mumsikūn*), which is what Abu Hayyan chose. The verb "withholding" takes ﴿'alā⁠﴾, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Keep your wife to yourself⁠﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. A group went to considering the sense of negation contained in "withholding," so that the exception can be exhaustive (*tafrīgh*). Thus it is as if it were said: "They guard their private parts, not releasing them to anyone except their spouses." Some of them said: this inference is not required; the exhaustiveness here is not necessary for the sense, so the exception is valid in affirmative form. In *al-Kashshaf* it is said that the best view is that what is in the verse is of the type of "I guarded the child's property upon him," when one controls it, restricting it to him so that it does not exceed him. The original sense is: "they guard their private parts upon the spouses, not exceeding them." Then it was said: "not guarding except upon the spouses," as emphasis upon emphasis. On this view, the sense of negation mentioned by al-Zamakhshari is implied from the context and from the demand of the exhaustive exception, and it is not derived from the sense of prohibition and withholding contained in "guarding," because the preposition of elevation (*ḥarf al-isti'lā'*) prevents this. [Al-Zamakhshari's view] ends here, and there is in it what there is.

And alas, how is the preposition of elevation considered to prevent that, when the verb "withhold" taking it is a common matter? Al-Farra' said, and Ibn Malik and others followed him: "'Alā⁠" here means *min* (from), i.e., "except from their spouses," just as *min* means *'alā* in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We helped him against the people⁠﴾ [al-Anbiya': 77], meaning "against the people." It was also said that it is connected to an implied element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) of the pronoun in ﴿ḥāfiẓūna⁠﴾, and the exception is exhaustive from the most general of states, meaning: they guard their private parts in all states, except in the state of being those who are in charge of and maintain authority over their spouses, from your saying: "So-and-so was over so-and-so, then he died leaving her," and from it their saying: "So-and-so is under so-and-so," and for this reason the woman was called a *firāsh* (bed). Or it is connected to an implied element that indicates ﴿not blameworthy⁠﴾, as if it were said: "they are blamed except upon their spouses," meaning: they are blamed for every intercourse except what has been permitted to them, for they are not blameworthy for it. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned both of these views.

[Some] objected that both of them are forced, and that they apparently have foreignness (*'ujmah*) in them. He raised an objection against the latter: that affirming blame for them within the course of praise is not appropriate, especially since it is not restricted to them. And that this is on the assumption of their disobedience, and it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then whoever seeks beyond that⁠﴾ etc. [al-Mu'minun: 7], and this does not remove it as was supposed, and it is not permissible for it to be connected to ﴿maluminā⁠﴾ (blamed) mentioned afterward, because Abu al-Baqa' said that what comes after the negative particle does not govern what precedes it, and that the genitive-governed noun does not govern what precedes it.

What is meant by ﴿what their right hands possess⁠﴾ is the female captives (*al-sarriyyāt*). The specification of that is due to the consensus that it is not lawful to have intercourse with a male slave. The expression about them with *mā* (what), according to the view that it is restricted to non-rational beings, is because they resemble goods in being bought and sold; or because their femininity indicates the weakness of their intellects, so they are treated as if they were rational beings. This is clear in the case where they are from the Circassians, the Romans, or the like; so how much more so when they are from the Zanj, the Abyssinians, and all the Sudanese. By my life, in that case, if they are not of the kind of beasts, then the kind of beasts is not far from them. The verse is specific to men, for concubinage (*tasarri*) for women is not permitted by consensus.

It is reported from Qatadah, who said: a woman took a boy as a concubine, and it was mentioned to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and he asked her: "What moved you to this?" She said: "I thought that what is lawful for men of the right hand's possession is lawful for me." Umar consulted the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ about it, and they said: "She interpreted the Book of Allah, exalted is He, other than its interpretation." Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Surely I will not make you lawful to any free man after him, ever." It is as if he punished her with that, averted the legal penalty (*ḥadd*) from her, and commanded the slave

[Page 7]

not to approach her. And if a woman was married to a slave, then she came to own him and freed him while in the state of ownership, the marriage is annulled according to the jurists of the metropolitan cities (*fuqahā' al-amṣār*).

Al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, and Ubaydullah ibn Abdullah ibn Utbah said: the two remain upon their marriage. ﴿For they are not blameworthy⁠﴾ is an explanation of what the exception implies, namely the non-guarding of their private parts from those mentioned, meaning: they are not blameworthy for leaving off guarding them from them.

It was also said that the *fa'* (so) is the answer to an implied condition, meaning: if they give their private parts to their spouses or their female slaves, then they are not blameworthy for that. The purpose is to explain the category of what is lawful to have intercourse with in general; otherwise they have said that intercourse with a menstruating woman, a female slave who has been married, or one who has been subjected to *ẓihār* is forbidden until she atones (*yakfur*), and this is agreed upon.

Regarding combining two sisters from the possession of the right hand, and combining a female slave with her paternal aunt or maternal aunt, there is a difference of opinion according to what is in *al-Bahr*.

Al-Amidi mentioned in *al-Aḥkām* that Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, argued for the permissibility of combining two sisters in ownership by the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿or what their right hands possess⁠﴾.

Or it is connected to an implied element that indicates ﴿not blameworthy⁠﴾, as if it were said: "they are blamed except upon their spouses," meaning: they are blamed for every intercourse except what has been permitted to them, for they are not blameworthy for it. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned both of these views.

[Some] objected that both of them are forced, and that they apparently have foreignness (*'ujmah*) in them. He raised an objection against the latter: that affirming blame for them within the course of praise is not appropriate, especially since it is not restricted to them. And that this is on the assumption of their disobedience, and it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then whoever seeks beyond that⁠﴾ etc. [al-Mu'minun: 7], and this does not remove it as was supposed, and it is not permissible for it to be connected to ﴿maluminā⁠﴾ (blamed) mentioned afterward, because Abu al-Baqa' said that what comes after the negative particle does not govern what precedes it, and that the genitive-governed noun does not govern what precedes it.

What is meant by ﴿what their right hands possess⁠﴾ is the female captives (*al-sarriyyāt*). The specification of that is due to the consensus that it is not lawful to have intercourse with a male slave. The expression about them with *mā* (what), according to the view that it is restricted to non-rational beings, is because they resemble goods in being bought and sold; or because their femininity indicates the weakness of their intellects, so they are treated as if they were rational beings. This is clear in the case where they are from the Circassians, the Romans, or the like; so how much more so when they are from the Zanj, the Abyssinians, and all the Sudanese. By my life, in that case, if they are not of the kind of beasts, then the kind of beasts is not far from them. The verse is specific to men, for concubinage (*tasarri*) for women is not permitted by consensus.

It is reported from Qatadah, who said: a woman took a boy as a concubine, and it was mentioned to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and he asked her: "What moved you to this?" She said: "I thought that what is lawful for men of the right hand's possession is lawful for me." Umar consulted the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ about it, and they said: "She interpreted the Book of Allah, exalted is He, other than its interpretation." Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Surely I will not make you lawful to any free man after him, ever." It is as if he punished her with that, averted the legal penalty (*ḥadd*) from her, and commanded the slave

[Page 7]

not to approach her. And if a woman was married to a slave, then she came to own him and freed him while in the state of ownership, the marriage is annulled according to the jurists of the metropolitan cities (*fuqahā' al-amṣār*).

Al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, and Ubaydullah ibn Abdullah ibn Utbah said: the two remain upon their marriage. ﴿For they are not blameworthy⁠﴾ is an explanation of what the exception implies, namely the non-guarding of their private parts from those mentioned, meaning: they are not blameworthy for leaving off guarding them from them.

It was also said that the *fa'* (so) is the answer to an implied condition, meaning: if they give their private parts to their spouses or their female slaves, then they are not blameworthy for that. The purpose is to explain the category of what is lawful to have intercourse with in general; otherwise they have said that intercourse with a menstruating woman, a female slave who has been married, or one who has been subjected to *ẓihār* is forbidden until she atones (*yakfur*), and this is agreed upon.

Regarding combining two sisters from the possession of the right hand, and combining a female slave with her paternal aunt or maternal aunt, there is a difference of opinion according to what is in *al-Bahr*.

Al-Amidi mentioned in *al-Aḥkām* that Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, argued for the permissibility of combining two sisters in ownership by the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿or what their right hands possess⁠﴾.

﴿So whoever seeks beyond that﴾, i.e., beyond what has been mentioned of the broad limit, which is four free wives and as many concubines as one wishes. The word ﴿beyond﴾ (*wara'a*) is in the accusative as the object of *ibtagha* (seeks), meaning "other than that." This is the view taken by Abu Hayyan. Some of the verifying scholars (*muhaqqiqun*) said: ﴿beyond﴾ is an adverb of place (*zarf*), which cannot be the direct object, but rather stands in the place of the direct object. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: that is, whoever initiates the seeking of what lies beyond that. ﴿Then those are the transgressors﴾, the complete ones in transgression, who go to its extreme, as the demonstrative and the definite form indicate, and as the intervening pronoun (*damir al-fasl*) implies, which makes them the class of transgressors or all of them. In the verse there is an observance of the wording of *min* (from) and its meaning. What lies beyond that includes fornication, sodomy, and bestiality, and there is no disagreement about this.

There is disagreement about intercourse with a slave-girl who has been made lawful for him to have intercourse with. The majority said: she too falls under what lies beyond that, and so it is forbidden. This is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin, and it is narrated from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abd al-Razzaq narrated from him that he was asked about a woman who made her slave-girl lawful for her husband, and he said: "It is not lawful for you to have intercourse with a private part other than your wife's private part, except a private part, if you wish you may sell her, if you wish you may give her away, and if you wish you may free her." It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that it does not fall under it, so it is not forbidden. Abd al-Razzaq narrated from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "If a man's wife, or his daughter, or his sister, makes his slave-girl lawful for him, then let him have intercourse with her, and she belongs to him." This is the view of Tawus. Abd al-Razzaq also narrated from him that he said: "It is more lawful than food. If she gives birth, her child belongs to the one who was made lawful for her, and she remains the property of her first master." And he narrated from Ata that he said: "It used to be done: a man would make his slave-girl lawful for his servant, his son, his brother, or his father, and a woman would make her slave-girl lawful for her husband. It has reached me that a man would send his slave-girl to his friend." The Shi'a went to this view. The verse is evident in this regard, since it is clear that a borrowed woman for intercourse is neither a wife nor a slave-girl owned in full. Likewise is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if you fear that you will not be just, then (marry) one, or what your right hands possess﴾ [An-Nisa: 3], for silence in a context of explanation implies restriction (*hasr*), especially when the context calls for mentioning everything in which justice is not obligatory. And in the non-obligation of justice, the borrowed woman is more general than all of them, since it is not required of her that she should not bear the obligation of the owner of the private part only. Likewise is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free, believing women, then (marry) from what your right hands possess﴾ up to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is for whoever among you fears hardship, but to be patient is better for you﴾ [An-Nisa: 25]. For if borrowing were permissible, the fear of hardship and the need to marry slave-girls, and to be patient in refraining from marrying them, would not be established. Similar is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And let those who cannot find marriage be chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾ [An-Nur: 33]. For if borrowing were permissible, those who cannot find marriage would not have been commanded to be chaste. Perhaps the previous narration from Ibn Abbas is not authentic.

Likewise, there is disagreement about temporary marriage (*mut'a*). The Shi'a also went to its permissibility, [page 8] and it is refuted by what we have mentioned of the clear verses concerning the prohibition of borrowing. Abd al-Razzaq and Abu Dawud in his *Nasikh* narrated from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad that he was asked about temporary marriage, and he said: "It is forbidden in the Book of Allah, the Exalted," and he recited: ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ (the verse). He established the manner in which the verse indicates this: that the one who enjoys her is neither a possession of the right hand nor a wife, so it must not be lawful for him. As for her not being a possession of the right hand, it is evident. As for her not being his wife, it is because they do not inherit from each other by consensus, and if she were a wife, inheritance would occur, by His saying: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾ [An-Nisa: 12]. Al-Kashf commented on this, saying that they may say: she is a wife, whom death reveals to have been separated from him, just as she is separated by the expiry of the term, in fulfillment of the right of the condition and the limitation. Its summary is to dispute the implication: if what is meant is that were she a wife during life, it would not benefit, and if what is meant is after death, then the implication is denied. If it is said: she is not separated by death, as in a permanent marriage, it is answered that this is an analogy with the very thing in which the two marriages differ, and it is invalid by consensus.

Shaykh al-Islam criticized this, because its meaning is hidden from him, saying: the disjunction has no clear meaning. And if it were said: if what is meant is that were she a wife during life, the implication is denied, and if what is meant is after death, it would not benefit, that would have some merit. He said, in refuting their argument, that they may say: she is a wife of his in general. As for whether every wife inherits, they do not concede that. Some of them said: the truth is that the verse is a proof against the Shi'a, for the apparent meaning of their statement is that she is not a wife at all, since they negate from her the consequences of marriage entirely, such as the waiting period (*'idda*), divorce, oath of abstention (*iila'*), the zihar (likening to a mother), attaining the status of chastity (*ihsan*), the possibility of mutual curse (*li'an*), maintenance, clothing, and inheritance, and they hold that one may enjoy as many as one wishes through temporary marriage. There is no doubt that negating the consequence is evidence for negating what it implies. It was objected that this would be true if it were granted that they negate all the consequences, but it is not granted. Negating some of the consequences is not sufficient in refuting them, if they say: marriage is of two kinds, complete and incomplete, for by negating that part only the first kind is negated, and that does not harm them.

It was said: what equity requires is that the verse is evident in the prohibition of temporary marriage, for the one who enjoys her is not called a wife in common usage, and does not intend from her what is the wisdom behind the legislation of marriage, namely procreation and reproduction for the preservation of the species, but merely the fulfillment of desire and the quieting of the agitation of semen and the like. He claimed that the argument from the verse for prohibition in this manner is complete, whether the consequences are negated or not, as is the view of some who hold it permissible, as we shall point out, if Allah the Exalted wills.

Perhaps what is closer to equity is to say: whenever it is said that the consequences, such as attaining chastity, the prohibition of exceeding four, and the like, are negated, the verse is evidence for the prohibition, because what is understood from "wife" in it is the wife to whom such things are binding, and this suffices as an argument for a subsidiary matter of this kind. Whenever it is not said that the consequences are negated, and one does not distinguish between it and permanent marriage except by the time limit and its absence, the verse is not evidence for the prohibition.

Here there remains a investigation that I have not seen anyone address, namely that it is mentioned in the two *Sahihs* that "the Prophet ﷺ forbade temporary marriage on the day of Khaybar," and in Sahih Muslim that "he, upon him be prayer and peace, forbade it on the day of the Conquest." Ibn al-Humam agreed that it was forbidden twice, once on the day of Khaybar and once on the day of the Conquest, and this implies that it was lawful before these two days. You have heard just now what indicates that this verse is Meccan by consensus. If it indicates prohibition, as you have heard from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, and Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim narrated the like from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and al-Hakim authenticated it, then it follows that it was forbidden in Mecca on the day the verse was revealed, and that is before these two days, so it would have been forbidden three times. I have not seen anyone state this explicitly. And if we accept this, another matter remains: the argument from it alone for the prohibition of temporary marriage is not complete for one who knows that it was made lawful after its revelation, as is not hidden.

It cannot be said: people have three conventions regarding Meccan and Medinan. The first is that the Meccan is what was revealed before the Hijra, and the Medinan is what was revealed after it, whether it was revealed in Medina, or in Mecca in the year of the Conquest, or in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, or during a journey. The second is that the Meccan is what was revealed in Mecca even after the Hijra, and the Medinan is what was revealed in Medina, and according to this the intermediate category is established: what was revealed during journeys is not called either Meccan or Medinan. The third is that the Meccan is what was addressed to the people of Mecca, and the Medinan is what was addressed to the people of Medina. In that case, this verse may be Meccan by the second convention, and be revealed on the day of the Conquest, the day temporary marriage was forbidden for the second time, and there would be no prohibition except twice. And the argument of those who argued from it, from the Companions, the Successors, and others, for the prohibition would be valid, even though they knew that temporary marriage was made lawful after the Hijra in some campaigns, which is beyond dispute. And if this convention is adopted for the Meccan status of the entire surah, which is agreed upon as you have heard from al-Bahr, a difficulty is resolved, namely that the zakat is taken to mean legal zakat, despite its obligation in Medina, by saying: the opening of the surah was revealed after the obligation of zakat in Medina, in the year of the Conquest, in Mecca. For we say: there is no doubt that the verse may be Meccan by the second convention, and be revealed on the day of the Conquest, and likewise it is possible that the whole surah, or most of it, is Meccan in that sense, and everything built upon that is valid on that basis. However, what is understood from "Meccan" and "Medinan" is the meaning first agreed upon, because the first convention is the most famous of the three conventions, as al-Jalal al-Suyuti said in *al-Itqan*.

So the apparent meaning of their saying that this surah is Meccan is that it was revealed before the Hijra. Indeed, the aforementioned al-Jalal has explicitly stated that it is Meccan, except for what is excepted from it, which you have heard to be Meccan according to the first convention and not the second, and such a matter is not prohibited by that except by firm transmission. Thus what has been mentioned is merely the permissibility of a matter, which does not support its establishment, and rather explicit transmission supports the opposite, and it is the reference in what we are discussing.

Al-Qadi Abu Bakr said in *al-Intisar*: "Knowledge of the Meccan and Medinan is only by the memory of the Companions and the Successors." And that they may be defined by analogy, as mentioned by al-Ja'bari and others, despite its uselessness, is nothing. Yes, if the argument of a Companion or Successor who knew that temporary marriage was permitted after the Hijra is taken as a declaration that it is excepted from its sister verses in the surah, and a ruling that it was revealed after the Hijra while they were before it, then the matter is clear. You will also come to know, if Allah the Exalted wills, what necessitates the exception of other than that. In sum, whenever it is said that the basis in such matters is explicit transmission, it becomes necessary to hold that the verse is Meccan in the sense that it was revealed before the Hijra. And the argument from it for the prohibition of temporary marriage after its permission following the Hijra becomes problematic, because the evidence for permission specifies its general application. The majority of the four imams hold that the general wording of the Qur'an may be specified by the Sunnah absolutely, and this is the preferred view. In that case one would need another proof, besides it, for the prohibition. And after the proof is established, the verse becomes another proof with its support. This proof is the sound reports of the prohibition by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, some of which have already been mentioned.

In Sahih Muslim, from him, upon him be prayer and peace: "I had permitted you to enjoy women, and Allah the Exalted has forbidden that until the Day of Resurrection."

Al-Hazimi narrated with his chain to Jabir, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to the campaign of Tabuk. When we were at the 'Aqaba on the side of Syria, women came, and we mentioned our temporary marriage with them while they were circling around our camp. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came, looked at them, and said: 'Who are these women?' We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, women with whom we have enjoyed temporary marriage.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ became angry until his cheeks reddened and his face changed color. He stood among us as a preacher, praised Allah the Exalted and extolled Him, then forbade temporary marriage. So on that day the men and women bade farewell to one another, and we did not return to it and will never return to it forever."

Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, also narrated its prohibition from him, upon him be prayer and peace.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 7 (part 2 of 2):

It is recorded in Sahih Muslim, and it is said that the Companions reached a consensus (ijma') that it is forbidden (haram).

It is authentically reported from some scholars that Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, returned to the view that it is forbidden, after having said it was permissible absolutely, or permissible only at a time of necessity. Ibn al-Humam used as evidence for his return what al-Tirmidhi narrated from him, that he said: "Temporary marriage (mut'ah) was only at the beginning of Islam. A man would arrive in a town where he had no acquaintances, so he would marry a woman for as long as he expected to stay. She would guard his belongings and look after his affairs for him. Then when the verse came: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy﴾, Ibn Abbas said: 'So every other type of intimacy is forbidden.'" He added: "I do not know what he meant by 'the beginning of Islam.' If he meant what was in Makkah before the Hijrah, the report indicates that it was practised until the verse was revealed. If the verse was revealed before the Hijrah, there is no difficulty in using it as evidence for prohibition, unless after its revelation it was still permitted, but that did occur. If he meant the early period after the Hijrah, and that it was permitted at that time until the verse was revealed, then that would be a claim that the verse was revealed after the Hijrah, which contradicts what is narrated from him that the surah is Makkan. The apparent meaning of his words is the first sense, and perhaps he holds that. Or it may be said that his use of the verse as evidence is based on its exception, as mentioned just above. Or it may be said that this report is not authentic." This is supported by the words of the scholar Ibn Hajar: "The report of Ibn Abbas's return is not authentic. Rather, it is authentic, as some have said, that a group [of scholars] agreed with him on permissibility but disagreed by saying that the rulings of marriage do not follow from it." It was on this basis that he disputed al-Zarkashi's claim of consensus, and said: "The disagreement is real, even if one claims a consensus denying it." End of quotation. It is understood from this that Ibn Abbas includes the one who enjoys temporary marriage among the wives, and in that case the verse is not evidence against it, so reflect on this.

It is attributed to Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, that he permitted temporary marriage, but this is a false accusation against him. Rather, like the other imams, he holds that it is forbidden. Indeed, it is said that he went beyond the view of prohibition by holding that the one who practises temporary marriage deserves the hadd (prescribed punishment), which the other scholars who hold it forbidden did not require, because of the presence of doubt (shubhah).

Similarly, there is disagreement about a man masturbating with his hand, which is called khadkhada, and about jald 'Umayra. The majority of the imams hold that it is forbidden, and they consider it to fall under "what is beyond that." Ahmad ibn Hanbal used to permit it, because semen is a surplus substance in the body, so it is permissible to expel it when there is need, like bloodletting and cupping. Ibn al-Humam said: "It is forbidden. But if desire overcomes a person and he does it intending to calm that desire, then it is hoped that he will not be punished." Some people prevented its inclusion in what was mentioned. In al-Bahr: "A discussion took place between me and the Chief Judge Abu al-Fath Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Muti' al-Qushayri, known as Ibn Daqiq al-'Id. He used this verse as evidence for prohibiting it. I said: 'That verse came in the manner of what the Arabs used to do, such as fornication and boasting about it in their poetry. This was so common among them that among their prostitutes there were those who had banners [to advertise themselves], and they did not disapprove of it. As for jald 'Umayra, it was not known among them, and none of them mentioned it in poetry as far as we know. So it is not included in "what is beyond that."'" End of quotation.

You know that if it is established that jald 'Umayra is a metaphor for masturbation with the hand among the Arabs, as the apparent wording of al-Qamus indicates, then it is apparent that this act existed among them, even if it was not widespread and common like fornication. Whenever it is one of the individual cases of a general term, its inclusion under that term does not depend on its being widespread, just like its other individual cases. In legal rulings: if it is the custom of the addressees to consume a particular food, for example, and a general address then comes forbidding "food," as in "Forbidden to you is food," the majority of scholars agree that the wording is applied to its general sense, prohibiting every food, in a way that includes both what is customarily eaten and what is not. Custom does not restrict the generality so as to forbid only what is customarily eaten, which is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. This is because the proof lies in the wording that was revealed, and it covers every edible thing by its wording. It has no connection with customs, and it is the judge over customs, so customs cannot be the judge over it. Yes, if the customary food had been specialised by the customary usage, such that the term "food" came to refer only to it, just as "beast" (dabbah) was specialised for four-legged animals, then the term "food" would be understood as referring to that only, and not to anything else, because the Lawgiver addressed the Arabs according to what they understood from their language. The difference is this: the custom first is merely a regular habit of eating that particular food, so it does not limit what the generality of the word "food" implies. Second, it is a regular specialisation of the name "food" to that particular food, so it does limit the original usage.

From this it is known that if the Arabs' custom was to apply the expression "what is beyond that" to masturbation with the hand, then it is included according to the majority, even if they did not customarily practise it. And if their custom was not to apply that expression to it, but it was applied to fornication and similar acts, then that act is not included in the generality according to the majority.

Some people used as evidence for its prohibition something else, such as what the shaykhs mentioned, namely the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The one who has intercourse with his hand is cursed."

And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Allah punished a nation that used to play with their private parts." And from 'Ata': "I heard that some people will be gathered with their hands pregnant, and I think they are those who masturbate with their hands. And Allah knows best."

The full discussion on this point should be sought in its proper place. It is not hidden that the verse indicates the prohibition of every act that falls under the generality in the most emphatic way. A parallel to this is the indication of the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse﴾ [al-Isra' 32] regarding the prohibition of the act of fornication, so understand this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 8:

﴿And those who are, to their trusts and their covenant, keepers.﴾ They are those who maintain their safekeeping and its proper upkeep. The original meaning of ra'y (ر ع ي, "to keep watch over") is the protection of an animal, either by providing it with the food that sustains its life or by warding off an enemy from it. Then the term was used for protection in general. The word amanat (أمانات) is the plural of amanah (أمانة, "trust"), which is originally a verbal noun (masdar). Here, however, what is meant by it is that which one has been entrusted with, since the act of keeping applies to the entity and not to the meaning. As for its plural form, this does not indicate that, since verbal nouns may be pluralized, as we mentioned not long ago. Likewise, 'ahd (عهد, "covenant") is a verbal noun, and what is meant by it is that which one has been bound to by covenant. According to most exegetes, the verse is general in regard to everything they have been entrusted with and bound to, whether from God Most High or from people, such as the legal obligations (taklif shar'iyyah), deposited property, oaths, vows, contracts, and the like. The word amanah is given in the plural while 'ahd is not, and it is said that this is because trusts are very varied and numerous in relation to every responsible person (mukallaf) from God Most High, and no responsible person is almost ever free of them, whereas this is not the case with covenant.

Some exegetes have permitted that it be specific to what they have been entrusted with and bound to by people, but this is not the right view. In my opinion, it is permissible that by the trusts is meant what God Most High has entrusted them with of their limbs and faculties, and what is meant by keeping them is guarding them against using them contrary to His command, glorified and exalted is He. And that by the covenant is meant what God Most High has bound them to of what He, glorified is He, has commanded them through His Book and upon the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ), and what is meant by keeping it is guarding it against neglecting it, by fulfilling it in the most complete manner. Thus, the keeping of trusts is like vacating (takhliyah), and the keeping of the covenant is like adorning (tahliyah). It seems that, after mentioning their guarding of their private parts, He, exalted is He, mentioned their guarding of what includes them and other things. It is also permissible that trusts be generalized so as to include wealth and the like, and the plural form is used for the sensible, observed multiplicity it contains. So reflect.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, in one narration, read ﴿لأمانتهم﴾ in the singular.

﴿Those who are, over their prayers﴾: the obligatory prayers prescribed for them. This is as Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu Salih, and Abd ibn Humayd from Ikrimah. ﴿Who guard﴾: by performing them at their proper times, with their conditions, completing their bowing and prostration and all their other pillars, as related from Qatadah.

A group related from Ibn Mas'ud that it was said: "Indeed, Allah, exalted is He, mentions prayer frequently in the Qur'an," ﴿Those who are constant in their prayer﴾ (70:23), ﴿And those who guard their prayers﴾. He said: "That refers to their appointed times." They said: "We did not think it meant anything other than performing it and not abandoning it." He said: "Abandoning it is disbelief." It was also said: guarding it means persisting in performing it in the most perfect manner.

The verb was used rather than the noun, as in the rest of the verse-endings preceding it, because of the renewal and repetition inherent in prayer. For this reason, it was written in the plural in the recitation of the Seven (al-Sab'ah, the seven canonical readers), except for the two brothers (al-Akhawayn, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i).

This is not a repetition of what He described them with at the beginning, namely humility (khushu') in the category of prayer, because there is complete difference between what is mentioned here and what is mentioned there, as is not hidden.

In opening and closing the attributes with the matter of prayer, there is an exaltation of its status. And placing humility first is to give it importance, for prayer without it is entirely not prayer, by consensus. They have said: "Prayer without humility is a body without a soul." It was also said: its being placed first is because of the generality of what is mentioned here (i.e., the sense of guarding applies to it).

Page 12

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verses 10–11:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the believers, in view of their being characterized by the qualities mentioned, and the demonstrative is preferred over a pronoun to indicate that they are distinguished by these qualities from others, and that they are placed in the position of those pointed to physically. The sense of distance in it is to announce the high rank and the far elevation of their station in excellence and nobility. That is: those described with the sublime attributes mentioned. ﴿They are the inheritors﴾, that is, the worthy ones to be called inheritors, to the exclusion of all others who did not possess those qualities among the believers. It has also been said: [they are the inheritors] of the desirable wealth and its precious treasures.

﴿Who will inherit the Firdaws﴾ is a descriptive (sifah kashifah), or an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan), or a substitute (badal). Whichever it is, it contains a clarification of what they inherit, and a restriction of the inheritance after its generality, in order to magnify and emphasize it. Al-Firdaws is the highest of the gardens.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and al-Tirmidhi related, and he said: "Hasan sahih gharib," from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that: "Al-Rubayyi' bint Nadr came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and her son al-Harith ibn Suraqah had been struck on the day of Badr by a stray arrow. She said: 'Inform me about Harithah; if he has reached Paradise I will be patient and seek reward, and if he has not reached Paradise I will strive greatly in supplication.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Indeed, there are gardens within Paradise, and your son has attained al-Firdaws al-A'la, and al-Firdaws is the hillock of Paradise, its middle and its best.'"

On this basis there is no difficulty in the restriction (ḥaṣr) in the sense we pointed out at first, for one who is not characterized by the qualities mentioned, even if he enters Paradise, does not inherit al-Firdaws, which is its best part. And even supposing he inherits it, he is not worthy of being called an inheritor, since that generally occurs only after toil and exertion. Their inheriting it from the disbelievers is because the latter forfeited it for themselves, for Allah created for each a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in Hell.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Abu Hurayrah who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'There is none of you but he has two dwellings, a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in Hell. When he dies and enters Hell, the people of Paradise inherit his dwelling. This is the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾.'"

It has also been said that inheritance is a metaphor for entitlement, and in that there is whatever exaggeration there is, since inheritance is the strongest cause of ownership. But the first was chosen because it is the explanation of the Messenger of Allah, upon him be prayer and peace, as al-Qurtubi authenticated.

﴿They therein﴾, that is, in the Firdaws. According to what Ibn al-Shihnah mentioned, it is among the words that may be feminine or masculine.

Some have mentioned that the feminine usage is in view of it being a name for Paradise or for its highest tier. The full discussion concerning al-Firdaws has already passed for you.

﴿Abiding﴾: they will not leave it forever. The clause is either a resumptive new sentence confirming what precedes it, or a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) from the subject of ﴿inherit﴾, or an object (maf'ulah), as Abu al-Baqa' said, since in it each of these is mentioned. The meaning of the statement is: they will not die, nor will they leave it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verses 10–11:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the believers, in view of their being characterized by the qualities mentioned, and the demonstrative is preferred over a pronoun to indicate that they are distinguished by these qualities from others, and that they are placed in the position of those pointed to physically. The sense of distance in it is to announce the high rank and the far elevation of their station in excellence and nobility. That is: those described with the sublime attributes mentioned. ﴿They are the inheritors﴾, that is, the worthy ones to be called inheritors, to the exclusion of all others who did not possess those qualities among the believers. It has also been said: [they are the inheritors] of the desirable wealth and its precious treasures.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 12:

﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay.﴾ When He, glory be to Him, first mentioned the conditions of the fortunate (al-su'ada'), He followed them with mention of their origin and the outcome of their affair, within what embraces them and others. In this there is magnifying of the favour upon them, an incitement to adopt praiseworthy qualities, and a bearing of the burdens of the severe obligations (al-taklifat). Or, when He mentioned the inheritance of Firdaws, He followed it with mention of resurrection (al-ba'th), since the inheritance depends upon it. Or, when He urged them to worship Him, glory be to Him, and to comply with His command, He followed it with what indicates His divinity (uluhiyyah), since worship depends upon that. The first is likely more apt regarding the connection of the verse with what precedes it. It is also permissible that the whole of the mentioned matters be meant collectively. The lam is in the response of the oath, and the waw is for resumption (li'l-isti'naf).

Page 13
Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is a conjunction joining one speech to another speech, even though the two differ in meaning. This is open to consideration. By "man" (al-insan) is meant the species (al-jins). The sulalah (extract) is from sallalta al-shay' min al-shay' (you extracted a thing from a thing) when you drew it out from it; so it is what is drawn out and extracted from a thing. The form fa'alah is a noun for what results from an action: sometimes it is intended from the action, as in khulasah (essence), and sometimes it is not intended from it, as in qulamah (nail-parings) and kunasah (sweepings). The sulalah belongs to the first category, for it is intended by the act of drawing out (al-sall).

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that this pattern indicates paucity (al-qillah). The first "min" is for origin (ibtida'iyyah), connected with "khalaqa." The second "min" may likewise be so, except that it is connected with "sulalah," in the sense of "maslulah" (drawn out), or it is connected with an omitted element occurring as a qualifier of "sulalah." In this case it may be partitive (tab'idiyyah) or explicative (bayaniyyah). It is also permitted that "min tin" be a substitute (badal) or an explicative appositive (atf bayan), with the preposition repeated. The creation of the species of man from what was mentioned is by considering the creation of the first individual and the origin of the species, namely Adam, peace be upon him, from whom all are created in a summary manner within his creation, as previously established. It was also said: the species was created from that by considering that it is a distant origin for the individuals of the species, for they come from the drops (nutfah) resulting from nourishment, which is the extract of clay and its essence. In this there is a description of the species with the attribute of most of its individuals, because the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, was not thus. Or it may be said that the omission of mention of his condition, peace be upon him, is because it is known, and the discussion was confined to the condition of his offspring. This is reported in some narrations from Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said that by "clay" is meant Adam, peace be upon him, on the basis of metonymy of origin (majaz al-kawn). By "sulalah" is meant the drop (nutfah), and by "man" the species, and he described it with what was mentioned by considering most of its individuals. Or it may be said, as was said just now. The obscurity of the indication for metonymy and the non-immediacy of "drop" from "sulalah" is not hidden. It was also said that by "man" is meant Adam, peace be upon him, and this was reported from a group. What we took first is preferable. The pronoun in His statement, exalted is He:

Verse 13: ﴿Then We made him a drop of sperm﴾ refers to the human species in terms of its individuals, who are other than Adam, peace be upon him. If by "the human being" at first Adam, peace be upon him, is meant, then the pronoun in "in it" (in the phrase about what is in the sea) refers to something not mentioned, namely the son of Adam, and this is permissible because the matter is clear and well known; but it is, as you see, far-fetched. Or the reference is to "the human being," and the speech involves the omission of a modifier, meaning: "Then We made his offspring." It has also been said that by "the human being" at first Adam, peace be upon him, is meant, and when the pronoun refers to him, it refers to what descended from him by way of the figure of speech called istikhdam. It is very far-fetched to mean by "the human being" the individuals of the children of Adam while the pronoun refers back to them, with a modifier being supposed at the beginning of the speech, meaning: "And We certainly created the origin of the human being," and so on. Similar to this is meaning by "the human being" the species, or Adam, peace be upon him, while the pronoun refers to ﴿an extract﴾, and the masculine form is by interpretation of "the extracted thing" or "the water," meaning: "Then We made the extract a drop of sperm."

The apparent reading is that ﴿a drop of sperm﴾ is, in all the other views, a second object of "made" (ja'ala), taking it in the sense of "rendered" (tasyir). In the last view this is clear. As for the view where the pronoun refers to "the human being," it is necessary to commit a metaphor of the first kind, namely that by "the human being" is meant what will become a human being. It is also permissible for "made" (ja'ala) to mean "created" (khalaqa), transitive to a single object, and for ﴿a drop of sperm﴾ to be in the accusative by removal of the preposition, a view chosen by some of the verifiers, meaning: "Then We created the human being from a drop of sperm" ﴿situated in a place of rest﴾, that is, a fixed place. It is originally from "qarra, yaqirru, qarran," meaning "was firmly established," and it is used of this as an intensive. What is meant by it is the womb. He described it by the words of the Exalted: ﴿secure﴾, that is, firmly established, although firmness is an attribute of the one who has a place, and here the drop is that one, by way of metaphor, as one says "a traveled road" (ṭarīq sā'ir). It is also permitted to say that the womb itself is firmly established, and the meaning of its firmness is that it does not get dislodged because of the heaviness of its burden, nor does it first eject what is in it; so this is a metaphor (kināya) for making the drop kept safe and guarded, and this is a fine view.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 23, verse 14:**

﴿Then We made the drop into a clinging clot﴾, that is, congealed blood. This happens by pouring the accidents of blood upon it, so that it becomes blood in its attributes. This is of the category of motion in quality (al-harakah fi al-kayf). ﴿Then We made the clot into a lump of flesh﴾, that is, a piece of flesh the size of what can be chewed, with no distinct features or differentiation in it. This transformation, it is said, is in the essence (bi-hasb al-dhat), like the transformation of water into stone and the reverse. Its reality is the removal of the first form from the matter and the pouring of another form upon it. This belongs to the category of generation and corruption (al-kawn wa al-fasad). It does not exclude motion in the quality of readiness (al-harakah fi al-kayfiyyah al-isti'dadiyyah). For the readiness of water, for example, for the first, corrupted form begins to diminish, while its readiness for the second, generated form begins to increase. The first keeps diminishing and the second keeps strengthening, until the matter reaches a point where the first form departs from it and the second form arises in it at once. These readinesses, which belong to the category of quality, thus succeed one another in a single subject. ﴿Then We made the lump into bones﴾, most or all of it, ﴿small bones and large bones﴾, as wisdom requires. This transformation is by shaping (al-taslib) that which is to become bones out of the lump. This too is a transformation in attributes, and so it belongs to the first category.

In the words of the Allamah al-Baydawi there is a certain allusion to the whole of what we have mentioned. It entails the view that the drop and the clot are one in reality, and that the difference between them lies only in accidents, such as redness and whiteness for example. Likewise, the lump and the bones are one in reality, and the difference lies only in things like softness and hardness. And the clot and the lump differ in reality, just as they differ in accidents.

It is apparent that in all these stages successive forms follow one another upon a single matter, in accordance with the succession of readinesses, until it reaches the human form. We hold this view unless evidence to the contrary is established, so reflect.

﴿Then We clothed the bones﴾, the known bones, ﴿with flesh﴾, that is, We made something covering each of them like a garment. That flesh may be from the flesh of the lump, in that not all of it was made into bones but only part of it, and the remainder extends over the bones until it covers them. It may also be another flesh that Allah, exalted is He, created over the bones from blood in the womb.

The word "bones" (al-'izam) is used in the plural rather than the other terms in the stages because they differ in form and hardness, unlike the others. Do you not see the shin bone, the finger bones, and the ends of the ribs? The number of bones in general is, it is said, two hundred and forty-eight, and this is the numerical value (by the abjad reckoning) of the word "rahim" (womb). Some have said that this is the number of the parts of the human body. And Allah knows best.

Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, Aban, al-Mufaddal, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Harun, al-Ju'fi, and Yunus on the authority of Abu 'Amr, and Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them, read "al-'izam" in the singular in both places, relying on the noun of genus (ism al-jins), which applies to the few and the many, with no ambiguity, as in his saying: "Eat in part of your bellies and you will be spared." The restriction of such usage to poetic necessity, as reported from Sibawayh, is open to question. In the singular here there is also a correspondence with what was mentioned before in the stages, as Ibn Jinni has noted.

Al-Sulami and Qatadah also, and al-A'raj, al-A'mash, Mujahid, and Ibn Muhaysin read the first in the singular and the second in the plural.

Abu Raja', Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr, and Mujahid also read the first in the plural and the second in the singular.

﴿Then We brought him into another creation﴾, distinct from the first creation with a distinction that is extremely remote, in that He made him a living being, speaking, hearing, and seeing, and deposited in every organ and every part of him wonders and marvels that cannot be grasped by description or expressed by explanation. From this it has been said:

"You claim that you are a small body, yet within you the greatest universe is folded."

It has been said that the other creation is the spirit, and what is meant by it is the rational soul (al-nafs al-natiqah). The meaning is: We brought into being for him, or in him, another creation. What comes first to mind from "bringing into being the spirit" is its creation. The apparent sequence with "then" (thumma) implies the coming into existence of the body, and this is the view of most Muslim thinkers, and Aristotle held it too. It has been said that bringing it into being is breathing it into the body, which for some is an expression for making it attached to the body, and for most Muslims is making it flow through the body. If by the spirit is meant the animal spirit, then there is no dispute about its coming into existence after the body and its flowing through it. It has also been said that the other creation is the sensory faculties. Al-Dahhak, who was almost laughed at for it, said, as reported from him by 'Abd ibn Humayd: the other creation is the teeth and the hair. He was asked: Is a child not born with hair on his head? He replied: Then where are the pubic hair and the armpit hair?

What we have indicated, that "thumma" here denotes temporal sequence, is what most of its uses require. It may also be that it denotes sequence of rank (al-tartib al-rutbi), since the second creation is greater than the first and its rank is higher. The coordinated items (al-ma'tufat) in the first part are sometimes introduced by "thumma" and sometimes by "fa", and not all of them are introduced by "thumma" or all by "fa", even though this would be permissible in similar contexts. This is to indicate the difference in the improbability (al-istihalat) involved. So what is joined by "thumma" is judged unlikely to come about from what precedes it, and so the improbability, whether intellectual or by rank, is placed in the position of temporal distance and sensory remoteness. For the coming into existence of a drop from earthen constituents is extremely strange. Likewise the white, flowing drop being made into congealed red blood is strange, unlike making blood into flesh, which resembles it in colour and appearance. Likewise the shaping of the lump until it becomes bone, and likewise the stretching of its flesh over it to cover it. This is what has been said, though it is not free of debate.

Imam Abu Hanifah took as evidence the words of the Exalted, ﴿Then We brought him into another creation﴾, and so on, for the ruling that if someone usurps an egg and it hatches in his possession, he is liable for the value of the egg and not for the chick, since it is another creation. Al-Kashshaf says: there is a concern about this argument on the basis of the principles of those who disagree with him, since its being distinct from the first does not remove it from the ownership of the original owner according to them. The author of al-Taqrib said: the chick is liable because it is a part of the usurped thing, not because it is identical with it or named by its name. There is debate on this, and there is much disagreement and lengthy discussion on the question, which may be sought in the detailed books of jurisprudence.

The Imam said: They said that the verse is evidence against the view of al-Nizam that the human being is the spirit and not the body. For the Exalted has made clear in it that the human being is composed of these things. It is also evidence against the view of the philosophers that the human being is not divisible and is not a body. They seem to have meant that the human being is the rational soul and the abstract spirit of command, for it is that which, in their view, is not a body, does not accept division in any way, and is neither inside the body nor outside it.

﴿So blessed is Allah﴾, exalted and sanctified is His majesty, glorified is He, in His all-encompassing knowledge and His dazzling power. ("Tabaraka") is a past-tense verb that does not conjugate, and it is most commonly attributed to a non-feminine subject. The shift to the sublime Name serves to cultivate awe and bring in dread, and to indicate that what has been mentioned of these wondrous acts belongs to the rulings of divinity. It also serves to announce that every one who hears what has been detailed of the traces of His power, mighty and majestic, or considers it, should hasten to speak of it in reverence and magnification of His affairs, exalted is He. ﴿The best of creators﴾ is an attribute of the sublime Name. The annexation of the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) is genuine, and so it gives definiteness when annexed to a definite noun, according to the more correct view.

Abu al-Baqa' said: it cannot be an attribute, because it is indefinite even when annexed, since the noun annexed to it is a substitute for "min" (from). This is true of the whole category of "af'al min-ka". He took it as a substitute (badal), though this is rare in derivatives. Or it is the predicate of an implied subject, meaning "He is the best of creators." But the basic principle is that nothing is assumed without need. The comparative (af'al) is specified by an implied noun, the ism of the comparative's object, indicated by "the creators": that is, "the best of creators in creation." Thus the goodness is attributed to the creation. It has been said that a parallel to this is his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "Indeed Allah is beautiful and loves beauty," meaning: His action is beautiful. The annexed noun was dropped and the annexed-to noun took its place, and so it became nominative and the pronoun became hidden. Creation here means determination (taqdir), a term that is applied to others than Allah, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you shape from clay the likeness of a bird﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110], and in the verse of Zuhayr:

"You indeed smooth what has been shaped, and some of the people shape but do not smooth."

Interpreting it as making (al-sun') is similar in meaning, as Ibn 'Atiyyah did. Interpreting it as bringing into existence from nothing (al-ijad) is not valid according to us, since no creator in that sense other than Him, exalted is He, exists, except on hypothesis and assumption. The Mu'tazilah interpret it that way, because they hold that the servant creates his actions and brings them into being independently. Thus for them there are multiple creators who bring into being, and the books of theology have taken up the refutation of them.

The meaning of the goodness of His creation, exalted is He, is His perfection and firm ordering of it. It may also be intended that goodness is the opposite of ugliness, and everything from Him, mighty is His majesty, is good, and has no attribute of ugliness at all, inasmuch as it comes from Him.
