So there is no evidence in it for the Mu'tazilah that He does not create disbelief and sins, as is not hidden.

It is reported that 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh used to write for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dictated to him the words of the Exalted, ﴿And We created man…﴾ until, when he reached ﴿Then We brought him into another creation﴾, 'Abd Allah spoke the words ﴿So blessed is Allah﴾ and so on before he had finished writing. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "It was revealed like this." 'Abd Allah said: "If Muhammad is a prophet to whom revelation comes, then I am a prophet to whom revelation comes." He apostatized and went to Mecca as a disbeliever, then became Muslim again before the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) death, and his Islam was good. It is said that he died a disbeliever.

Some have criticized the soundness of this report on the grounds that the surah is Meccan, while the apostasy, as the report implies, took place in Medina. It is answered that reconciliation is possible: the verse was revealed in Mecca, and he (ﷺ) had him write it down in Medina, and so what happened happened. Or one may hold that the verse is Medinan because of this report. The statement that the surah is Meccan is based on the majority. On this basis, al-Jalal al-Suyuti's restriction of the exception to the words ﴿until when We seize their affluent ones﴾ up to His saying ﴿in despair﴾ would be deficient, so reflect. This agreement is also reported from Mu'adh ibn Jabal.

Ibn Rahawayh, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and Ibn Mardawayh reported, on the authority of Zayd ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dictated to me this verse, ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ up to His saying ﴿another creation﴾. Then Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, said: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed, and Mu'adh said to him: "At what did you laugh, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "By it I have concluded."

It is also reported from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. al-Tabarani, and Abu Nu'aym in Fada'il al-Sahabah, and Ibn Mardawayh, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: When ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ was revealed, up to the end of the verse, 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾, and so it was revealed as he had said. Ibn 'Asakir and a group reported on the authority of Anas that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to take pride in this and mention that it was one of his four agreements with his Lord, mighty and majestic.

Moreover, this is part of the excellent composition of the noble Qur'an, in that the emergence of many of its verses points to its inimitability. I have praised some poetry in this regard, and it has been said:

"Poems, if they are recited before a gathering, the listeners know their rhymes from their openings."

It may be objected: human beings have indeed spoken, from the start, something similar to the composition of the noble Qur'an, and this is damaging to its inimitability. The answer is that what is beyond human power, according to the correct view, is what is the length of the shortest surah of it. Moreover, the inimitability of this noble verse depends on what precedes it, as the particle "fa" indicates, for it is a concluding interjection (i'tiradun tadhyili) confirming the content of what precedes it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 15:

﴿Then indeed you, after that﴾ i.e., after what has been mentioned of the wondrous matters, as indicated by the meaning of distance contained in the demonstrative (ism al-isharah), which implies the exalted rank of the one pointed to and its far station in excellence and perfection.
Page 17
And its being distinguished by this, placed in the position of sensible matters, ﴿shall surely die﴾, i.e., shall certainly come to death without doubt, as is indicated by the nominal form of the sentence, by the particle inna, the emphatic lam, and the form of the adjective (na't), which denotes permanence. Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Ibn Abi 'Abla and Ibn Muhaysin read "limaʾitun" (lima'itun), which is an active participle (ism fa'il) intended to denote occurrence (huduth). Al-Farra' and Ibn Malik said: "Mayyit" is only used in reference to the future.

Then, indeed, you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection (عِنْدَ النَّفْخَةِ الثّانِيَةِ, at the second blowing of the Trumpet) from your graves (﴿تُبْعَثُونَ﴾) for reckoning and for recompense with reward and punishment. The Exalted did not stress the matter of resurrection as He stressed the matter of death, despite the great number of those who doubt it and deny it, being content with presenting what makes intensive emphasis unnecessary, and what firmly establishes the pillars of the claim in the most complete manner: His creation of man from an extract of clay, then His transferring him from stage to stage until He brought him into being as another creation, one that encompasses wonders and gathers marvels. Indeed, in that is the most evident proof of His wisdom and of His great power, the Mighty and Majestic, over his resurrection and return, and that He, the Majestic and Exalted, does not neglect his affair or leave him after his death as something utterly forgotten, settled in the womb of non-existence as though he had never been a thing. And since the preceding sentence contained the emphasis that He, may His affair be exalted, made man's creation most perfectly wise and most accomplished, He, glory be to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, laid great emphasis on the sentence indicating his death, although it is not denied, because that is a cause for the intellect to find it exceedingly remote, to the point that one who has not witnessed it, and has only heard that God, His majesty be great, made man's creation most wise and most accomplished to the utmost degree, might come close to denying its occurrence. This is a subtle point for increasing the emphasis in the sentence indicating death, and for not increasing it in the sentence indicating resurrection. I have not seen that I preceded anyone to it. It has also been said regarding this: when He, may His affair be exalted, mentioned in the preceding verses the obligations that He mentioned, He drew attention to the fact that He, glory be to Him, originated the creation of man and turned him through the stages until He brought him to a stage that is the utmost of his perfection, and by which his being obligated with such obligations is valid, namely that he be living, rational, hearing and seeing. That required mention of a stage in which the recompense for what He obligated him with would take place, namely that he be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection. So He, glory be to Him, drew attention to it by His saying: ﴿Then indeed you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection﴾. Thus the most important purpose, after explaining his creation and his fitness for obligation, is explaining his resurrection. But it came in the midst of the discourse on death, because it is a barrier between his stage in which he became fit for deeds that call for recompense and between his resurrection; so it is necessary to cut it off in order to reach that. It is as though it were said: O wondrous creature, indeed your quiddity and reality will perish and cease to exist, then indeed it, in its very same parts, scattered bones, decayed skins, and dissolved remains in the regions of East and West, will be raised and dispersed for the Day of Recompense, to reward whoever did well in what We obligated him with, and to punish whoever did evil in it. So the second clause, which is the sentence indicating resurrection, did not need emphasis as the first did, namely the sentence indicating death, because it is like a preface to it, and its emphasis refers back to it. From this one knows the secret of shifting the discourse from the third person to the second person. End. And in it is what is in it of remoteness.

And it has been said: the greater emphasis was placed on the first clause only because the addressees persisted in heedlessness, so they were treated as those who deny it, while the second was left unemphasized because its proofs are clear and its demonstrations manifest. Al-Tibi said: this is a fine statement, if the superior composition supported it. And it may be said: the intense natural aversion to death, from which hardly anyone is free, took the place of intense denial, so the sentence indicating it was emphasized. As for resurrection, insofar as it is life after death, souls do not dislike it, and insofar as it is a presumed occasion of hardships, they dislike it. So since its state is neither like the state of death nor like the state of life, but in between, the sentence indicating it was emphasized with a single emphasis. This is an aspect of emphasis that none of the scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamāʾ al-maʿānī) has mentioned, and it does no harm that it is so, provided it is sound in itself. The repetition of the particle of delay (thumma) indicates the difference in ranks. The verse has included mention of nine stages, and death falls in it as the eighth stage. This coincides with the fact that one born at eight months of gestation rarely survives. The Exalted did not mention the stage of life in the grave, because it belongs to the same category as the return.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 17:

﴿And We have certainly created above you﴾
Page 18
It is an explanation of the creation of what their survival requires, following the explanation of their own creation. It has also been said that it is an argument for the Resurrection, meaning: We created in the direction of height, without considering its being "above" them, because that relation only arises after their creation. ﴿seven heavens﴾ are the seven heavens. ("Tara'iq") is the plural of "tariqah" in the sense of "matruqah" (that which is trodden), from "tarq al-na'l" (the trodding of a sandal), and "al-khawafi" (the layers), since He placed its layers one above another. This was said by al-Khalil, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in layers﴾ [al-Mulk: 3; Nuh: 15]. Each of the seven has a relation and connection to being trodden, so there is no preference of one over the others. It has also been said that it is the plural of "tariqah" in its well-known meaning, and the heavens were named thus because they are the paths of the angels, peace be upon them, in their descent and ascent for the benefit of the servants, or because they are the paths of the stars in their courses.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is permissible that "tara'iq" means "extended things" (mabsutat), from "taraqat al-hadid" (he beat the iron), for example, when it spreads it out, and this does not contradict the view of their being created ex nihilo (bikriyyah). It has also been said that they were named "tara'iq" because each heaven is a path and a form different from the form of the other. But you know that the apparent meaning is that the form is one. Yes, God, exalted is He, has placed in each heaven what He did not place in the other, so it is permissible that they are called "tara'iq" for that reason. ﴿And We were not of the creation﴾, meaning of all the created beings, of which the seven heavens are a part, ﴿heedless﴾, neglecting their affairs; rather, We bestow upon everything what wisdom requires. It is also permissible that by "creation" is meant people, and the meaning is that Our creating the heavens was for their benefits, and We are not heedless of their interests. The definite article (al) in both cases is for generality (istighraq). It is also permitted that it be for specificity (ahd), on the understanding that "creation" refers to the mentioned created thing, namely the seven heavens, meaning: "And We were not heedless of them," rather We preserve them from ceasing and disorder and manage their affairs. The explicit noun in the place of the pronoun is for the sake of attention to their matter. The singular "khalq" in all the other interpretations is because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar), or because the multiple is, in His sight, exalted, in the ruling of a single thing.

[p. 19]

﴿And We sent down from the sky﴾ water, which is rain according to many of the exegetes (mufassirun). By "the sky" is meant the direction of height, or the clouds, or its well-known meaning. Nothing can overcome Allah, the Exalted. On this reading, the apparent form would have been "from it" in place of "from the sky," so that the pronoun would return to the "paths." However, he departed from that to the pronoun form, because sending down from it does not require that it be "paths." Rather, it requires only that it be the direction of height. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the direct object serves to give attention to what is placed first and to create anticipation for what is delayed. The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿in measure﴾ describe "water." That is, We sent down water attended by the quantity that suffices them for their needs and interests, or with a fitting measure for securing their benefits and repelling their harms. On this reading, it is permissible for it to occupy the position of a state (ḥāl) relative to the pronoun. It has been said that it is a description of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "a sending down attended by that." It has been said that the prepositional phrase has other than this function. ﴿Then We lodged it in the earthⴾ, meaning We made it firm and settled within it. From this is the water of springs and the like. Most of the philosophers claim that this water comes from the transformation of vapour trapped in the earth into water when it inclines toward one of its directions and cools, and that rainwater has no part in it. Its being "from the sky" is considered on the basis that the rays of the stars in it have a role in it in terms of efficient causation.

Ibn Sina said in his Najat: These vapours trapped in the earth, when they burst forth as springs, supply the seas by pouring rivers into them. Then vapours rise from the seas, marshes, and especially the hollows of mountains, and then they are condensed again back into them, standing in place of what dissolves from them, cyclically and perpetually. What is in the verse supports what Abu al-Barakat al-Baghdadi among them held. For he said in al-Mu'tabar: The cause of springs, channels, and what runs in their course is what flows from snows and rainwater, because we find that they increase with its increase and decrease with its decrease. And the transformation of the airs and vapours confined in the earth has no part in this, for the inside of the earth is colder in summer than in winter. So if that were the cause of their transformation, springs, channels, and well water would have to be greater in summer and less in winter, whereas the matter is contrary to that, as experience demonstrates. End of quotation. Qadi Husayn al-Mubidi chose that each of the two matters has a part, and he objected to the proof of Abu al-Barakat by saying that it only shows that the transformation is not a complete cause, but as for it having no part at all, it does not show that.

The truth is what the Book of Allah, the Exalted, bears witness to, for He, glory be to Him, is most knowing of His creation. Whatever the philosophers mention in such matters, they have no proof for it that yields certainty, as the commentator on Hikmat al-'Ayn pointed out. It has also been said that by this water is meant the water of five rivers.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah, the Exalted, sent down from Paradise to the earth five rivers: Sayhun, which is the river of India; Jayhun, which is the river of Balkh; the Euphrates (Dijlah and al-Furat), which are the two rivers of Iraq; and the Nile, which is the river of Egypt. Allah sent them down from one spring of the springs of Paradise, from the lowest level of its levels, upon the two wings of Jibril, peace be upon him. He deposited them in the mountains and made them run in the earth."

He made them benefits for people in the varieties of their livelihoods, and that is the word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We sent down from the sky﴾ water ﴿in measure, then We lodged it in the earth﴾. When the coming forth of Ya'juj and Ma'juj occurs, Allah, the Exalted, sends Jibril, peace be upon him, and he lifts from the earth the Qur'an, all knowledge, the Black Stone from the corner of the House, the Station of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, the Ark of Musa, peace be upon him, with what is in it, and these five rivers. He raises all of that to the sky. This is the word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed We are able to take it away﴾. When these things are lifted from the earth, its inhabitants lose the good of this world and the Hereafter. It is not hidden from one who investigates that this report was recorded by Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib with a weak chain. Yes, the hadith of four rivers from Paradise: Sayhan and Jayhan, which are other than Sayhun and Jayhun, because those two are rivers in the frontier cities near al-Massisa and Tarsus, while Sayhun and Jayhun are the rivers of India and Balkh, as you have heard according to what Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said. The Euphrates and the Nile are sound, but the discussion concerns the interpretation of the verse with that. It is narrated from Mujahid that he understood "water" to encompass both rainwater and sea water, and said: There is no water on earth except that it is from the sky. You know that what better accords with the reports and with what is mentioned afterward in the noble verse is that what is meant is other than sea water.

﴿And indeed We are able to take it away﴾, meaning able to remove it by bringing it out of its watery state, or by sinking it so that its extraction becomes impossible, or by something similar. ﴿Indeed We are able﴾, just as We were able to send it down. So the sentence is in the position of a state. In the indefinite form of ﴿taking away﴾ there is an indication of the multiplicity of its ways, because the indefinite noun generalizes even though it is in an affirmative context, and through this the emphasis in the affirmation is understood. This verse is more emphatic than the word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, who then would bring you flowing water?﴾ [al-Mulk: 30].

The author of al-Taqrib mentioned eighteen aspects of eloquence. The first is that this is on the basis of supposition and estimation, and this definite form is in the sense that it is more indicative of the realization of what they are threatened with, even if it has not occurred. The second is the emphasis with inna. The third is the lam in the predicate. The fourth is that this (in the verse) concerns water sent down from the sky in general, while that (in the other verse) concerns water attributed to them. The fifth is that what is sunken may still remain, unlike what is taken away. The sixth is the emphasis found in the indefinite form of ﴿taking away﴾. The seventh is attributing it here to a gone-away object, unlike ﴿sunken﴾ there. The eighth is the grandeur of the speaker's own self in the sense of awe. The ninth is what is in "able" of indicating power over it, and an act that proceeds from the one who has power is more eloquent. The tenth is what is in its plural form. The eleventh is what is in the word "with it" (bihi) indicating that whatever holds it back has no sender. [p. 20] The twelfth is its freedom from being followed by hopes, whereas there the mention of "bring" is the object of hope. The thirteenth is the placement of what contains the threat, namely the taking away, on what is like its object, or its object according to the two schools, the Basran and the Kufan. The fourteenth is the difference between the nominal and verbal sentences in terms of stability and otherwise.

The fifteenth is what is in the word "becomes" (aṣbaḥa) of indicating transition and change. The sixteenth is that taking away is explicitly stated here. There is also something understood from the context of the interrogation. The seventeenth is that there is a negation of a particular water, namely flowing water, unlike here. The eighteenth is considering all these matters together, each of which suffices to be emphatic. Then he said: This is what comes to mind now, and Allah, the Exalted, knows best. End of quotation. In the self there is some doubt about counting the last as an aspect.

It may be added to that, saying: The nineteenth is that Allah, the Exalted, Himself reports it without an order to another here, unlike there, where He commanded His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to say it. The twentieth is that the addressee is not specified here, while the disbelievers are specified for the address there. The twenty-first is the comparison derived from making the sentence a state, as we pointed out, for it indicates the realization of power, and there is no comparison there. The twenty-second is the attribution of power to Allah, the Exalted, twice. Some distinguished scholars of the contemporary age, from the noble intelligence of their noble minds, have added, the best of the contemporary age, namely the third of al-Rafi'i and al-Nawawi, brother of Mulla Muhammad Afandi al-Zahawi, and he said: The twenty-third is the inclusion within the threat here of a threat of their being removed from the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, because "took it away" (dhahaba bihi) implies the companionship of the agent with the object, and the going away of Allah, the Exalted, from them together with the water means the going away of His mercy, glory be to Him, from them and their being cursed and expelled from it. This is not the case there. The twenty-fourth is that the time of the taking away is not specified here, unlike in "if it becomes" (in aṣbaḥa), where it is understood that the transformation happens in the morning according to one of the two usages of aṣbaḥa as a defective verb. The twenty-fifth is that the direction of the taking away is not specified as being downward. The twenty-sixth is that the threat here is with something they have never been tested with, unlike what is there. The twenty-seventh is that if the promised taking away here occurs, they are certainly destroyed. The twenty-eighth is that nothing remains here for them to cling to, even weakly, in hoping that the promised event will not happen, whereas there, where the morning is attributed to the water as sunken, and it is known that water does not become sunken by itself, as the verification of the sage's position also holds, there is room for someone to suppose the conditional, even with its truth, to have an impossible antecedent, so they feel secure from its occurrence. The twenty-ninth is that the promised taking away here may in a first glance be understood as occurring immediately, unlike there, where the future is determined for its occurrence because of the particle "if" (in). It is clear that a threat of what may happen immediately is more terrifying, and a threat of what is certain to occur in the future is less so. The thirtieth is that what is here admits only of threat, unlike what is there, which admits, even if it is known afterward, that its meaning is a favour: that "if your water becomes sunken, then who will bring you flowing water, other than Allah, the Exalted?" It is supported by what follows it, the word of Allah: "Our Lord and the Lord of the worlds." End of quotation. So reflect, and do not be heedless, and Allah, the Exalted, is the guide to the secrets of His Book.

Emphasis has been chosen here, according to what some verifiers have said, because the context requires it, since it is for enumerating the signs of the horizons and of the souls in a manner that includes indication of power and mercy together with the complete greatness of the one characterized by both. For this reason it begins with the pronoun of majesty with emphasis, unlike where it is completed. For that is a completion to urge worship and to encourage it, and this is sufficient for that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 19:

﴿Then We produced for you thereby﴾, that is, by that water. This is the apparent meaning according to the early scholars (al-Salaf), while the later scholars (al-Khalaf) said: the intended meaning is "We produced [them] near it" ﴿gardens of palm trees and grapevines﴾. He mentioned these two first because of their abundance and because of the great benefit derived from them, especially in the Hijaz, al-Ta'if and Madinah. ﴿For you therein﴾, that is, in the gardens, ﴿are abundant fruits﴾

﻿﻿﻿ ﻿ ﻿ ﻿ ﻿ ﻿ ﻿ ﻿ ﻿ ﻿

with which you enjoy yourselves and take pleasure, beyond the usual sustenance of basic food. What is meant by them is other than the fruits of the palm trees and the grapevines.

﴿And from them﴾, that is, from the gardens, and what is meant is from their crops and fruits. The "min" (from) is for beginning (ibtida'iyyah), and it has been said that it is partitive (tab'idiyyah). Its content is the object of ﴿you eat﴾, and what is meant by eating is its literal meaning.

It is also permissible that it be a metaphor or a metonymy for livelihood in general, that is: "And from them you are provided for and obtain your livelihood," from the saying "So-and-so eats from his trade." It is also permissible that the two pronouns refer to the palm trees and the grapevines, that is: for you in their fruits are kinds of fruits: fresh dates, grapes, dates (tamr), raisins (zabib), and date syrup (dibs) from each of them, and other things, and food that you eat. Thus their fruit combines enjoyment and sustenance, unlike the fruit of other than these two. On this view, "fruit" (fakihah) is used in an absolute sense for their fruit.

Al-Raghib mentioned two opinions regarding fakihah: the first is that it is all fruits, and the second is that it is what excludes grapes and pomegranates. The author of al-Qamus chose the first and said: the statement of one who excludes dates and pomegranates from it, citing the words of the Exalted, ﴿In them is fruit, and palm trees, and pomegranates﴾ [al-Rahman: 68], is false and rejected; I have explained this in detail in al-Lami' al-Mu'allim al-'Ujab. End of quote. You know that the jurists differ regarding fakihah. Imam Abu Hanifa held that it is apples, melons, apricots, quince and the like, not grapes, pomegranates or fresh dates. His two companions said: the excepted items are also fruit, and this is the fatwa. There is no disagreement, as in al-Qahistani, quoting al-Karmani, that dried fruit such as raisins, dates and pomegranate seeds is not fruit.

In al-Durr al-Mukhtar, it is stated that the disagreement between the Imam and his two companions is a disagreement of time and place, so the criterion for one who swears not to eat fruit is custom, and he breaks his oath by eating what is regarded as fruit by custom. This was mentioned by al-Shamani and endorsed by al-Ghuzzi. It is not hidden that one thing may be called fakihah in the custom of one people and not called so in the custom of others. In al-Nahr, from al-Muhit, it is reported that walnuts and almonds are fruit; this is in their custom, but in our custom they are not eaten for enjoyment. End of quote. Furthermore, I have not seen any of the lexicographers or jurists count dibs (date syrup) as fruit, so consider this carefully and do not be negligent.

[Page 22 marker omitted]

﴿And a tree﴾ in the accusative is in coordination (ʿatf) with ﴿gardens﴿ (in the previous verse). It was also read in the nominative, as a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate (khabar) is omitted. The preferable reading is to assume the predicate placed before it: "We brought forth for you a tree ﴿that springs forth from Mount Sinai﴾." Mount Sinai (Ṭūr Sīnāʾ) is the mountain of Mūsā (peace be upon him), where his Lord (glorified is He) spoke to him. It lies between Egypt and Aylah, which today is called al-ʿAqabah. It is said that it is in Palestine, in the land of al-Shām. It is also called Ṭūr Sīnīn. The majority of the Arabs pronounce the sīn of Sīnāʾ with a fatḥah and a long vowel. This is how ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, and Yaʿqūb recited it, as did most of the seven readers. It is the name of the locality, and Ṭūr is the name of the specific mountain, or of any mountain, and it is annexed to Sīnāʾ, as they all agreed. On the first view, its indefiniteness is intended, as with all proper names when they are annexed. On the second view, Ṭūr Sīnāʾ is like the minaret of the mosque.

It is permitted that it be like Imruʾ al-Qays, in the sense that the whole annexed construction (muḍāf and muḍāf ilayhi) is made a proper name for that place. It is said that Sīnāʾ is the name of a particular stone, and the mountain was annexed to it because it was found there. This was narrated from Mujāhid. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ, it says: "Ṭūr Sīnāʾ is a mountain in al-Shām. Ṭūr is annexed to Sīnāʾ, and Sīnāʾ is a tree." It is also said that it is the name of the mountain, and the annexation is an annexation of the general to the specific, as in Jabal Uḥud.

This view was reported in al-Baḥr from the majority. However, the view that it is the name of a locality has been deemed sound. It is then diptote (mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf) because of the long alif (alif mamdūdah), so its pattern is faʿlāʾ, like ṣaḥrāʾ. It is also said that it is diptote because of definiteness (ʿalamiyyah) and foreignness (ʿujmah). It is also said that it is because of definiteness and feminine gender, by interpreting it as a locality. Its pattern is then faʿāl, not fiʿlāl, since this pattern does not occur in Arabic except rarely, in a doubled root, as in khazʿāl, meaning a camel's limp, which al-Farrāʾ reported. Abū al-Baqāʾ did not accept it. Most scholars hold that it is not Arabic, but either Nabataean or Abyssinian, and the root meaning is "the good" or "the blessed." Some have permitted that it be Arabic, from al-sanāʾ with a long vowel, meaning "elevation," or from al-sinā with a short vowel, meaning "light."

Abū Ḥayyān objected to this, saying that the two roots are different, because the ʿayn of al-sanāʾ or al-sinā is nūn, while the ʿayn of Sīnāʾ is yāʾ. This was answered by saying that the one who holds this view takes it to be a pattern of fayʿāl, makes its ʿayn the nūn, its yāʾ an added letter, and its hamzah a replacement for a wāw. Al-Ḥaramayn, Abū ʿAmr, and al-Ḥasan read Sīnāʾ with a kasrah on the sīn and a long vowel. This is a dialect of the Banū Kinānah. It is also diptote because of the long alif, according to the Kufans, since they hold that the hamzah of faʿlāʾ can be a feminine marker. According to the Basrans, it is diptote because of definiteness and foreignness, or definiteness and feminine gender, since the alif of faʿlāʾ, in their view, is not a feminine marker but is added to fiʿlāl, as in ʿilbāʾ and ḥizbāʾ. It is paired with qirṭās, sardāḥ, and its hamzah replaces a wāw or a yāʾ, since the addition can be with either.

Abū al-Baqāʾ said: the hamzah of Sīnāʾ with a kasrah is original, like ḥimlāq, and it is not a feminine marker, since there is no word like ḥamrāʾ in the language. The yāʾ is original, since there is no word sanāʾ in the language. Some have allowed that it is fayʿāl, like dīmās. Al-Aʿmash read sīnā with a fatḥah and a short vowel. It was also read as sanāʾ with a kasrah and a short vowel, so its alif is a feminine marker, if it is not foreign.

The intended tree is the olive tree. It is singled out from among all trees because it has well-known benefits on its own. It has been said that it is the first tree that grew after the Flood and lives a long time. In al-Tadhkirah it is said that it lasts a thousand years. Its soundness is not far-fetched, but the reason given for it, namely that it is connected to the high star, is far from sound. In the tafsir of al-Khāzin, it is said that it lasts three thousand years. Specifying it with the description of coming out of the Ṭūr, although it also comes out of other places, is because it grows most where its breadth exceeds its slope, where the cold is intense, and where the soil is mountainous, white or red. This is either to honour it, or because that is its original place of growth. Perhaps making it an honour is the better view, and then this is praise of it on account of its place.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿growing with oil﴾ is praise of it on account of what it is in itself. The bāʾ denotes accompaniment and association, as in your saying: "He came with the clothes of travel." It is connected to an omitted verb that serves as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the tree. The meaning is: it grows while associated with oil. Oil is the extract of everything that has grease. Here it refers to olive oil. Its association with oil is by way of the association of its fruit, since the fruit is in fact what carries the oil.

It is permitted that the bāʾ be connected to the verb as its transitive complement, as in your saying: "I took Zayd away." It is as if it were said: "It causes oil to grow," meaning it contains and produces it. There is no hiding that this is correct, but the causing of oil to grow is not familiar in usage.

Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Sallām, Sahl, Ruways, and al-Jaḥdarī read tunbitu with a ḍammah on the initial tāʾ and a kasrah on the bāʾ, as a form of the causative (afʿāl) pattern. This is explained as deriving from anbata in the sense of nabata, so the hamzah in it is not causative. It also occurs like this in the verse of Zuhayr:

I saw those in need around their tents, / their people for them, until the herb had grown.

al-Aṣmaʿī denied this and said the reading in the verse is nabt without a hamzah. It is possible that the hamzah is causative, with an implied object, meaning: the herb produced its fruit or what they eat. Some explained the verse on this basis, saying: the meaning is "it causes its olives to grow with oil," and the prepositional phrase here is a circumstantial clause from the object or from the hidden pronoun in the verb. It is also said that the bāʾ is extra, as in the verse: ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:195). Attributing growing to the tree, and even to the oil, is figurative. Al-Khafājī said: it is also possible that anbata is transitive to a second object by the bāʾ.

Al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī, and Ibn Hurmuz read tunbatu with a ḍammah on its first letter and a fatḥah on the letter before the last, in the passive voice. The prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause. Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh read tunbitu as a verb, with al-duhna in the accusative. Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik and al-Ashhab read bi-l-dihān, the plural of duhn, like simāk for rumḥ, the plural of rumḥ (spear). As for what they narrated from the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, "tukhriju al-duhn," and the reading of Ubayy, "tuthmiru bi-l-duhn," these are treated as commentary, according to what is in al-Baḥr, since they contradict the consonantal text of the Mushaf which is agreed upon. Also, the transmitted reports from them are like the reading of the majority.

﴿And a relish for those who eat﴾ is coordinated (maʿṭūf) with oil. The difference between them, which coordination requires, is in terms of concept. Otherwise, their essence is one, according to many commentators. It is common for the difference of two concepts to be treated as the difference of two essences, as in the verse:

To the mighty king, and the son of the noble, / and the lion of the battalion in the crowd.

The meaning is: it grows with the thing that combines being an oil with which one anoints and from which one makes lamp-fuel, and being a condiment in which bread is dipped, that is, dipped for the sake of eating with it. In al-Maghrib it says: "It is said: he dyed the cloth with good dye, and a dyer (ṣabbāgh). From this comes ṣabgh and ṣabbāgh in condiments, because bread is dipped into it and coloured by it, like vinegar and olive oil." The apparent meaning is that it is specific to any liquid condiment, and al-Miṣbāḥ states this explicitly. Some have stated that using ṣabgh for this is figurative, and perhaps what al-Maghrib says contains a hint of this.

It is narrated from Muqātil that he said: "al-duhn is olive oil and al-ṣabgh is the olive." On this view the coordination is between two things that differ in essence, which is the most common kind of coordination. One must say about this: ṣabgh is a condiment in general, which is what is eaten with bread usually, whether liquid or solid. In our countries, olives are mostly eaten by the poor with bread, while the rich eat them with things like rice, and rarely with bread. I have been fond of them since I was young, and I often eat them both with other food and alone. As for olive oil, I have not seen anyone in Baghdad who dips bread in it, and whoever among them eats food with it is rare, and most of them are surprised at whoever eats it. The reason for this is its scarcity among them and their lack of understanding of it, so their souls shrink from it. I myself used to shrink from it long ago, but gradually I grew accustomed to it, praise be to Allah, Exalted. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to eat it.

It is authentically reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) had a sheep's tongue cooked for him in oil, and he ate from it.

Abū Nuʿaym in al-Ṭibb reported from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Eat olive oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it is a cure for seventy diseases, including leprosy.'"

al-Tirmidhī in al-Aṭʿimah reported from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Eat olive oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it comes from a blessed tree."

However, some said: this command applies to whoever is able to use it and whose temperament suits it. This is so, and therefore there is no objection to whoever does not use it because it does not suit his temperament. Rather, the apparent ruling is that it is forbidden to use it if it harms him, just as they ruled that a person with bile excess is forbidden to use honey. There is no difference in this between eating it and anointing oneself with it, since anointing with it may also harm, as eating does. Ibn al-Qayyim said: "Oil in hot countries like the Ḥijāz is one of the means of preserving health and improving the body, and it is almost essential for its people. As for cold countries, it is harmful, and excessive use of olive oil on the head there is dangerous for the eyesight." End of quotation.

ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh read wa-ṣibāghan, which has the same meaning as ṣabgh, as has already been indicated, and from it comes dabgh and dabbāgh. Its accusative is by coordination with the position of bi-l-duhn. In the tafsīr of Ibn ʿAṭiyyah: ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Qays read wa-matāʿan li-l-ākilīn, and this is taken as commentary.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 21:

﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is surely a lesson for you﴾ is an explanation of the blessings that reach them from the direction of the animals, following the explanation of the blessings that flow from the direction of water and plants. He has explained that these, although they are themselves a blessing from which they benefit in various ways, are a lesson (ʿibrah, a lesson drawn from observation) that they must take heed of, reflect upon, and infer from their conditions the immensity of the power of Allah, ʿazza wa-jall, and the all-encompassing extent of His mercy, and that they should thank Him and not deny Him. He singled this out for the animals because the place of the lesson in them is more evident.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We give you to drink of what is in their bellies﴾ is a detailing of what in them are the locations of lessons. As for "what is in their bellies," it is an expression that refers either to the milks, in which case min (مِن) is partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah) and "the bellies" (al-buṭūn) means the interiors (al-ajwāf), since the milk is in the udders; or it refers to the fodder from which the milk is formed, in which case min is for beginning (ibtidāʾiyyah) and "the bellies" is in its literal sense. In either case, the pronoun in ﴿bellies﴾ (buṭūnihā) refers to the livestock, by considering the attribution of what belongs to a part to the whole, not to the females among them, as a form of istikhdam, because the generality of what follows rejects that. It has also been read with a fatḥah on the nūn and with the tāʾ, meaning: the livestock gives you to drink (tusqīkum al-anʿām).

﴿And for you in them are many benefits﴾ other than what has been mentioned, such as their wool, their hair, and their fleece, ﴿and from them you eat﴾. The apparent meaning is that eating is in its true literal sense, and min is partitive, because some parts of the livestock are not eaten. The fronting of the object for the sake of the verse-ending (al-fāṣilah), or for restriction relative to donkeys and the like (al-ḥaṣr al-idafī), or for restriction in view of what is implied in (taʾkulūn) of the continuous habitual custom, is possible. This was an explanation of their benefit from the very substances of the animals, while what preceded it was an explanation of their benefit from its uses and what is obtained from them. It is permissible in my view, though I have not seen anyone state it explicitly, that eating be a metaphor or a kināyah for sustenance in general, as you have heard before; that is: and from them you are provided for, and you obtain your livelihoods.

in the land and the sea, with yourselves and your loads. The pronoun in (upon them) refers to the cattle (al-an'am), in terms of attributing to the whole what belongs to some of them, also. It is also permissible that it refers to them (al-an'am) on the basis that what is meant by them is camels, by way of metonymic usage (istikhdam), because they are the ones that are ridden upon among them, and the counterpart to the ship, for they are "ships of the land." Dhu al-Rummah said, regarding his she-camel Saydahah:

"A ship of the land, its halter under my cheek"

This is acceptable. As for taking the cattle, from the outset, to mean camels, this does not suit the context of divine favour (imtinan) nor the flow of the discourse. In combining the two (cattle and ships) in the act of being carried upon, there is an emphasis on their capacity to bear loads. It has been said: this is what prompted the delay of this benefit, even though it is among the benefits obtained from them, after mention of the benefit of eating, which is directly connected to their substance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 23:

﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 23, 63] This begins an explanation of people's neglect and their failure to reflect and take heed regarding the blessings that He, glorified is He, enumerated, and the loss of them that befell them. In this there is a warning to Quraysh.

The placing of the story of Noah, peace be upon him, before all the other stories is something whose wisdom is not hidden. Its placement right after His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾ has an excellence of position that cannot be described. Introducing it with an oath serves to show the utmost concern with its content. The discussion of Noah's lineage, peace be upon him, the length of his stay among his people, and similar matters has already passed. The more correct view is that his mission, peace be upon him, was not universal; rather he was sent to a specific people. ﴿So he said﴾, being compassionate toward them and seeking to draw them to the truth: (O my people, worship Allah), that is, worship Him alone, as His saying, exalted is He, in Surah Hud [11:2] makes clear: ﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾. The restriction to Him was omitted to indicate that worship is exclusively this, and that worship alongside associating partners is not worship at all. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾ is a resumptive clause providing the reason for the worship being commanded, or the reason for the command to it. (Other than Him) is in the nominative as an attribute of (god), based on its position, which is nominative either as the subject of (for you) or as a predicate whose subject is (for you), or as an omitted element. (For you) serves to specify and clarify, meaning: there is no god in existence for you other than Him, exalted is He. It is also recited as (other than Him) in the genitive, taking the word (god) as the basis. ﴿Will you not then fear Allah?﴾ The interrogative particle is for denying the actual state of affairs and finding it abominable, and the fa' is for coordination with an implied element demanded by the context, meaning: do you recognize this, that is, the content of His saying, exalted is He: "You have no god other than Him," so that you do not fear His punishment, which is what your abandonment of worshipping Him alone and your associating with Him, mighty and majestic is He, in worship deserves, [namely] things that do not deserve existence were it not for Allah's bringing them into being, let alone deserving worship. So the denial is of the non-fearing despite the realization of what necessitates it. It is also possible that the implied sense is: "Do you not take heed? So you do not fear," in which case both matters are denied, and the emphasis then concerns quantity, whereas in the first case it concerns quality. Estimating the object of (you fear), as we have indicated, is preferable to some scholars' estimation of it as the loss of blessings. We do not concede that the context demands this, as is not hidden.

The chiefs (al-mala') who disbelieved among his people said — "al-mala'" meaning the nobles (al-ishraf). The description of the chiefs with disbelief, although all of them shared it, is to indicate the completeness of their ancient lineage and the severity of their obstinacy in it. The purpose of this is nothing but to censure them, not to distinguish them from other nobles who believed in him (peace be upon him), since none of their nobles believed in him, as is made clear by their saying: ﴿And we see none following you except those who are the lowest of us﴾. Al-Khafaji said: it is valid that the description with this is for distinction, even if some of their nobles did not believe at the time of speaking these words, because among his people (peace be upon him) who followed him were nobles; as for their saying ﴿We see you not﴾ [Hud: 27] etc., it is according to their assumption, or because of the scarcity of nobles who followed him. Whatever the case, the meaning is: the chiefs said to their common folk, "This is not ﴿but a human like you﴾", i.e., in kind and attribute, with no distinction between you and him. They described him (peace be upon him) with this in exaggeration of lowering his lofty rank and debasing him from the station of prophethood. They described him with the words of the Exalted: ﴿He wants to gain superiority over you﴾, to anger the addressees against him (peace be upon him) and to incite them to oppose him. Tafaddul means seeking superiority, and it is a metonymy for lordship, as if it was said: he wants to make himself your master and to precede you by claiming prophethood while being like you. It is said: the form tafa''ala is used metaphorically for perfection, for one who exerts himself for something does it in the most perfect manner; so it is as if it was said: he wants the perfection of superiority over you. ﴿And had God willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ — an explanation of the impossibility of human messengership in general according to their corrupt assumption, after establishing his humanity (peace be upon him). That is: and had God Most High willed to send a messenger, He would have sent messengers from among the angels. It was said ﴿He would have sent down﴾ because the sending of angels happens only by way of descent; so the object of the will is the absolute sending understood from the apodosis, not the very content of it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾ [al-Nahl: 9]; and there is no harm in this. As for the claim that the object of the will is omitted only when it is a strange matter and the content of the apodosis, this is a rule for the omission that is regular in it, not absolutely, for it, like the other objects, may be omitted and supplied according to the contextual indications. On this basis it is permissible to say: the supplied meaning is, "And had God Most High willed His worship alone, He would have sent down angels who convey that to us from Him, Mighty and Majestic; and this would have been from them a disparagement of His (peace be upon him) saying to them ﴿Worship God﴾." Likewise His Exalted saying: ﴿We have not heard of this among our fathers, the earliest ones﴾; rather it is a disparagement of what was mentioned even on the first supposition, and this is based on the view that "this" refers to the speech containing the command to worship God Most High alone, and the speech is on a supposed omitted noun, i.e., "We have not heard of the like of this speech among our fathers who passed before his mission (peace be upon him)." The noun was supposed because the non-hearing of the speech of Noah mentioned is not fit for rejection, for hearing the like of it is sufficient for acceptance. It was also said: the reference is to this very speech apart from its particulars, so there is no need to supply a noun, and this is a sound opinion. Then their saying this is either because they and their fathers were in a period without prophets (fatra), or because of the extreme excess of their denial and obstinacy and their immersion in error and corruption; whatever the case, it must have been what they said at the beginning of his call (peace be upon him), as indicated by the particle fa (then/so), which shows sequence, in His saying: ﴿So the chiefs said﴾, etc.

It was also said: "this" refers to Noah (peace be upon him), in the sense: "We have not heard of the news of his prophethood." It was said: it refers to his name, which is the word "Noah." The meaning: if he were a prophet, he would have a mention among our earliest fathers. On these two opinions, their saying mentioned is from the later members of his people who were born a long time after his mission; so the "earliest fathers" means those who passed before them in his time (peace be upon him). Its utterance from them was at the later stages of his affair (peace be upon him). It was also said: after the passing of their fathers, and it does not necessarily have to be at the later stages. On both of these too, their saying

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 25:

﴿Ilhu huwa﴾ meaning: he is not, ﴿except a man in whom there is madness﴾ meaning: insanity, or jinn who possess him (yakhbilunahu), and for this reason he says what he says. ﴿So wait for him﴾ meaning: bear with him, be patient with him, and wait ﴿until a time﴾ in the hope that he will recover from what he is in, this being understood in light of the extremes of their stubbornness and obstinacy, and their turning away from what they had described him, peace be upon him, with of humanity, and their desire to attribute to him what you see. Yet they know that he, peace be upon him, is the most rational of people and the most sober in speech. And what has preceded is to be understood as referring to the contradiction of their corrupt claims. May Allah fight them; how are they deluded?

﴿Qāla﴾ ("He said") is an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'nāf bayānī), as if it were asked: "What did he say, peace be upon him, after hearing these falsehoods from them?" The answer is that he said, when he saw them persisting in what they were in and going on in misguidance to the point that he despaired of their faith entirely, and he had already been revealed: ﴿that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ [Hud: 36]. ﴿My Lord, help me﴾ by destroying them completely. This is based on the view that it is a summary report of his words, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers a dweller﴾ [Nuh: 26], and so on.

The bā' in His words, ﴿bi-mā kadhdhabūnī﴾ ("because they denied me"), is either causal (li-l-sababiyyah) or substitutive (li-l-badal), and mā is verbal-masdariyyah (mā al-maṣdariyyah, the "ma" that forms a verbal noun with the following verb). The meaning is: "because of their denial of me," or "in place of their denial of me." It is also permitted that the bā' be instrumental (ālleast, ālliyyah) and that mā be relative (mawṣūlah, "that which"), meaning: "help me with that with which they denied me," namely the punishment which you promised them within my words: ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ [al-A'raf: 59; al-Shu'ara': 135; al-Ahqaf: 21]. The sum of this is: "help me by bringing that about." The weakness of omitting such a returning pronoun from speech is not hidden.

Abū Ja'far and Ibn Muḥaysin read «Rabbu» with a ḍammah on the bā' (rabbu, rather than rabbi). Its justification is not hidden.

Then We revealed to him, following this, or it was said: because of this, "Build the ark under Our eyes" (meaning: with Our especial protection and care for you, guarding you from transgression or from error in its construction) "and Our revelation" (meaning: Our command and Our instruction on how to build it). The fa' in Allah's words, ﴿So when Our command comes﴾, indicates that what follows is consequent upon the completion of the building of the ark. By "the command" is meant the punishment, as in His words, ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah﴾ [Hud: 43]. It is the single one of the matters, not the command to board, which is the single one of the orders, as has been said. By its "coming" is meant the full approach of it, that is, the beginning of its appearance, i.e., when the sign of the ark's completion comes, Our punishment. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and the oven gushed forth﴾ is an explanation and clarification of the coming of the command. It is narrated that it was said to him, peace be upon him: "When the oven gushes forth, board, you and those with you." The oven was that of Adam, peace be upon him, and it came into the possession of Noah, peace be upon him. When water gushed from it, his wife informed him, and they boarded. They differed about its location. It was said that it was in the mosque of Kufa, that is, at its place on the right of one who enters from the Kindah Gate today. It was said that it was at 'Ayn Wardah in Syria. It was said that it was in al-Jazirah near Mosul. It was said that "the oven" means the surface of the earth. It was said that "the oven gushed forth" is like the idiom "the battle became hot." 

It is related from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he explained ﴿and the oven gushed forth﴾ as the rising of dawn. It was said: its meaning is that the gushing of the oven happened at the rising of dawn, but this is far-fetched. The full discussion of this has already been presented to you earlier.

﴿Then insert into it﴾, i.e., enter into it. It is said salaka fihi, meaning he entered into it, and salakahu fihi, meaning he caused it to enter into it. From this is His saying: ﴿What has brought you into Saqar?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42]. ﴿Of every﴾, i.e., of every community, ﴿two pairs﴾, i.e., two singles which are paired, as His saying ﴿two﴾ indicates, for it is clear in the singles and not in the pluralities.

Most of the reciters read "kulli zawjayn" with the genitive construction, on the basis that the object is "ithnayn", i.e., insert from every one of My community the male and female, two paired individuals, like a camel and she-camel, a horse and mare. It is narrated: "He, peace be upon him, did not carry on the ark from these except what gives birth and lays eggs." As for what is generated from decay, such as bedbugs, flies and worms, he did not carry any of them. Perhaps something like mules is attached in not being carried, with this kind, because it comes about through breeding between two types; so carrying from both of them suffices from carrying from it, if the carrying was so that the species would not be cut off, as is apparent, so it would need a new creation, as He created at the beginning of the matter.

The verse is explicit that the command to enter was before the building of the ark. In Surah Hud [40]: ﴿until when Our command came and the oven gushed forth, We said: Load into it from every kind two pairs﴾. So the proper view is that this is to be understood as a report of a different command, an immediate command, issued at the gushing of the oven upon which the conditional command was hung, out of concern for the matter of what was commanded; or that this is the very same prior command, but since the conditional command, before the condition attached to it was realized, is with respect to making the commanded thing obligatory like nonexistence, it was treated as though it had only occurred upon the realization of the condition, and so it is reported in the form of an immediate command.

﴿And your family﴾: it was said it is conjoined to "ithnayn" on the reading with the genitive construction, and to "zawjayn" on the reading with tanwin (nunation). The meaning's disruption on this is not hidden. So it is in the accusative governed by a verb conjoined to ﴿fasluk﴾, i.e., and insert your family. By them is meant the community of response, those who believed in him, peace be upon him, whether they were of his relatives or not. The use of "family" for this is attested. He was led to take it here in this sense, and not the well-known meaning, so as to include whoever believed among those who were not relatives, for they are mentioned in Surah Hud, and the Qur'an explains one part of it by another. On this, His saying ﴿except those against whom the word has already preceded﴾ is a disjunctive (munqati') exception. Some have chosen to take "family" in its well-known sense, meaning his wife and sons from among them, as in Surah Hud, and then the exception is connected (muttasil), as it was there. The non-mention of those who believed is because it is sufficient to state it explicitly there, together with what the exception indicates, and likewise what follows it, as an indication that it is appropriate to include them.

The delay of the command to insert the family, on both interpretations, relative to what was mentioned of inserting the pairs, is because inserting the pairs requires him, peace be upon him, to undertake the work and requires his family to assist him, whereas they enter by their own choice. And because in what is delayed there is a kind of detailed specification, by mentioning the exception and other things, so putting it first would disrupt the harmony of the noble composition.

By "the word" is meant the decree of destruction. By the preceding of that is meant its realization in pre-eternity, or the writing of what indicates it in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) before the world was created. 'Ala was used because the preceding is harmful, just as the lam was used in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best has preceded from Us﴾ [al-Anbiya': 101], because the preceding is beneficial.

﴿And do not address Me concerning those who did wrong﴾, i.e., do not speak to Me about them with intercession and seeking deliverance for them from drowning or the like. And when the intended ones are those against whom the word has preceded, the use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is not hidden in its purpose.

﴿Indeed, they are drowned﴾: this is a reason for the prohibition, or for what indicates it, namely the non-acceptance of intercession for them. I.e., they are decreed against, drowning without doubt, because of their wrongdoing through association and all sorts of sins. And one whose state is this should not be interceded for, nor should one intercede for him. And how could that be proper, when his destruction is among the blessings for which one is commanded to praise Allah, as is indicated by it.

[Page 27]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 28:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when you and those with you are settled upon the ship﴾, [those] from your family and your followers, ﴿then say: "All praise is due to Allah, who has saved us from the wrongdoing people."﴾ Indeed, praise for being saved from them includes praise for their destruction. The reason it was said as it is mentioned, and not "say: All praise is due to Allah, who has destroyed the wrongdoing people," is that the blessing of being saved is more complete. Al-Khafaji said: In that there is an indication that one should not rejoice in the calamity of anyone, even an enemy, insofar as it is a calamity for him; rather [one rejoices] because of what it includes of safety from his harm, or the purification of the earth from the filth of his polytheism and his misguidance.
Page 28

You know that praise here is a companion of thanks (al-shukr), so when it is specified by the blessing that reaches the one who gives thanks, it is not valid for it to relate to the calamity insofar as it is a calamity, and this is evident. And in his being commanded, peace be upon him, to praise [Allah] for the salvation of his followers, there is also an indication that it is a blessing upon him as well.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 29:

﴿And say: "My Lord, cause me to descend"﴾ in the ark ﴿a blessed descent﴾, that is, a descent (inzal) or a place of descent, ﴿blessed﴾ — causing an increase of good in both abodes; ﴿and You are the best of those who cause to descend﴾, that is, the best of whoever is described by that. The supplication with this, if it is after boarding, then what is meant is the continuation of that descent, and perhaps the intended meaning is the continuation of blessing. It is also permitted that it be a supplication for success in alighting at the most blessed of its (the ark's) stopping places, since it is spacious. And if it was before boarding, the matter is clear. A group related from Mujahid that this is the supplication which Nuh, peace be upon him, was commanded to say when descending from the ship, so the meaning is: "My Lord, cause me to descend from it onto the earth at a blessed place," and so on. Qatadah took this view. He recommended that the rider of the ship say, upon descending from it, ﴿My Lord, cause me to descend﴾, etc. Some of them favoured the first view, since the conjunction (ʿaṭf) apparently indicates that the two statements are made at the time of settling (on the ship). The word (﴿qul﴾, "say") is repeated for the multiplicity of supplications, and the first includes the warding off of harm, which is why it was placed first, while this one is for the attainment of benefit.

His peace be upon him being commanded to precede his supplication with what befits it of praise of Him, Mighty and Majestic, as a means of seeking a response, for praise of the benefactor calls forth his beneficence; and they have said: "Praise of the generous one dispenses with asking him." His peace be upon him being singled out for the command, though all share in boarding, is to show his excellence, peace be upon him, and that none other than him among them is fitting for it, because of nearness to God Most High and attaining the honour of presence in the station of excellence; together with an allusion to His greatness, Mighty and Majestic, and that He, glorified be He, does not address every one of His servants; and an indication that in his supplication and praise, peace be upon him, there is sufficiency beyond what is other than it.

Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Ablah and Aban read "munzalan" (﴿مَنزِلًا﴾) with a fatha on the mim and a fatha on the zay, meaning a place of descent. Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿAsim, read "munzilan" (﴿مَنزِلًا﴾) with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the zay. Abu ʿAli said: it is possible that the noun (manzil) in this reading is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it is possible that it is a place of descent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 30:

﴿Indeed, in that﴾ — that which he mentioned of what was done to him, peace be upon him, and to his people — ﴿are signs﴾ — magnificent ones — by which those endowed with sight are guided, and those who take heed are admonished. ﴿And indeed We were ever testing﴾ — "inna" here is the lightened form of "inna" (from inna, "indeed"), and the lam is the lam of distinction (al-lam al-fariqah) between it and the negating "in" (in al-nafiyah). "In" is not negating, and the lam carries the meaning of "illa" (except). The clause is circumstantial (hal), meaning: indeed, the matter was that We were striking the people of Noah with a great affliction and a severe punishment; or: testing Our servants with these signs, to see who takes heed and remembers. What is intended is: treating them in the manner of one who tests. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have left it as a sign, so is there any who will take heed?﴾ [al-Qamar: 15].

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verses 31–32:

﴿Then We brought into being after them﴾, i.e., after the destruction of the people of Noah, peace be upon him, ﴿another generation﴾. They were ʿAd or Thamud. ﴿And We sent among them a messenger from among themselves﴾. He was Hud or Salih, peace be upon them both. The first view is the one transmitted (al-marthur) from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and most of the exegetes (mufassirun, scholars of tafsir) adopted it. It is supported by the words of Allah, the Exalted, quoting Hud: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 69], and by the fact that the story of ʿAd comes after the story of Noah in Surat al-Aʿraf, Surat Hud, and elsewhere. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and al-Tabari chose the second view, and they argued for it by the mention of the Shout (al-sayha) at the end of the story. It is well known that the people of Salih are the ones destroyed by it, not the people of Hud. The answer to this will come, if Allah wills. The word "generation" (qarn) is taken as an adverbial of time for the sending, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Thus We have sent you to a community﴾ [al-Raʿd: 30], and it has no end point, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿We certainly sent Noah to his people﴾. This is to indicate from the outset that the one sent to them did not come from outside their land, but rose up among them. ("And [an]") in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿that worship Allah﴾ is explanatory (mufassira, i.e., introducing an explanation of what precedes), because the sending contains the meaning of saying. That is, We said to them through the tongue of the Messenger: worship Allah. He also permitted that it be verbal (masdariyya, i.e., forming a verbal noun with the following verb), with no obstacle to connecting it to the imperative verb, and with an understood preposition before it, meaning: We sent among them a messenger, saying: worship Allah alone. (﴿You have no god other than Him. Will you not then fear Allah?﴾) The discussion of this is like the discussion of its parallel that has passed in the story of Noah, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 33:

﴿وقالَ المَلأُ﴾ That is, the nobles (al-mala')﴿مِن قَوْمِهِ﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of them. And His saying, ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وكَذَّبُوا بِلِقاءِ الآخِرَةِ﴾ — that is, [they denied] the meeting with what is in it of reckoning, reward and punishment, or with the Resurrection, or with the second life — is a description (sifah) of al-mala', brought as a reproach against them and as an alert to their excess in disbelief. It is permissible that it be for specification (tamyiz), if in that generation there were nobles who believed.

The placing of ﴿مِن قَوْمِهِ﴾ here before the description, though it was delayed in the earlier narrative, is so that the separation between the explanation and what it explains would not be prolonged were it brought after the description and what is in its scope of what is attached to the relative clause, along with the possibility of it being understood as connected to the worldly life; or so that it would not separate the conjoined from the conjoined-to, were it brought after the description and before the conjunction. Thus it has been said.

It has been objected that there is no need to commit to making ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ a description of al-mala' and to show a point for the aforementioned placement, since it is clearly permissible to make it a description of "qawmihi" (his people). It was answered that the motive for this choice is the conjunction of His saying, ﴿وأتْرَفْناهم في الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾ — that is, We gave them ease and expanded for them in it — upon the relative clause; so it becomes a descriptive clause of meaning for what is described by the relative pronoun. And the familiar usage is describing the nobles as "those given ease (al-mutrafun)," not others. Likewise the situation is if it is not conjoined and is made a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ("kadhdhabu"). But you know that we do not grant that the familiar usage is describing the nobles as "those given ease." And even if we grant it, describing them thus may remain while making the relative clause a description of "qawmihi," by making the clause ("atrafnahum") a circumstantial clause from ﴿al-mala'﴾ without "qad," or with "qad" implied; that is, the nobles said about our Messenger ﴿ما هَذا إلا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ﴾ etc., while We had bestowed favour upon them.

The apparent reading, in wording, is that the clause ("atrafnahum") is conjoined to the relative clause, and the more eloquent in meaning is making it a circumstantial clause from the pronoun, since it conveys harm done to one who has done good, and that is stronger in reproach.

The conjunctive "wa" was brought with ﴿وقالَ المَلأُ﴾ here and was not brought there; rather the sentence was brought as a resumptive, explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) in another place, because what we are dealing with here is a narration of the difference between the two speeches — I mean the speech of the sender and the speech of those sent to — not a narration of a dialogue, since those sent to said what they said to one another. The apparent reason for rejecting that resumption there, whereas here it is required, is that it is in the narration of a dialogue between the sender and those sent to, and the situation of address requires that. Thus stated in al-Kashf. But this does not close the matter of the question, for it may be asked: why is the dialogue narrated there while the difference between the two speeches is here, and why was it not reversed? Something like this refutes those who explain the mention here and the omission there by variety of style (tafannun), by saying: if it had been reversed, omitting here and mentioning there, variety would also have resulted. I have not seen the secret in that clearly.

As for the use of "wa" here and "fa" in ﴿فَقالَ المَلأُ﴾ in the story of Noah, peace be upon him, it has been said: perhaps it is because the speech of the nobles here was not connected to the speech of their messenger, unlike the speech of the people of Noah, peace be upon him. And God Most High knows best the realities of matters.

There is no concealing what is in their saying ﴿ما هَذا إلَخْ﴾ of exaggeration in belittling the matter of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and making light of him. May God fight them; how ignorant they are.

His saying, Most High: ﴿يَأْكُلُ مِمّا تَأْكُلُونَ مِنهُ ويَشْرَبُ مِمّا تَشْرَبُونَ﴾ is an affirmation of the equality (mumathalah). The apparent reading is that the second "ma" is a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun is a genitive pronoun deleted together with the preposition, due to what precedes it indicating it. The deletion here is like its deletion in your saying: "marartu bi-lladhi marartu" (I passed by the one I passed by), fulfilling its conditions. Its goodness here is that "tashrabun" is the closing word (fasilah).

In al-Tahrir, al-Farra' claimed the deletion of the returning genitive pronoun together with the preposition in this verse, and this is not permissible according to the Basran grammarians. The verse either has no deletion, or only the object is deleted; for if "ma" is a verbal-noun (masdariyyah) it needs no returning pronoun, and if it is a relative pronoun then the deleted returning pronoun is an accusative pronoun in the object position, attached to the verb, and the estimate is "mimma tashrabunahu" (of what you drink). Thus far al-Tahrir. This is an derivation according to the rule of the Basrans, and it forfeits the eloquence of the parallel structure. Moreover, the first aspect requires interpreting the verbal-noun as an object-noun (ism al-maf'ul), and after that it needs some strain to make the meaning sound; the second aspect too needs that same strain, since no one drinks from their drink, nor from that which they drink, but rather one drinks from another individual of the kind. So the generic sense must be intended in both aspects.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 34:

﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves﴾ in what he has mentioned of states and attributes, that is, if you comply with his commands, ﴿then indeed you would be losers﴾ in your minds, and deceived in your opinions, since you have humbled yourselves. The lam here is a preparatory lam (lam al-muwatta'ah) for the oath, and the clause ﴿indeed you would be losers﴾ is the answer to the oath. As for (idhan), in what I incline to, it is adverbial (zarfiyyah), related to what the predication between the subject and the predicate indicates of established occurrence, or it is related to the predicate itself; and the lam does not prevent operating in such a case. The answer to the conditional is omitted, and what has been mentioned indicates it.

Abu Hayyan said: If this were the answer, the fa' would have been required in it, so that one would say: "fa-innakum" and so on. Indeed, if it were with the fa' in a composition other than the Noble Qur'an, that composition would not be permissible except according to al-Farra', while the Basrans do not permit it, and in their view it is an error. End of quote.

Some scholars have said that "idha" here is for the conditional and the answer, but this is forced, and nothing prompts to it except the assumption that one must follow the well-known view, and that the truth in such matters is confined to what the majority hold. In Hama' al-Hawami' and likewise in al-Itqan by al-Jalal al-Suyuti, on this topic, there is what will benefit you to consult, so consult it.

**Page 31**

﴿Does he promise you﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a clause that begins a new statement while continuing the previous argument), offered to confirm what precedes it, namely their deterrence from following him, peace be upon him, by denying the occurrence of what would call them to belief in him and by deeming it unlikely. The phrase ﴿that you﴾ is taken with an implied preposition, meaning *bi-annakum* (that you). It is also permissible not to supply the preposition, as in *wa'attuka al-khayra* (I promised you good).

﴿when you die﴾ is read with a kasra on the *mim* from *mata yamutu* (to die), and it is also read with a damma on the *mim* from *mata yamutu*, as in *mata yamootu*. ﴿and you have been dust and bones﴾ means that some parts of your bodies were flesh and their likes were dust, and some of them were bones, decayed and stripped of flesh and sinews. The mention of dust first is due to its strangeness in terms of being unlikely, and its transformation from the visible parts. Alternatively, the meaning is that your predecessors were pure dust and your successors were bones.

﴿that you﴾ is an emphatic repetition (*ta'kid*) of the first ﴿that you﴾, because of the long separation between it and its predicate, which is the words ﴿will be brought forth﴾. ﴿when﴾ is an adverbial clause of time connected to it, meaning: Does he promise you that you will be brought forth from your graves alive, as you were at first, when you die and have become dust?

Al-Farra', al-Jurmi and al-Mubarrad chose this grammatical analysis (*i'rab*). This does not necessitate that the bringing forth occurs at the time of death, as is not hidden. This differs from what Abu Nizar, who was titled Malik al-Nuhat (King of the Grammarians), imagined. Al-Sakhawi refuted him, and al-Jalal al-Suyuti transmitted this refutation from him in *al-Ashbah*. What is transmitted from Sibawayh is that ﴿that you﴾ is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for the first ﴿that you﴾, and it carries the meaning of emphasis. The predicate of the first *inna* is omitted, because the predicate of the second indicates it. The meaning is: Does he promise you that you will be raised when you die? This omitted predicate is the governing element of ﴿when﴾. It is not permissible for it to be the predicate itself, because a temporal adverb cannot be predicated of a body. If it is interpreted by omitting a noun (*mudaf*), meaning that your bringing forth when you die, then it is permissible. Al-Mubarrad rejected the substitution because it is not an independent construction, since the predicate of the first *inna* is not mentioned.

Al-Akhfash held that ﴿that you will be brought forth﴾ is equivalent to a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the nominative, governed by an omitted verb whose estimated form is *yahduthu ikhrajukum* (your bringing forth occurs). According to this estimate, the conditional clause may be the predicate of the first ﴿that you﴾, and that omitted verb serves as the answer of ﴿when﴾. It is also permissible for that verb to be the predicate of *inna* and to govern ﴿when﴾. Some transmit from al-Akhfash that he makes ﴿that you will be brought forth﴾ the agent of ﴿when﴾, just as he makes *al-khuruj* (the going out) the agent of *yawm* (day) in your saying: *yawm al-jumu'a al-khuruj* (on Friday, the going out), in the sense of: the going out occurs on Friday.

Some have permitted that ﴿that you will be brought forth﴾ be the subject (*mubtada'*), with ﴿when you die﴾ as its predicate, in the sense of: your bringing forth when you die. The clause then becomes the predicate of the first *inna*. Al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) says: This analysis is easy and free of artificiality. Al-Sakhawi attributed it in *Safar al-Sa'ada* to al-Mubarrad. However, what the eloquence of the noble composition requires is what we have mentioned from al-Farra' and those with him.

In the reading of Abdullah: ﴿Does he promise you when you die﴾, with the omission of the first ﴿that you﴾.

﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ is a noun meaning "far away" or "how distant," and in origin it is an interjection (ism sawt). Its agent is a concealed pronoun within it, referring to the affirmation, the truth, the occurrence, or something similar that the context makes understood. It is as though it were said: "far is the affirmation, or the truth, or the occurrence." The Exalted's saying ﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ is a repetition for emphasis of the distance.
