The usual practice with this word is that it comes repeated, but it came unrepeated in the verse of Jarir:

*"Far away (hayhata) is the abandoning of the one at al-'Aqiq whom we keep company with."*

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ explains the referent of that pronoun. The lam is attached to an implied element, as in *saqyan lahu* (a supplication for him to be watered). That is, the affirmation or the occurrence characterized by distance is "for what you are promised." It should not be said that it is attached to the pronoun referring back to the verbal noun, as in his saying:

*"War is only what you have known and tasted, and he is not one to speak of it lightly."*

For the employment of the pronoun of the verbal noun, although the Kufans held this, is extremely rare, and the Book of God should not be interpreted in accordance with it. It has been said: "Why should it be affirmed when the line is open to interpretation?" All of this applies even when the pronoun is explicit; what then of when it is concealed? The claim that the agent is an omitted noun, not a concealed pronoun, and is a verbal noun like *al-wuqu'* (the occurrence) or *al-tasdiq* (the affirmation), with the prepositional phrase attached to it, is one that should not be given any attention at all, especially when that omitted verbal noun is definite, as is clear.

It is permissible that the agent be the pronoun of the distance, with the lam being explanatory, as though it were said: "He (the distance) made distance and occurred; then it was asked: 'For what?' and it was answered: 'For what you are promised.'" It has also been said that the agent of ﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ is ﴿ما تُوعَدُونَ﴾, and the lam is an "eloquent sword" (i.e., a decisive, cutting lam). This was supported by the reading of Ibn Abi 'Abla: *"Hayhata, hayhata ma tu'adun,"* without the lam. It was rebutted on the ground that the addition of such a lam to the agent is not known.

It has also been said: *hayhata* means "distance," and it is a subject (mubtada') that is indeclinable (mabni), taken in view of its original form. Its predicate is ﴿لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾, meaning: the distance is for what you are promised. This interpretation is attributed to al-Zajjaj.

Abu Hayyan, in al-Bahr, criticized this, saying that it should be an interpretation of meaning, not a tafsir of i'rab (grammatical analysis), because the verbal-noun status of ﴿هَيْهاتَ﴾ has not been established.

Harun reported from Abu 'Amr the reading *"hayhatan hayhatan"* with both vowelled with fatha and nunated, for indefiniteness, as is the case with all verb-nouns (asma' al-af'al, nouns functioning as verbs) when they take tanwin. In that case it is a verb-noun that is indefinite. It has been said:

*"It is, on this reading, a declinable noun (ism mutamakkin) in the accusative, functioning as a verbal noun."*

Abu Haywa and al-Ahmar read it with damma and tanwin. The author of al-Lawami' said: "It is possible on this that *hayhata* is a declinable noun in the nominative, functioning as the subject of the sentence, with ﴿لِما تُوعَدُونَ﴾ as its predicate, and the repetition is for emphasis. It is also possible that it is a verb-noun and the damma is for indeclinability, like *hawb* in driving camels, but it was given tanwin because it is indefinite." End of quotation. It has also been said: it is a declinable noun in the nominative functioning as the agent, meaning: "it occurred after." It is reported from Sibawayh that it is a plural, like *bay'at* (eggs), and some of them derived from this that its two components are equal in the sound of the letters, so they said its singular is *hayha*, like *bay'a* (an egg).

In a report from Abu Haywa, he vowelled it with damma without tanwin, likening it to *qabla* and *ba'da* (before and after). Abu Ja'far and Shayba read it with kasra on both without tanwin. This was also reported from 'Isa, and it is a dialect of Tamim and Asad. It is also reported from him, and from Khalid ibn al-Ilyas, that they both read it with kasra on both and with tanwin.

Kharija ibn Mus'ab reported from Abu 'Amr, and al-A'raj and 'Isa as well, reading it with sukun on both. Among them are those who keep the *ta'* and pause on it, as in *musallimat* (plural feminine forms), and among them are those who change it to a *ha'* likening it to the feminine *ta'*, and pause on the *ha'*. It has been said: the pausing on the *ha'* follows the written form.

What is understood from Majma' al-Bayan is that *hayhata* with fatha is written with a *ha'*, like *arta* (a tree), and its original form is *hayhay'a*, like *zalzala*; the second *ya'* was changed to an *alif* because it is vowelled and the preceding letter is open. Likewise *hayhata* with damma and tanwin. On this basis it is a singular declinable noun. When it is considered a plural, it is written with a *ta'*, and that is when it is vowelled with kasra, with or without tanwin. This was reported from Ibn Jinni.

He read *"ayhaha"* with the first *ha'* changed to a hamza, and pausing with sukun on the *ha'*. What I incline to is that all these readings are dialects and the meaning is one. In this word there are more than forty dialects, and this has been mentioned in al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil and elsewhere.

[p. 32]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 37:

﴿Ilhi illa hayatuna al-dunya﴾ ("It is nothing but our life of this world")

Its original form was: "Inna al-hayata illa hayatuna al-dunya." Then the pronoun was placed in the position of "al-hayah" (life), because the predicate indicates it and explains it. So the pronoun refers to something that comes later in the sentence. Its reference in this way is permissible in certain cases, among them when it is explained by the predicate, as here. Thus they said.

It has been objected that the predicate is described by an adjective, so the adjective must be taken into account in the pronoun, as is well known for a pronoun referring to a described noun. In that case the sense becomes: "Inna hayatana al-dunya illa hayatuna al-dunya" ("Indeed our worldly life is nothing but our worldly life").

The answer is that the pronoun may refer to the described noun without its adjective. This, in the matter of the Hereafter, returns to the view that the pronoun refers to what is understood from the genus of life, in order to convey the sense that they intended in denying resurrection. It is as if they said: "There is no life except our worldly life." From this it is known that the error of one who said, "It is like 'my poetry is my poetry'" (sha'ri sha'ri). Of the same kind, according to the opinion of those who say, "They are the Arabs, saying whatever they wish," and the poet's line:

"It is the soul; whatever I burden it with, it bears; and for time there are days that oppress and that bring justice."

In al-Kashshaf it is said: The meaning is not "the soul is the soul," because the second term would not then be suitable as an explanation, and the sentence following it would not be a clarification. Rather the pronoun refers to a mentally known referent, which is pointed to and then described by what follows, as in "This is your brother." End of quotation. So reflect on this and do not neglect it.

As for the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Namutu wa nahya﴾ ("We die and we live"), this is a sentence explaining what they claimed, that life is the worldly life. By this they meant that some of us die and some are born, and so on. The intended meaning of "life" is not another life after death, for in that case the sentence would not be suitable as an explanation, and its speaker would not be blamed. It contradicts their words: ﴿Wa ma nahnu bi-mab'uthin﴾ ("And we are not to be resurrected").

It has also been said: they meant by "death" the non-existence that precedes existence, or they meant by "life" the survival of their offspring, for the survival of offspring is treated as the life of the fathers. This is very far-fetched. Similar to it, according to what is said, though I do not see it this way, is the view that these people held to transmigration (tanasukh, the passing of souls from one body to another). Their "life" would then be the attachment of the soul that had departed their bodies to other elemental bodies, which had moved through stages until they became fit for that departed soul to attach to them. So Zayd, for example, when he dies, his soul attaches to another body that has been prepared in the womb for attachment, and then he is born. Then, when he dies again, his soul attaches to another body in the same way, and so on without end. This is the doctrine of some of the transmigrationists, namely the Milyuniyya and the Nahliyya.

[Page 33]

It may be said that this is according to the manner of the words of Allah the Exalted to 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿Inni mutawaffika wa rafi'uka ilayya﴾ ("Indeed I will take you to Myself and raise you to Me") [Al 'Imran: 55], according to one opinion, since the conjunction there is "wa" (and), which does not require sequence. Therefore it is permissible that the life they meant was the life before death. It is also possible that they said "nahya wa namutu" (we live and we die), but when it was reported about them it was said: ﴿Namutu wa nahya﴾ so that it would be more suitable to His words: ﴿Ilhi illa hayatuna al-dunya﴾. Then the intended meaning of their words "wa ma nahnu" (and we are not) and so on is the continuation and emphasis of the denial.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 38–39:

﴿In he huwa﴾ i.e., "he is not" ﴿but a man who has fabricated against Allah a lie﴾ regarding what he claims of His, exalted is He, sending him, and regarding what he promises us of Allah, exalted is He, resurrecting us. ﴿And we are not, for him, believers﴾, i.e., we do not affirm what he says. The intent is also the continuation and emphasis of the negation. ﴿He said﴾, i.e., their Messenger, when he despaired of their faith, after he had followed every path in calling them, humbly beseeching Allah, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿My Lord, help me﴾ against them, and avenge me upon them ﴿for that they denied me﴾, i.e., because of their denying me and their persistence in it, or in place of their denial. It is also permissible that the bā' be instrumental (ālīyyah) and mā be a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), as has passed in the story of Noah, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 38–39:

﴿In he huwa﴾ i.e., "he is not" ﴿but a man who has fabricated against Allah a lie﴾ regarding what he claims of His, exalted is He, sending him, and regarding what he promises us of Allah, exalted is He, resurrecting us. ﴿And we are not, for him, believers﴾, i.e., we do not affirm what he says. The intent is also the continuation and emphasis of the negation. ﴿He said﴾, i.e., their Messenger, when he despaired of their faith, after he had followed every path in calling them, humbly beseeching Allah, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿My Lord, help me﴾ against them, and avenge me upon them ﴿for that they denied me﴾, i.e., because of their denying me and their persistence in it, or in place of their denial. It is also permissible that the bā' be instrumental (ālīyyah) and mā be a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), as has passed in the story of Noah, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 40:

﴿Said﴾ — the Exalted says, in response to his supplication and as a promise of what he asked for: ﴿after a little while﴾, i.e., after a short time. Here the question arises of what the connection is between the preposition and the noun it governs. It was brought in to emphasise the meaning of fewness. ("Qalil", little, is an adjective of a noun of time that has been omitted, and the phrase has been made to stand in its place. Its occurring in this manner is common.) It is also permitted that *ma* be a complete indefinite noun (*nakira tamma*, a noun that is complete in itself), with "qalil" as its substitute, or that it be an indefinite noun described by "qalil". The preposition "'an" here carries the sense of distance, and it is connected to the Exalted's words: ﴿they will surely become regretful﴾. Its connection to either the verb or the descriptive phrase is possible. This was permitted even though the oath particle *lam* intervenes, because the prepositional phrase is like an adverbial of time, which admits latitude that other elements do not.

Abu Hayyan said: The majority of our companions hold that the oath particle *lam* cannot be preceded by the complement of what follows it, whether that complement is an adverbial of time, a prepositional phrase, or something else. On this view, the phrase is linked to an omitted element indicated by what precedes it, and the estimate is: "after a little while you will be victorious" or what follows it, i.e., "they will become [regretful] after a little while, surely they will become..." etc. The view of al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda is that it is permitted to place before this *lam* the complement of what is within its scope, without restriction. The verb "yusbihu" here means "yasiru" (to become), i.e., by Allah the Exalted, they will surely become regretful for what they did of denial after a short time. That is at the time the punishment descends in this world and they witness it. It was also said: after death. In *al-Lawami'*, it is reported from some of them that it is read "latasbahanna" with a *ta'* in the second person. So if someone were to go in the direction that the speech is from the Messenger to the disbelievers after his supplication has been answered, it would be permissible.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 41:

﴿So the Cry seized them﴾, that is, the cry of Jibril (peace be upon him). He cried out to them (peace be upon him) and thereby destroyed them. This is apparent according to the view that the "qarn" (generation) were the people of Salih (peace be upon him). As for the one who said they were the people of Hud (peace be upon him), this is problematic on its apparent sense, since what is explicitly stated in other surahs is that they were destroyed by a violent wind. He answered that Jibril (peace be upon him) cried out at them from within the wind, as has been reported in some hadiths. Mentioning each separately indicates that each one alone would have sufficed to destroy them. It is also permissible that by the "Cry" is meant a terrible punishment and an annihilating torment, as in his saying:

"The age cried out at the family of Barmak with a cry, and they fell upon their chins from its severity."

﴿with the truth﴾ is connected to the seizing, that is, with the established matter that has no repelling. This is as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the agony of death came with the truth﴾ [Qaf: 19]. Or it means with justice from Allah, exalted and majestic, from your saying: "So-and-so judges with the truth" when he is just in his judgments. Or it means with the true promise that the Messenger made it within His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In a little while they will surely become regretful﴾.

﴿So We made them debris﴾, that is, like the debris of the torrent, which is what it carries of leaves and decayed twigs. It is pluralized as "aghtha'" irregularly, and its "tha'" may be doubled, as in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"As if the peaks of the head of al-Mujayjir at dawn, from the torrent and the debris, were a spindle's whorl."

﴿So away with the wrongdoing people﴾. It may be understood as a report or as a supplication. "Bu'd" is the opposite of "qurb" (nearness), and "halak" (destruction); their verbs are like "karuma" and "faraha," and the common usage is the first for the first and the second for the second. It is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, that is: they were removed with a removal from the mercy of Allah, exalted, or from all good, or from salvation, or they perished with a perishing. According to Sibawayh, the verb governing this infinitive must be omitted when it is a supplication, as stated in ad-Durr al-Masun. The "lam" is to clarify who is cursed or whose distance is reported; it is therefore connected to an omitted element, not to "bu'dan." The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate that their removal was because of their wrongdoing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verses 42–43:

﴿Then We brought into being after them﴾, i.e., after their destruction, ﴿other generations﴾. According to most exegetes, they are the people of Salih, the people of Lut, the people of Shu'ayb, and others besides them.

﴿No community can precede its appointed term﴾, i.e., no community among the destroyed nations gets ahead of the time that was appointed for its destruction. Here the particle "min" (from/any) is brought in, in the phrase "min sayfi khatib" (a rhetorical device meaning "min" emphasizes that the negation is absolute), to reinforce the generality (istighraq) derived from the indefinite noun occurring in a negative context. The overall meaning is: no nation among the nations is destroyed before the arrival of its term. ﴿Nor can they delay it by an hour﴾. The plural pronoun refers to ﴿community﴾ according to its meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verses 42–43:

﴿Then We brought into being after them﴾, i.e., after their destruction, ﴿other generations﴾. According to most exegetes, they are the people of Salih, the people of Lut, the people of Shu'ayb, and others besides them.

﴿No community can precede its appointed term﴾, i.e., no community among the destroyed nations gets ahead of the time that was appointed for its destruction. Here the particle "min" (from/any) is brought in, in the phrase "min sayfi khatib" (a rhetorical device meaning "min" emphasizes that the negation is absolute), to reinforce the generality (istighraq) derived from the indefinite noun occurring in a negative context. The overall meaning is: no nation among the nations is destroyed before the arrival of its term. ﴿Nor can they delay it by an hour﴾. The plural pronoun refers to ﴿community﴾ according to its meaning.

﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿We brought into being﴾, but not in the sense that their sending was delayed beyond the bringing into being of all the generations mentioned together. Rather, it means that the sending of each messenger came after the emergence of a particular generation assigned to that messenger. It is as if it were said: "Then, after them, We brought into being other generations, to each of which We sent a messenger specific to it." The interposition of the parenthetical clause between the two coordinated items serves to hasten the explanation of the destruction of those generations in a summary manner. The linking of the sending to the messengers is similar to the linking of killing to the slain in the expression "whoever kills a slain person," and the scholars have various interpretations of this.

﴿Tatra﴾ derives from al-mutawātirah (consecutiveness, one thing following another), which is successive sequence with an interval and a pause, as al-Aṣmaʿī said and as al-Ḥarīrī preferred in *al-Durrah*.

In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*, al-mutawātirah is al-mutābaʿah (succession), and there is no mutawātirah between things unless a pause (fatrah) occurs between them; otherwise it is mudārakah (overtaking). The same appears in *al-Qāmūs*. It is related from Abū ʿAlī that he said: "Al-mutawātirah is when a report follows a report, or a book follows a book, without a great interval between them." In *al-Baḥr* it is reported from some scholars that mutawātirah is succession without a pause. It is also said that it is succession in general. The first tāʾ is a substitute for a wāw, as in turāth and tujāh, and the derivation confirms this.

The majority of readers and the Arabs read it without tanwīn, so its alif is the alif of feminine formation, like the alif in daʿwā and dhikrā. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). The apparent view is that it is a ḥāl of the object, and the meaning, as Abū Ḥayyān, al-Rāghib and others said, is "then We sent Our messengers in succession." It is also said to be a ḥāl of the subject, meaning "We sent them in succession."

It is also said to be an adjective of a suppressed verbal noun, i.e. "a successive sending." It is also said to be an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) of ﴿We sent﴾, because it has the sense of "We made them follow one another."

Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Qatādah, Abū Jaʿfar, Shuʿbah, Ibn Muḥaysin and the Imam al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, read ﴿tatrā﴾ with tanwīn, and this is the dialect of Kinānah. In *al-Baḥr* he said: "According to those who read with tanwīn, the alif should be the alif of ilḥāq (extension of a root), as in arṭā and ʿalqā. But the alif of ilḥāq in verbal nouns is rare, and it is said that it is not found in them at all."

Al-Farrāʾ said: "It is said tatarun in the nominative, tatarin in the genitive, and tatran in the accusative, so it is like ṣabrun and naṣrun, and its pattern is fiʿl, not faʿlā. When it is said tatrā with the alif, its alif is a substitute for the tanwīn, as in ṣabartu ṣabran when pausing." This was rejected on the grounds that it has not been heard with the three vowels applied to the rāʾ, and whoever claims it must prove it. Also, its being written with a yāʾ rejects this view. What we have mentioned about ﴿tatrā﴾ being a verbal noun is the well-known view. It is also said that it is a plural, and it is said that it is a collective noun (ism jamʿ). On both views it is also a circumstantial qualifier.

His, exalted is He, statement ﴿Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) explaining the coming of each messenger to his nation. Since they denied him at the time of conveying the message, the "coming" may mean either the conveying or the literal arrival, to indicate that they denied him at the very first encounter. The attribution of "messenger" to "nation," together with the attribution of "all of them" earlier to the first-person plural of majesty, serves to establish that each messenger came to his specific nation, not that all of them came to all nations. It also indicates the complete repugnance and error of the deniers, in that they denied the particular messenger sent to them. It is also said that He, exalted is He, attributed the messenger to the sending toward Him, exalted and majestic, and to the coming to those to whom he was sent, because the sending, which is the starting point of the matter, is from Him, exalted is He, and the coming, which is its endpoint, is to them.

﴿So We made them follow one another﴾ in destruction, just as some of them followed others in committing its cause, which is denying the messenger. ﴿And We made them into tales﴾: ﴿aḥādīth﴾ is the plural of uḥdūthah (a story that is told out of wonder or for amusement), like aʿājīb, the plural of ʿujūbah (something one marvels at). That is, We made them into stories told in a manner of wonder and amusement. According to al-Akhfash, uḥdūthah is used only for evil.

It is permitted that it be the plural of ḥadīth, which is an irregular plural contrary to analogy, like qaṭīʿ and aqāṭīʿ. Al-Zamakhsharī calls it a collective noun (ism jamʿ). The meaning is: "We destroyed them, and nothing remained but their news." ﴿So away with a people who do not believe﴾: here He limited their description to their not believing, just as He limited the account of their denial to a summary. As for the earlier generations, when the excess and transgression beyond bounds in disbelief and aggression that was mentioned about them is related, they are described as wrongdoers.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 45:

﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs﴾, that is, with the well-known signs, which are the nine signs, and the discussion of their detail and what has been said about them has already passed. ( Harun ) is either a substitute (badal) or an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan). He is mentioned as Musa's brother, peace be upon them both, to indicate that he followed Musa in being sent. ﴿and a clear authority﴾, that is, a manifest proof or one that makes the truth evident. What is meant by it, according to some, is the staff, and it is mentioned separately although it falls under the signs, because it is distinguished by its qualities, to the point that it becomes like something other than them. It is also permitted that what is meant by it is the signs themselves, and the conjunction is then a conjunction of two things that are identical in referent, because their concepts differ, like the conjunction of an attribute upon an attribute while the essence is one, and a parallel of this has passed just above. Or it may be like your saying: "I passed by the man and the blessed soul," where "clear authority" is stripped off from the signs themselves and joined to them for emphasis. Its being mentioned in the singular is because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar), or because of the unity of what is intended. It is related from al-Hasan that what is meant by the signs are the religious obligations, and by the clear authority the miracle. Abu Hayyan said: It is permissible that what is meant by the signs is the miracles themselves, and by the clear authority the manner of their indication, because although they share with the signs of the prophets, peace be upon them, the basic indication of truthfulness, they differ in the strength of their indication of that. This is as you see. It is possible to say: What is meant by the authority is Musa's, peace be upon him, dominance in discourse and reasoning concerning the Creator, may He be exalted and glorified, and the strength of his resolve and his boldness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 46:

﴿To Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, i.e., the nobles of his people. They were singled out for mention because the sending of the Children of Israel, which was the matter for which the two of them (peace be upon them both) had been sent, depends on their opinions. It is also possible that by al-Mala' (the chiefs) is meant his people in general, since this term has been used in the sense of "the community" without restriction. ﴿But they acted arrogantly﴾ by refusing to submit to what they were commanded and called to, namely faith, the sending of the Children of Israel, and the abandoning of their torment. The call was not confined to the sending of the Children of Israel and their release from bondage, for in Surah [al-Nazi'at: 17-19] ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾ ﴿Then say, "Would you like to purify yourself?"﴾ ﴿And I would guide you to your Lord, so you would fear Him﴾. And also, in what we are discussing there is something that indicates that the call was not restricted to this.

﴿And they were a haughty people﴾: arrogant, or overbearing through oppression and injustice. The meaning is that exaltation (ʿuluww) was their habit.

﴿So they said﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿they were arrogant﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ) that establishes the arrogance. The meaning is that they said among themselves, by way of counsel: ﴿Shall we believe two humans like us?﴾ He used the dual of "human" (basharayn) because bashar is used for one person, as in His words ﴿a perfect human being﴾ [Maryam: 17], and it is used for the plural, as in His words ﴿If you see any human being﴾ [Maryam: 26]. He did not make "like" (mithl) dual, looking at the fact that it has the status of a verbal noun (maṣdar). Had he used bashar in the singular, it would have been correct, since it is a collective noun (ism jins) that applies to one and to more. The same holds if he had made mithl dual, for it occurs in the dual in His words ﴿they see them as twice their number﴾ and in the plural in His words, glory be to Him, ﴿then they will not be like you﴾, looking at the fact that it functions as an adjective. However, the preferred reading is the dual in the first case and the singular in the second: the dual with the first indicates how few the two were and how isolated they were from their people, despite the large number of the chiefs and their assembly, while the singular with the second indicates how closely they resembled each other, so that they were with the two humans as though they were one thing. This is more indicative of what they intended.

These stories, as you see, indicate that the basis of the resemblance of those who deny prophethood is the analogy of the state of the prophets, peace be upon them, to their own states. This rests on their ignorance of the details of the affairs of human reality and of the variation among its individuals on the ascending levels of perfection and the descending depths of deficiency. Some of them are at the highest of the high (ʿIlliyyin), namely those singled out by pure souls, supported by holy power, who, because their essences are pure, are connected to both the subtle and the dense worlds. They receive from one side and convey to the other, and their attachment to the interests of creatures does not prevent them from devoting themselves to the presence of the Real. Others are at the lowest of the low, and they are like those ignorant ones who are like cattle, nay, they are further astray in the way.

It is strange that they were not content for prophethood to belong to a human, while most of them were content for divinity to belong to a stone. May God fight them; how ignorant they are. The interrogative particle (hamza) here expresses denial, meaning: we will not believe two humans like us. ﴿And their people﴾ means the rest of the Children of Israel, ﴿are servants to us﴾, meaning they are serving us, obeying us, subject to us like slaves. In ﴿servants﴾ (ʿābidūn) there is a subsidiary metaphor (istiʿāra tabaʿiyya), looking at the common usage of the language.

Al-Khafaji reported from al-Raghib that he stated explicitly that ʿābid in the sense of servant is literal. Abu ʿUbayda said: the Arabs call everyone who submits to a king an ʿābid. Al-Zamakhshari allowed reading it as the literal sense of worship, for Pharaoh claimed divinity and so claimed worship from the people in the literal sense.

It is objected that the apparent meaning is that this statement came from the chiefs, and this rejects that reading. Their having said it through the tongue of Pharaoh is like the way the elite of a king say: "We are people of a large subject population and a vast, wide kingdom," intending that "our king has a subject population," and so on, which is contrary to the apparent meaning. It has also been said, on the assumption that the speaker is Pharaoh, that his claim of divinity does not necessarily entail that the Children of Israel worshipped him, or that he believed or claimed that they worshipped him in the literal sense. You know that once it is granted that the speaker is Pharaoh and that he claimed divinity, this does not preclude that by ʿibād (servants) he meant literal servitude, even if he did not believe in it, because, as some reports indicate, he often displays the opposite of what he conceals, to the point that these reports indicate that his claim of divinity was of this kind. Yes, the first interpretation, explaining ﴿servants﴾ as ﴿serve﴾ in the sense of ﴿obey﴾, is one that can be ascribed to Pharaoh and his chiefs. It seems they intended by this a disparagement of the two Messengers, peace be upon them, and a lowering of their exalted rank from the station of messengerhood, from another angle besides their humanity. The lām in ﴿to us﴾ is connected to ﴿servants﴾, and it was placed before it for the sake of the rhyme (fawāṣil). It has also been said that it is for restriction, meaning: they are servants to us, not to them two. The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of ﴿we believe﴾, emphasizing the denial of belief in them two, on the basis of their corrupt assumption, which is founded on analogizing religious leadership to worldly leadership, which depends on precedence in attaining worldly fortunes of wealth and status, just as the Quraysh did when they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two towns?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. Their ignorance is that the criterion for being chosen for messengerhood is precedence in acquiring exalted qualities and noble dispositions, which God, exalted is He, bestows as a favor on whom He wills of His creatures.

[Page 37]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 48:

﴿So they denied them both.﴾ They persisted in their denial of them, insisted upon it, and acted arrogantly with great arrogance. ﴿So they were among those who were destroyed.﴾ By drowning in the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea). The sequence (ta'qib) is considered in terms of the last part of the period of denial in which they persisted. It has also been said: the sequencing of the denial with that (destruction) is based on the premise that the intended meaning is that they were sentenced to destruction. It has also been said: the fa' is purely causal (al-sababiyyah), i.e., "so they were, because of their denial of the two messengers, among those who were destroyed."

﴿And We certainly gave﴾ after their destruction and the deliverance of the Children of Israel from their kingdom, ﴿Musa the Book﴾, meaning the Tawrat (Torah). Since Musa (peace be upon him) was given it to guide his people to the truth, as is the nature of divine books, it is as though they (the Children of Israel) were given it. Thus it is said: ﴿so that they may be guided﴾, meaning to the path of truth in knowledge and in action, because of what it contained of matters of belief (i'tiqadiyyat) and matters of practice (amaliyyat).

It is also permissible that the statement contains an elided noun (mudaf, an omitted word that must be understood), meaning: "We gave the people of Musa," and the pronoun in ﴿so that they may be guided﴾ refers to them. It has also been said that by "Musa" (peace be upon him) is meant his people, as one says "Tamim" and "Thaqif" for the tribe. This was criticized on the grounds that what is known in such usage is the naming of the tribe after its ancestor (abu al-qabilah), whereas the use of "Musa" for his people does not belong to this category, although there is no objection to it in principle. The pronoun in ﴿so that they may be guided﴾ was not taken to refer to Fir'awn and his chiefs (mala'ihi), because it is evident that the Torah was revealed only after their drowning of the Children of Israel. It may be supported by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ [al-Qasas: 43], on the basis that what is meant by "the earlier generations" includes Fir'awn and his people and those before them among the destroyed, such as the people of Nuh (Noah) and Hud, and not merely those nations destroyed before them. This is because the restriction of the report of Musa's receiving the Book to being after the destruction of the earlier nations is already known; so if Fir'awn and his people were not included, there would be no benefit in it, as has been said.

Harun (Aaron) is not mentioned along with Musa, peace be upon them both, for brevity, by limiting the mention to the one who is, as it were, the origin of the giving. It has also been said that this is because the Book was revealed at Mount Tur, and Harun (peace be upon him) was absent with the Children of Israel.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 50:

﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ That is, a sign indicating the great extent of Our power through his birth from her without contact with a human. The sign is one matter shared by both of them, and therefore it was stated in the singular (ufridat).

He also permitted that the speech be understood with an elided noun (taqdir mudaf), meaning: We made the condition of the son of Mary and his mother a sign; or: We made the son of Mary and his mother possessors of a sign. And that it be understood with the elision of "sign" from the first clause because the second indicates it, or the reverse, meaning: We made the son of Mary a sign, since there appeared in him, peace be upon him, extraordinary acts (khawariq) such as his speaking in the cradle with what he said as a child, his raising of the dead, his healing of the blind and the leper, and other things as an adult; and We made his mother a sign in that she gave birth without contact.

Al-Hasan said: she, peace be upon her, also spoke in her childhood, when she said: ﴿It is from God; indeed God provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37], and she never put a breast in her mouth. 

Al-Khafaji said: "You may say that explaining the singular of 'sign' by what has been mentioned is only needed if it is intended that she is a sign of God's power. But if it means a miracle (mu'jizah) or a preparatory sign (irhas), then it is not, because it belongs to 'Isa, peace be upon him, for his prophethood, not to Mary." End of quote. What he says is not hidden from us, but the view I hold is what was previously stated. The expression of 'Isa, peace be upon him, as "son of Mary," and of Mary as "his mother," is to indicate from the outset the aspect of both of them being a sign. His being related to her, even though relations are normally to fathers, indicates that he has no father. That is: We made the son of Mary alone, without having a father, and his mother who bore him alone, without the father's participation, a sign. His being mentioned first, peace be upon him, is because he is the principal in what has been mentioned of being a sign, as it has been said that the mention of his mother first in the words of God Almighty: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91] is because she is the principal in what is attributed to her of chastity and the breathing (of the spirit).

Then know that what the Muslim scholars agree upon is that Mary has no son other than 'Isa, peace be upon him.

Some Christians, may God fight them, claimed that after she bore 'Isa she married Yusuf the carpenter and bore three sons by him. The principal view among them is that she was, in her youth, betrothed to Yusuf the carpenter, who contracted marriage with her but did not approach her. When he saw her pregnant with 'Isa, peace be upon him, he intended to release her; but he saw in a dream an angel who informed him of the reality of the situation. When she gave birth she remained with him together with 'Isa, peace be upon him, and he began to raise him and care for him along with children he had from another wife. As for her, he never approached her at all. The Muslims do not accept that she was contracted to Yusuf, but they accept that she was his betrothed and that he cared for her and cared for 'Isa, peace be upon him, and they say: that was due to his kinship with her.

﴿And We gave them refuge﴾ That is, We made them take shelter ﴿on a height﴾, which is that which rises from the earth, short of a mountain.

The interpretation here has differed. Waki', Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn 'Asakir narrated with a sound chain from Ibn 'Abbas that he said regarding the words of God Most High: ﴿on a height﴾: "We have been informed that it is Damascus." Ibn 'Asakir narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Salam, from Yazid ibn Shajarah the Companion, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and from Qatadah from al-Hasan that they said: "The height is Damascus." Regarding this there is a raised (marfu') hadith narrated by Ibn 'Asakir from Abu Umamah with a weak chain.

A group narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "It is ar-Ramlah in Palestine," and Ibn Mardawayh narrated this from his hadith as a raised report.

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and a group, narrated from Murrah al-Bahazi who said: "I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: The height is ar-Ramlah." Ibn Jarir and others narrated from al-Dahhak that he said: "It is Bayt al-Maqdis." He and others also narrated from Qatadah that he said: "We were told that the height is Bayt al-Maqdis." They also mentioned from Ka'b that its land is the navel of the earth and the nearest of it to the heaven by eighteen miles, and for this reason the Mi'raj and the raising of 'Isa, peace be upon him, were from it. This view is more consistent with the application of "height" to what you have heard of its meaning. Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Wahb and Ibn Jarir and others from Ibn Zayd that the height is Egypt. It is also narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam that he said: "It is Alexandria." They mentioned that every village of Egypt is on a high elevation, because the Nile in its flooding covers all its land; so if the villages were not on the hills they would be drowned. He mentioned that the reason for this sheltering was that the king of that time intended to kill 'Isa, peace be upon him, so his mother fled with him to one of these places that were mentioned. Thus in al-Bahr. 

I have seen in the Gospel of Matthew that when 'Isa, peace be upon him, was born in Bethlehem in the days of King Herod, a group of Magi came from the East to Jerusalem saying: "Where is the one born king of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the East and have come to worship him." When Herod heard, he was troubled and gathered the chief priests and scribes of the people, and asked them where the Messiah would be born. They said: "In Bethlehem." Then he secretly summoned the Magi and determined from them the time when the star appeared to them, and sent them to Bethlehem and said to them: "Search diligently for this child, and when you find him, inform me so that I may worship him with you." They went and found him with Mary, and they prostrated and offered gifts, and they saw in a dream that they should not return to Herod, so they went back to their country. Yusuf saw in a dream an angel saying to him: "Arise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and stay there until I tell you, for Herod intends to seek the child to destroy him." So he arose and took the child and his mother by night and went to Egypt, and he remained there until the death of Herod. When Herod died, Yusuf saw the angel in a dream saying: "Arise, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child's life are dead." So he arose and took them and came to the land of Israel. When he heard that Archelaus had become king over Judea after his father Herod, he feared to go there, and he was warned in a dream, and he went to the borders of Galilee and settled in a city called Nazareth. End of quote. If this is correct, then it is apparent that the height is in the land of Egypt or Nazareth in the land of Syria, and God Most High knows best.

Most of the readers read "rubwah" with a damma on the ra', and this is the dialect of Quraysh.

Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i read "ribwah" with a kasra, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "rubah" with a damma on the ra' and with an alif. Zayd ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with both of them, al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, al-Farazdaq, and al-Sulami, according to what Sahib al-Lawami transmitted, read it with a fatha and with an alif. It was also read with a kasra and with an alif: ﴿dhat qarar﴾, meaning settled, of level land, and the intended meaning is that it is in a spacious valley in which the soul of whoever dwells there is expanded. Mujahid said: "possessing fruits and crops." The intended meaning is that it is a suitable place for people to settle in, because of the crops and fruits in it, and this is more fitting with the words of God Most High: ﴿and a spring (ma'in)﴾, meaning a flowing water. Its form is fa'il, with the mim being original, from the meaning of flowing. Its root is extending in a thing, and from it comes "amana al-nazar" (he looked intently).

In al-Bahr: "ma'ana al-shay'a ma'anatan" means it increased; or it is from al-ma'un. Its application to flowing water is due to its benefit. It was also permitted that its form be maf'ul, like makhit, with the mim being augmentative, from 'anahu, he reached it with his eye, like rakabahu when he struck him with his knee. Its application to flowing water is because it is usually apparent and visible to the eye. He described the water with this because it gathers the expansion of the chest, the pleasantness of the place, and the abundance of benefits.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 51:

﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾ is a narration (hikayah) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a general manner, of what every messenger in his era was addressed with. It is placed after the narration of the sheltering of ʿIsa and his mother, peace be upon them both, upon the elevated ground, as a notification that the arrangement of the foundations of blessings was not among the special features of ʿIsa, peace be upon him; rather, the permission of good things is an ancient law (shar') upon which all the messengers, peace be upon them, proceeded, and they were enjoined with it. That is, it was said to each messenger: "Eat of the good things and do righteous deeds." He expressed those multiple commands related to the messengers in the plural form when narrating, as a summary for the sake of brevity; or as a narration of what was said to ʿIsa and his mother, peace be upon them both, when they were sheltered upon the elevated ground, so that they might follow the messengers in partaking of what they were provided. As if it were said: "We sheltered them to an elevated ground having a place of rest and a spring, and We said, or [We were] saying to them," that is, "We informed them, or [We were] instructing them, that all the messengers were addressed with this: so eat and act, following them." It is also permitted that it be a call (nida') to ʿIsa, peace be upon him, and a command to him to eat of the good things.

For there has come in a mursal hadith from Hafs ibn Abi Jabalah, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said concerning His statement, Exalted is He, "O messengers" etc.: "That is ʿIsa son of Maryam; he used to eat from the spinning of his mother." And from al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi that it is a call to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and an address to him, and the plural is for glorification. Al-Nisaburi preferred this. What occurred in the commentary on al-Talkhis, following al-Radi, that the intent of glorification by the plural form in other than the first-person pronoun did not occur in the ancient speech, is an error, since it is abundant in the speech of the Arabs absolutely, indeed in all languages; al-Tha'alibi has explicitly stated this in Fiqh al-Lughah. The meaning of "the good things," according to what Shaykh al-Islam and others chose, is what is found pleasant and delightful of permissible foods and fruits, and it was argued for by the fact that the context requires it, and the command is for permission and enjoyment. In it is a refutation of the monasticism (rahbaniyyah) which the Christians innovated. It was also said that the meaning of "the good things" is what is lawful (halal), and the command is obligatory (taklifi); it is supported by its being followed by His statement, Exalted is He, "And do righteous deeds," that is, a righteous deed. It may also be supported by what Ahmad recorded in al-Zuhd, and Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, from Umm ʿAbd Allah, sister of Shaddad ibn Aws, may Allah be pleased with her, that she sent to the Prophet ﷺ a bowl of milk at his breaking of the fast while he was fasting. He sent his messenger back to her: "From where is this milk for you?" She said: "From a sheep of mine." He sent back to her: "From where is the sheep for you?" She said: "I bought it with my own wealth." So he drank from it, peace and blessings be upon him. When the next day came, Umm ʿAbd Allah came to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I sent you milk and you sent back the messenger to me with it." So he ﷺ said to her: "With this were the messengers before me commanded: that they should not eat except what is good, and not act except righteously."

Likewise with what Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and others recorded from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'O people, Allah, Exalted is He, is Good and accepts only what is good. Allah, Exalted is He, commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, so He said: "O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds" [23:51], and He said: "O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided you" [2:172].' Then he mentioned the man who prolongs the journey, disheveled and dusty, whose food is unlawful, whose drink is unlawful, whose clothing is unlawful, and who is nourished with the unlawful, who raises his hands to the sky: O Lord, O Lord! How then could he be answered?'"

And the priority given to the command to eat the lawful is because eating the lawful helps in righteous deeds.

It has come in some reports that Allah, Exalted is He, does not accept the worship of one in whose belly is a morsel of the unlawful. And it is authentically related: "Any flesh that grew from something unlawfully gained, the Fire is more deserving of it." Perhaps the priority of the first command, on the interpretation that the good is what is delightful of permissible things, is because it is more fitting to His statement, Exalted is He, "And We sheltered them to an elevated ground having a place of rest and a spring." And in the command after it to do righteous deeds there is an exhortation to gratitude.

﴿Indeed I, of what you do﴾ of the apparent and hidden deeds ﴿am All-Knowing﴾, so I will recompense you for it. In al-Bahr it is stated that this is a warning to the messengers, peace be upon them, in outward form, while the intended audience is their followers.

And indeed this, [i.e., the creed (millah) and the law (shari'ah)], which is pointed to with "this" to indicate the full clarity of its matter in soundness and rectitude, and its being ordered by that into the line of visible affairs, [is] your community, i.e., your creed and your law. The address is to the Messengers, peace be upon them, in the manner already mentioned. It was also said that it is general, for them and for others, and this was narrated from Mujahid. The clause, as al-Khafaji said, is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause [that precedes it]: ﴿Indeed I am Knowing of what you do﴾. So the "wa" is part of the quoted speech. It was also said that it is part of the reporting (hikayah), and that [the speaker] has coordinated one saying with another, and the implied meaning is: "We said, O Messengers, eat…" etc., and "We said to them: Indeed this is your community." Its remoteness is not hidden.

It was said: the "wa" is not for coordination, and the clause after it is a new, independent sentence, not coordinated with what precedes it. But this is, as you see, [weak]. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿one community﴾, is a circumstantial clause (ḥal) derived from the predicate (khabar), and the element governing it is the sense of the demonstrative, meaning: I point to it while it is a single shari'ah
page 41
in the fundamental principles which do not change with the change of eras. It was also said that ﴿this﴾ refers to the communities of the earlier Messengers, and the meaning is that this, your group, is one group, united upon faith and the oneness of worship. ﴿And I am your Lord﴾, i.e., without anyone having a share in lordship with Me. This clause is coordinated with the clause "indeed this" etc., which is itself coordinated with what came before. Both fall within the scope of the causal explanation for righteous deeds, because the apparent meaning is that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed I am Knowing of what you do﴾, is the reason for that. Perhaps what is meant by righteous deeds is that which includes sound beliefs and correct actions. That reward and lordship require this is evident. As for the requirement that the unity of the law in its unchanging fundamentals [entails] this, it is on the basis that it is evidence of the truth of the beliefs, and the reality of the beliefs requires performing them, and performing them requires performing other righteous deeds. Rather, it was said: belief is not valid together with abandoning action. On this basis, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so fear Me﴾ is like an explicit statement of the conclusion, and the discourse is similar to your saying: "The world is originated, because it is changing, and everything changing is originated, so the world is originated."

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim it is stated that the pronoun of address in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿your Lord﴾ and in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿so fear Me﴾ is for the Messengers and the communities all together, on the basis that the command with respect to the Messengers is for stirring up and inciting, and with respect to the community is for warning and obligation. The "fa'" (so) is for the ordering of the command, or the obligation of complying with it, upon what precedes it of the exclusivity of lordship to Him, glorified is He, and the unity of the community, for each of these requires taqwa (God-consciousness) absolutely. The meaning is: "so fear Me" in [avoiding] splitting the staff (i.e., causing division) and opposition, by failing to fulfill what is required by what has been mentioned.

The Two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Abu 'Amr read "wa-anna" with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the nun. This is explained by assuming a preposition: i.e., "and because indeed this…" The prepositional phrase is connected to "fa-ttaqun" (so fear Me). Al-Khafaji said: the discussion of the "fa'" that enters upon it is like the discussion of the "fa'" in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So fear Me alone﴾, and it is for causation and for coordination with what precedes it, which is "work righteousness" (a'malu). The meaning is: "Fear Me, because the intellects agree upon My lordship, and the sound beliefs require taqwa." End of his words. And it is not free of something. It was also permitted that, on this reading, "indeed this…" be coordinated with "what you do," and the meaning would be: "Indeed I know what you do and that this, your community, is one community…", so it falls within the scope of what is known. This was judged weak, because there is no eloquence in the meaning on this basis. It was also said that it is the object of an omitted verb, i.e., "and know that this is your community…", and this omitted verb is coordinated with "work righteousness." It is not hidden that this estimation is contrary to the apparent sense.

Ibn 'Amir read "wa-anna" with a fatha on the hamza and a light nun (takhfif), taking it as the light form of the heavy "anna." The justification of the fatha is known from what we have mentioned.

﴿فَتَقَطَّعُوا أمْرَهُمْ﴾ [So they split their affair]: The pronoun (in *amrahum*, "their affair") refers to what is implied by *al-ummah* (the community), whether it means "the religion" (*al-millah*) and its adherents, or "the group." It is also permissible that *al-ummah* at first means "the religion," and that the pronoun, when it returns to it, means "the group." This is an instance of *al-istikhdam* (a rhetorical device in which one term is used in one sense and a pronoun referring back to it is used in another). The purpose is to relate what appeared among the nations of the messengers, peace be upon them, of opposition to the command. The *fa'* (so) indicates that their disobedience follows the command, in order to intensify the condemnation of their state. *Taqta'a* is used in the sense of *qata'a*, just as *taqaddama* is used in the sense of *qadama*. The "affair" refers to the affair of their religion, either by supposing an omitted noun (*mudaf*) or by treating the genitive construction as referring to a known matter (*'ahdiyyah*). That is, they split the affair of their religion and made it into different religions, although it is one. It is also permissible that *al-taqatta'* means *al-tafarruq* (dispersal). *Amrahum* is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning: "they scattered and formed factions regarding their affair." According to this reading, *amrahum* may also be an accusative of specification (*tamyiz*, a noun that clarifies the sense of a preceding term) according to the Kufan grammarians (*al-Kufiyyin*), who permit the definite form of the *tamyiz*. ﴿بَيْنَهم زُبُرًا﴾ [among themselves into scriptures]: that is, into pieces. *Zuburan* is the plural of *zabur*, in the sense of "a part." This is supported by the reading «زُبَرًا» with a *damma* on the *zay* and a *fatha* on the *ba'*, which is well known and established as the plural of *zubrah*, in the sense of "a piece." It is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) relating to «أمْرَهُمْ» or to the *waw* of «تَقْطَعُوا», or a second object (*maf'ul thani*), since the verb is implicitly used in the sense of *ju'ilu* ("they were made"). It has also been said that it is the plural of *zabur*, in the sense of "a book," from *zabarat* in the sense of *kataba* ("she wrote"), and that it is the second object of *taqta'u*, which is implicitly used in the sense of making, meaning: they split the affair of their religion, making it into books.

It is also permissible that it is a circumstantial accusative relating to «أمْرَهُمْ», if *taqta'u* is considered intransitive, meaning: they scattered regarding their affair, its state being like the heavenly scriptures among them. It has been said that it is a stipulated circumstantial accusative (*hal muqaddarah*), or an accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning: "in scriptures." The interpretation of *zuburan* as "scriptures" was related by a group of narrators from Qatadah, as in *al-Durr al-Manthur*, but its meaning is obscure in this sense and it hardly holds except by an interpretation. Reflect on this.

It was also read «زُبَرًا» with a sukun on the *ba'* for ease, like *rusul* becoming *rusl*, as in «رُسُلٍ» [a form of *rusul*]. Here ﴿فَتَقَطَّعُوا﴾ comes with the *fa'*, signaling that this split followed the command immediately, and this carries an intensification of blame, as we have indicated. In Surat al-Anbiya' it comes with *waw*, which allows the meaning of *fa'* and also allows that their splitting was delayed after the command. Here comes ﴿وأنا رَبُّكم فاتَّقُونِ﴾ [And I am your Lord, so fear Me], which is more emphatic in warning and admonition than what comes there, namely His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿وأنا رَبُّكم فاعْبُدُونِ﴾ [And I am your Lord, so worship Me] (21:92). This is because the present verse comes after the destruction of many groups, the people of Noah and the nations after them. In that surah, although the story of Noah and what precedes it also came first, what followed it was a sign of complete kindness and gentleness in the stories of Job, Zechariah and Mary. Therefore the command to worship fits one whose attribute is this, may He be exalted and glorified. This is what Abu Hayyan said. What he mentioned first is not fully sufficient for the purpose, and what he mentioned second has been objected to: it is based on the premise that the verse is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) to the preceding stories, or to the story of Jesus, peace be upon him, as the beginning of a new discourse. In that case it would not yield this meaning unless it is meant that it occurred in the narration for this particular connection. Reflect.

﴿كُلُّ حِزْبٍ﴾ [Every party] of those who formed factions ﴿بِما لَدَيْهِمْ﴾ [with what they have] of the affair they have chosen ﴿فَرِحُونَ﴾ [rejoicing]: pleased, delighted, with open hearts. The meaning is that they are pleased with it, believing it to be the truth. In this there is a condemnation of those factions, of a sort that is contained in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 54:

﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time.﴾ This is an address to him (ﷺ) concerning the Quraysh, who fragmented over the matter of the true religion. Al-ghamrah (the overwhelming flood, i.e., the water that covers the stature of a man) is, in origin, from concealment (al-sitr), and what is meant by it is ignorance, by way of the common element of overpowering and engulfing. It is as if, when Allah, glorified is He, mentioned, within the account of what occurred among the nations of the Prophets, peace be upon them, their dispersal and their division over what ought to have been unified and agreed upon in religion, and their rejoicing in their false deeds and their worthless beliefs, He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): "Then leave them in their ignorance, this ignorance beyond which there is no ignorance, abandoning them, forsaking them, and indicating despair that the word would benefit them." Included in the consolation, in the mention of the limit, namely His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿until a time﴾, is that what is meant by that is the time when He kills them, which is the day of Badr, according to what is related from Muqatil; or their death in disbelief, which necessitates punishment; or their punishment. In the indefiniteness and the vagueness there is what is not hidden of awe-inspiring severity.

It is also permissible to say: He likened the state of these people, together with what they are upon of attempting falsehood and immersing themselves in it, to the state of one who enters a deep water for play, and the common element is the wasting of time after toil in work. The discourse in this case follows the pattern of its predecessor, namely His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Every faction, with what they have, rejoicing﴾. When they were made rejoicing in delusion, they were also made players. The first is more evident. The discourse may also be taken as a figurative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah) upon it; indeed, it is preferred by the eloquent, as is not hidden.

Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), Abu Haywah and al-Sulami read «fi ghamarātihim» in the plural, because each one of them has a ghamrah.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 55:

﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children,﴾ that is, what We give them and make an increase for them. Here "ma" (what) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), the noun of "anna" (that), and its being a relative pronoun does no harm, because it is so in the Imam (the master copy of the Qur'an) for a secret we do not know.

﻿[Page 43]

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿of wealth and children﴾ is an explanation of it. The placing of wealth before the children, although they are more honoured than it, has already had its reasoning explained.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 23, verse 56:

His statement, glorified is He: ﴿We hasten to them in good things﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of inna, and the linking element (al-ra'id, the pronoun referring back to the subject) is omitted. The meaning is: "Do they think that what We supply them with of wealth and children, We hasten to them with it in that wherein is their good and their honour?" This is on the basis that the interrogative hamza is for denying the reality and declaring it abhorrent. The omission of this returning element is due to the length of the speech, together with the prior mention of its counterpart in the relative clause (al-sila), although the omission of such a element is rare. Hisham ibn Mu'awiya said:

The linking element is the apparent noun, which is al-khayrat (الخَيْراتِ). It is as if the meaning were "We hasten to them in it," and then the noun was made apparent, so it is said "fi al-khayrat." This is consistent with the view of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat), who permitted the construction such as "Zayd qama Abu 'Abd Allah," when Abu 'Abd Allah is a kunya (teknonym) for Zayd. It has been said: it is not permissible that the predicate be ﴿from wealth and children﴾, because God Most High supplied them with that, so it is not blamed, and the belief in its increase is not condemned as they are, as the denying interrogative indicates. This was objected to: it is not far-fetched that what is meant is what We make an beneficial increase for them in the Hereafter, not wealth and children, but belief and righteous deeds, like His saying, Most High: ﴿The day when wealth will not benefit, nor children, except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 88]. And in this there is what there is.

What we have mentioned, that ma is a relative pronoun (mawsula), is the apparent view. As for one who permitted it to be a verbal noun (masdariyya), making the verbal noun formed after the composition (sabk) the subject of inna and its predicate "nusari'u" (We hasten), on the basis of the estimate "musara'a" (hastening), with the premise that the original was "an nusari'a," so that an was deleted and the verb became marfu' (nominative), the Noble Qur'an has not fulfilled its right. Likewise is the one who made it kaffa (a particle that removes the government of inna), as al-Kisa'i did, and Abu Hayyan transmitted this from him. He permitted pausing on "banin" (children) on this basis, explaining that what follows yahsabu (they think) has come to form a predicate and a subject in meaning, even if it is in the sense of a single noun. And this, as you see, is not so.

Ibn Wathhab read "innama numaddu-hum" with a kasra on the hamza of inna. Ibn Kathir, in one transmission, read "yumaddu-hum" with ya'.

Al-Sulami and Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra read "yusari'u" with ya' and kasra on the ra'. If its subject is the pronoun of God, Most High, then the discussion concerns the linking element as you have heard. If it is the pronoun of the relative noun, then that is the linking element. It is also reported from Ibn Abi Bakra mentioned that he read "yusari'u" with ya' and fath on the ra', in the passive voice. Al-Hurr al-Nahwi read "nusri'u" with nun, the present tense of asra'a. It was also read, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, "yusri'u" with ya', present tense of asra'a too, and its subject has the two possibilities already indicated.

﴿But they do not perceive﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon an implied element that the speech draws along with it. The meaning is: "No, We do not do that; rather they do not perceive," that is, it is not within their nature to perceive that they are, except like cattle, rather they are more astray, so that they might reflect and consider whether this is a respite (istidraj) or a hastening and an eagerness towards good things. From here it has been said: whoever disobeys God Most High, and sees no deficiency in what He, glorified is He, has given him of the world, let him know that he is being led on gradually and has been deceived. Qatada said: Do not judge people by their wealth and their children, but judge them by faith and righteous deeds.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verses 57–58:

﴿Indeed, those who are, out of fear of their Lord, apprehensive﴾ The discussion of this is similar to what passed regarding its counterpart in Surah al-Anbiya', except that the continuation of apprehension here, in this world and in the Hereafter, is for the believers without hesitation. ﴿And those who, in the signs of their Lord﴾ that are sent down and set up in the horizons and in the souls, ﴿believe﴾ — the bi' (ba') here denotes accompaniment (lil-mulabasah) and is connected to His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿believe﴾, meaning they affirm (yuşaddiqun). The intended meaning is affirming what they signify, since there is no praise in affirming their existence. The use of the present tense (al-mudari') rather than the noun form (al-ism) indicates that whenever they come upon a sign, they believe in it and affirm what it signifies.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verses 57–58:

﴿Indeed, those who are, out of fear of their Lord, apprehensive﴾ The discussion of this is similar to what passed regarding its counterpart in Surah al-Anbiya', except that the continuation of apprehension here, in this world and in the Hereafter, is for the believers without hesitation. ﴿And those who, in the signs of their Lord﴾ that are sent down and set up in the horizons and in the souls, ﴿believe﴾ — the bi' (ba') here denotes accompaniment (lil-mulabasah) and is connected to His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿believe﴾, meaning they affirm (yuşaddiqun). The intended meaning is affirming what they signify, since there is no praise in affirming their existence. The use of the present tense (al-mudari') rather than the noun form (al-ism) indicates that whenever they come upon a sign, they believe in it and affirm what it signifies.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 59:

﴿And those who do not associate anything with their Lord﴾ — that is, they devote their worship sincerely to Him, Mighty and Majestic. Thus the intended meaning is the negation of hidden association (al-shirk al-khafi), such as showing off in worship (al-riya'), so it is said.

Some of the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) have chosen generality, meaning: they do not associate anything with Him, the Exalted, neither open association (al-shirk al-jali) nor hidden association (al-shirk al-khafi). This is perhaps the better view. Their being described as believing in the signs of God, the Exalted, does not dispense with this.

It is also permitted that what is meant by what came before is their being described with tawhid al-rububiyyah (affirming God's lordship), and what is meant here is their being described with tawhid al-uluhiyyah (affirming God's sole right to worship). The first was not restricted to because most of the disbelievers are described with tawhid al-rububiyyah: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?", they would surely say, "God."﴾ [Luqman: 25; al-Zumar: 38]. And the mention of the title "Lord" (al-rububiyyah) does not contradict this, for it occurs in the three places to indicate causation (al-'illiyyah), and that title is suitable to be the reason for tawhid al-uluhiyyah, as is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 60:**

﴿And those who give what they give﴾, i.e., who give what they have given of charities, ﴿while their hearts are fearful﴾, fearing that it will not be accepted from them, and that it will not be performed in the fitting manner, so that they will be held to account for it. ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, al-Aʿmash, al-Hasan and al-Nakhaʿi recited:

*yaʾtūna mā ātaw* (they come with what they have brought), from *al-itiyān* (coming), not *al-ītāʾ* (giving) in either of them.

Ibn Mardawayh and Saʿid ibn Mansur narrated from ʿĀʾishah that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it in this way.

The exegetes (*mufassirūn*) applied to it the term "the recitation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)", meaning that the narrators (*muhaddithūn*) transmitted it from him (ﷺ), though the reciters (*qurrāʾ*) did not transmit it through their own chains. The meaning according to it is that they perform acts of worship as they have done, while their hearts are fearful. Something similar has also been reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir and a group narrated from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, regarding the saying of Allah, ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾, is it the man who steals, commits fornication and drinks wine, and yet fears Allah the Exalted?' He said: 'No, rather it is the man who fasts, gives charity and prays, and yet fears that Allah the Exalted will not accept it from him.'"

The clause *"qulūbuhum wajilah"* (their hearts are fearful) in both recitations is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to the plural pronoun in the first relative clause. The use of the present tense there indicates continuity, and in the second recitation it indicates certainty. The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿that they will return to their Lord﴾, are construed with an implied causal *lām* (the *lām* of cause), and it is connected with *wajilah* (fearful), meaning: fearful of non-acceptance and of not being performed in the fitting manner, because they will return to Him, the Exalted, and be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection. At that time the realities will be revealed, and the servant will need a deed that is accepted and fitting. ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7, 8].

It is also permitted that the phrase be construed with the *min* of origin (*ibtidāʾiyyah*), which the word *wajil* takes after it, meaning: fearful *of* the fact that their return is to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, on the basis that the object of the fear is that this (their deed) will not be accepted from them and will not be performed in the fitting manner, so that they will be held to account for it at that time, not merely the fact of their return to Him, the Mighty and Majestic. The first interpretation may be supported by the recitation of al-Aʿmash, *"annahum"* (with a kasra on the hamza). Perhaps the use of the nominal sentence, in which the return is expressed as a predicate rather than a verb in the present tense, is for emphasis on the certainty of the return, as if it were among established and continuous matters. So it has been said.

It is also permitted, though remotely, that the intended return mentioned is the return to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, through servanthood (*ʿubūdiyyah*). In that case the reason for using the nominal sentence is clearer than to be hidden. The reason for explaining the fear of non-acceptance, and of their deed not being performed in the fitting manner whatever it may be, by the fact that they return to Him, the Exalted, in servanthood, is that it is not obligatory for Him, may He be glorified, to accept their deed, since He is the Owner, and the owner may do with his property what he wills. And their deficiency, however they are, is manifest in comparison with His perfection, may His majesty be exalted. The deficient is likely not to produce what is fitting for the Perfect, especially when that Perfect is Allah the Mighty and Majestic, whose perfection has no end. I do not think you see in this aspect any burden other than the burden of the servant, so reflect.

Then, the four conjunctions (*mawāṣalāt*), according to what Shaykh al-Islam and others have said, refer to one single group characterized by what was mentioned within the scope of their connection among the four attributes, not to separate groups each characterized by one of the mentioned attributes. As if it were said: "Those who are fearful of their Lord's dread, and who believe in the signs of their Lord, etc." He repeated the relative pronoun only to signal that each of those attributes independently has a distinct, outstanding excellence of its own, and to treat each independent attribute as if it were the independent subject characterized by it. This applies to both recitations in His words, ﴿And those who give what they give﴾.

Al-ʿAllamah al-Tibi has a statement on this point that I do not think you will find agreeable, since in it he says that "those who do not associate anything with their Lord" and "those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful" are the sinners from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and that is extremely remote.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) has mentioned that the fourth attribute is the ultimate station of the *Ṣiddiqīn* (the truthful).
