Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 61:

﴿Ulā'ika﴾ (those) is a demonstrative referring to those mentioned, in view of their being characterized by those qualities; and the remoteness implied in it serves to indicate their high rank in excellence. It is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿they hasten to the good things﴾. The sentence formed by the subject and its predicate is the predicate of inna, and the discourse is a resumed sentence (isti'naf) introduced to explain who is entitled to hastening toward the good things, following the despair of the disbelievers regarding them and the refutation of their false assumption. That is: ﴿those﴾ who are described by the noble attributes detailed above, specifically and not those disbelievers, ﴿hasten to attain the good things﴾, among which are the immediate good things promised for righteous deeds, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 148], and His statement, glorified is He: ﴿And We gave him in this world a good, and indeed he in the Hereafter is among the righteous﴾ [al-Nahl: 122]. Thus He affirmed for them what was negated for their opposites, except that the style has been changed, for He did not say "those are hastened to by the good things," but rather attributed the hastening to them, indicating that they deserve to attain the good things through the excellence of their deeds. The choice of the particle fi (in) over ila (to) is to signal that they are immersed in the various kinds of good things, not that they are outside of them heading toward them by way of hastening, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133].

﴿And they are for it﴾, that is, for the good things, among which is what you have heard. The prepositional phrase is connected to His statement, exalted is He: ﴿foremost (sabiqun)﴾. This may be treated as if it were intransitive, meaning "those who perform the act of outstripping," or its object may be omitted, meaning "outstripping the people" or "outstripping the disbelievers." The verb is used with lam and with ila, so one says: "sabaqat ila kadha" and "li kadha." By their outstripping toward the good things is meant their attaining them and obtaining them.

Abu Hayyan made this sentence an emphasis of the first sentence. It was also said that sabiqun is transitive to the pronoun directly and the lam is extra (zā'ida), and the justification for its extra use is that the governing word is a secondary (far'i) form, and the pronoun object was placed before it, meaning: "and they are outstripping it." The meaning of their outstripping it is also intransitive in sense, namely attaining, meaning: "and they attain it before the Hereafter, since it is hastened for them in this world." So there is no objection to what has been said: if one thing outstrips another, it indicates that the outstripper precedes the outstripped; how then can it be said that "they outstrip the good things"? The need to intend the intransitive sense in this way is greater than in the previous way, and for this reason, even with the commitment to extra usage in it, it has been said that it is a strained interpretation.

It is also permissible that the intended meaning of the good things be acts of obedience, and the pronoun in ﴿for it﴾ refers to them as well, the lam being causal, and it is connected to what follows it. The meaning: they eagerly desire acts of obedience and worship with the utmost desire, and for their sake they are performers of outstripping, or for their sake they are outstrippers of people toward reward or toward Paradise. It was also permitted, on the assumption that the good things mean acts of obedience, that ﴿for it﴾ be the predicate of the subject, with ﴿foremost﴾ being a second predicate after a predicate. The meaning of ﴿they are for it﴾ is that they are prepared to perform the like of it from great matters. This is like your saying to one from whom a need is sought, when it is not hoped for from anyone else: "You are for it," and this is from the eloquent speech of the Arabs. On this is His statement:

"Difficult matters that have grown complex and overwhelmed us, O Messenger of Allah, you are for them."

Al-Tabari preferred this aspect on the grounds that the lam is firmly established in this meaning. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, is reported to have said something that is clear in making ﴿for it﴾ the predicate, though it is not clear in making the pronoun refer to the good things in the sense of acts of obedience. In al-Bahr, transmitted from him, the meaning is: happiness preceded for them in eternity, so they are for it. You know that most of these aspects are contrary to the apparent meaning, and that the first explanation of the good things is more fitting to the preceding verse. Some people claimed that the pronoun in ﴿for it﴾ refers to Paradise, and others claimed that it refers to the nations, and that is, as you see, far-fetched.

Al-Hurr al-Nahwi read "yusri'una" as the present tense of asra'a. It is said: "asra'at ila al-shay'" and "sari'at ilayhi" with one meaning. And "yusari'una," as al-Zajjaj said, is more emphatic than "yusri'una." Its justification is that the form of mufa'ala involves two parties, so it stirs the soul to outstrip, because whoever competes with you in something, you desire to surpass him in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 62:

﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah) brought in to encourage what He described those mentioned (ulaʾika al-mushar ilayhim) as doing, namely the performance of acts of obedience, by explaining its ease and that it does not exceed the bounds of capacity and obedience. That is: Our practice is such that We do not burden any soul among souls except with what is within its capacity and the measure of its strength. Some say the intended meaning is the continuity of the negation (istimrar al-nafy), by the aid of the context, not the negation of continuity. Or it is for granting leniency (al-tarkhis) regarding what falls short of the level of the deeds of those people, by explaining that He, exalted is He, does not burden His servants except with what is within their capacity; so if they do not reach the ranks of the foremost (al-sabiqun) in performing acts of obedience, there is no blame upon them after they have exerted their utmost effort and expended their capacity.

Muqatil said: Whoever cannot stand to pray, let him pray seated, and whoever cannot sit, let him pray by gesturing (ima').

His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And with Us is a Book that speaks with the truth﴾ is a completion of what precedes it, by explaining the states of the deeds they were charged with and the rulings consequent upon them of reckoning, reward and punishment. By "the Book" is meant the records of deeds which they read at the reckoning, as indicated by the description, as in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿This is Our Book, which speaks against you with the truth; indeed We used to have copied down what you were doing﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 29]. "The truth" (al-haqq) is that which corresponds to reality, and its "speaking" is a metaphor for its manifestation; that is: with Us is a Book that manifests the truth corresponding to reality as it is, in essence and attribute, and makes it clear to the beholder just as speech makes it clear and displays it to the hearer. Thus there will become manifest there the grand and the subtle of deeds, and reward will follow from them: if good, then good; and if evil, then evil. It has been said: the intended meaning of "the Book" is records they will read, in which is what was established for them in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) of recompense; but this is weaker than the first view. And among what is said to be meant by it is the noble Qur'an; and His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ serves to explain His, glorified and exalted is He, grace and His justice in recompense in the most complete manner, following the explanation of His subtle kindness in imposing obligations and recording deeds as they are. That is: they will not be wronged in the recompense by diminishing reward or increasing punishment; rather they will be recompensed according to the measure of their deeds which they were charged with and which their records spoke of truthfully. It is also permitted that it be a confirmation of what preceded regarding imposition and recording of deeds; that is: they will not be wronged by being charged with what is beyond their capacity, nor by having some of their deeds recorded—among which are the deeds of those who are not among the foremost—on the basis that these fall short of the rank of the deeds of the foremost; rather each one is recorded according to its measure and its grade.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 63:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿Nay, their hearts are in confusion about this.﴾ It is an idrab (a transitional turning away, shifting from the preceding topic) from what came before it and a return to describing the state of the disbelievers. The pronoun (damir) refers to the disbelievers, meaning: Nay, the hearts of the disbelievers are in heedlessness and ignorance of this which is explained in the Qur'an, namely that with Him, exalted is He, there is a Book

[Page 47]

that speaks with the truth, and their evil deeds will be displayed to them before the witnesses, and they will be recompensed for them, as is indicated by what will come, if God the Exalted wills, in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed My verses were recited to you﴾ etc. It has also been said: the reference is to the noble Qur'an and what it explains in general, and this was narrated from Mujahid. It has also been said:

it refers to what those described as doing righteous deeds are upon, and this was narrated from Qatada. It has been said: it refers to the religion as a whole. It has been said: it refers to the Prophet ﷺ. The first view is the most apparent. ﴿And they have deeds﴾, many evil deeds, ﴿beyond that﴾, that which was mentioned, namely their hearts being in confusion about what was mentioned. These are the various kinds of their disbelief and sins, among which is their slandering of the noble Qur'an, referred to in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Arrogant about it, talking nightly, abusing.﴾

Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the intended meaning of ghamra (confusion) is the disbelievers and doubt, and that ﴿that﴾ is a reference to what was just mentioned, and the meaning is: they have deeds beyond disbelief. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Qatada that ﴿that﴾ (in the sense of "like this") is a reference to what the believers were described as doing of righteous deeds, meaning: they have deeds that go beyond what the believers were described as doing, that is, the opposites of what they were described as doing, which fall within the scope of the relative clauses (silat, the clauses that complete a relative construction). This is the utmost in censure for them. ﴿They are doing them﴾, meaning: they persist in them, are habituated to doing them, and are harmed by them, not weaned from them. (And ﴿doing﴾) is a verb governing the pronoun before it, and the lam is for emphasis.

Abu Muslim said: the pronoun in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Nay, they﴾ etc. refers to the believers described with the attributes mentioned earlier, as if He, glorified is He, said after describing them: ﴿And We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, and its limit is what these fearful ones have brought, ﴿and with Us is a Book that records their deeds, speaking with the truth, so they will not be wronged﴾, but rather their reward for their deeds will be paid to them in full. Then He, glorified is He, described them with bewilderment in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Nay, their hearts are in confusion﴾. It is as if He, the Exalted and Majestic, said: they, despite that fear and dread, are like those bewildered about their deeds, whether they are accepted or rejected. ﴿And they have deeds beyond that﴾, meaning: they also have supererogatory acts and the various forms of good they are upon, end of quotation. The Imam said: this is preferable, because when it is possible to refer the speech to what is connected to it, namely the mention of the fearful ones, it is better than referring it to what is further removed from it, especially since a person may desire to do good by mentioning that his deeds are preserved, just as he warns against evil by it. A person may also be described, due to the intensity of his thinking about the matter of his afterlife, as having his heart in confusion, and it is meant that the thought has taken possession of him regarding the acceptance of his deed, whether he brought it, and whether he performed it as required or fell short. This, according to this view, is an indication of their apprehension and fear. End of quotation. What is in it is not hidden from one whose heart is not in confusion.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 23, verse 64:

﴿Until, when We seize their affluent ones with punishment﴾ ḥattā (until), according to what is in al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary), is the one after which speech begins, and it is at the same time a limit (ghayah) for what precedes it. It is as if it were said: they will continue doing their deeds until, when We seize them, etc. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is only a beginning (ibtida'), and nothing more. The first and second idhā both prevent it from being a limit for ʿāmilūn (the verb "they are doing"). There is an issue here. The idhā is conditional, its condition is ﴿We seized﴾ (akhadhnā), and it is annexed to it. Its response is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿idhā hum yajʾarūn (then they cry out)﴾. It is governed by it. The idhā in it is sudden (fujā'iyyah), standing in the place of the fa' (of the response). Al-Hawfi said: ḥattā is a limit, and it is coordinating (ʿāṭifah). Idhā is an adverb annexed to what follows it, containing the meaning of a condition. The second idhā is in the position of the response of the first. The meaning of the speech governs the first idhā, and what governs the second is ﴿akhadhnā﴾. End.

This is a confused statement, and it is unlikely to come from a scholar of such standing. The mutrafūn (affluent ones) are those who have been lavished with blessings. The punishment (ʿadhāb) intended is what befell them on the day of Badr of killing and capture, as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. Many of their champions and leaders were killed and captured on that day. The ju'ār is like the khuwār (bellowing). It is said: jaʾara al-thawr yajʾaru when the bull bellows, and jaʾara al-rajul ilā Allāh (the man cried out to God) when he humbly supplicates with prayer, as in al-Sihah (Jawhari's lexicon). In al-Asas (Zamakhshari's lexicon): jaʾara al-dāʿī ilā Allāh means he cried out and raised his voice. What is intended is shouting, either generally or with a plea for help.

The two plural pronouns refer to what the earlier pronouns refer to in (their affluent ones, to them, and their hearts) and others. They are the disbelievers of Makkah, but with the intention of those who remained after the affluent ones were seized by killing. Ibn Jurayj said: those punished are the dead of Badr, and those who cry out are the people of Makkah, because they wailed and sought help. In Insan al-ʿUyun (Ibn Sayyid al-Nas's biography of the Prophet): or the Quraysh wailed over their dead at Badr for a month, their women shaved their hair, and they would bring the man's horse or mount, cover it with curtains, wail around it, and take it out into the alleys, until it was advised to them to stop that out of fear of mockery.

Al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: what is meant by ju'ār is anguish (jazaʿ), since it is the cause of shouting. But this is far-fetched, because the indication of the metaphor is obscure. It is narrated from al-Dahhak that what is meant by punishment is the punishment of hunger. That is because the Prophet ﷺ supplicated against them, saying:

"O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar. O Allah, make it upon them years like the years of Joseph."

So his supplication was answered, peace and blessings be upon him, and a year of famine befell them in which they ate carrion, hides, bones burned, and al-ʿalhaz (a paste of blood and hair). In the reports there is what indicates that this was before the Hijrah, and there is also what indicates that it was before it. Al-Bayhaqi reconciled this by saying that perhaps it happened twice, and that will come shortly, God willing. The singling out of the affluent ones for mention is because when the affluent one goes hungry, others go hungry all the more. It is also said: what is meant by punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter, and the singling out of the affluent ones with what was mentioned is because of the utmost clarity of the reversal of their state and the overturning of their affairs, and because that is harder for them. Moreover, although they were protected and guarded by the protection of others through their strength and dignity, they met what they met of a dreadful state. So it is more fitting and more befitting that those other than them, from the guards and servants, should meet it.

Shaykh al-Islam said: this view is the truth, because the punishment of the Hereafter is that at which they are suddenly struck into crying out, and so they are answered with rejection and despair of victory. As for the punishment of the day of Badr, no crying out was found in them at it, as His statement, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And We had already seized them with punishment, but they did not humble themselves to their Lord, nor did they supplicate﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 76]. For what is meant by this punishment is what befell them on the day of Badr of killing and capture, as a certainty. As for the punishment of hunger, although Quraysh humbled themselves before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in it, he did not answer them with despair, since it was narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, supplicated for its removal, and it was removed from them. End. You will know, God willing, what is in it. Indeed, taking the punishment as that is more suitable, given that what lies within the scope of ﴿ḥattā﴾ is a limit for what precedes it.

Do not cry out for help today. [Understood as] said by way of implicit speech, i.e., We say to them that. The statement is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) serving to explain their despair and the fact that their crying out will benefit them nothing. By "today" is meant the present time in which what has befallen them has befallen them, and the restriction to this time serves to increase their despair and to intensify the statement that their crying out will not benefit them.

Shaykh al-Islam said: this terrifying "today" and the announcement of their losing the time of crying out [are the purpose]. By "speech" is meant, as has been said, what is by the tongue of the state (lisan al-hal), as in the line: "The basin is full, and Qutni said [so]." It is also permissible that it means the literal speech and its issuing, either from Allah the Exalted or from the angels, peace be upon them. According to this view, the apparent meaning is that the speech takes place in the Hereafter; its occurring in this world, with them not hearing it, is not free from some [difficulty]. Its assumed form is an imperative verb whose subject is his pronoun (ﷺ), i.e., "Say to them from Us: Do not cry out," which is very distant. Some people permitted that the assumed speech be the response of the conditional "idha" (when), and then "idha hum yaj'arun" (when they are crying out) would be a qualifier of the condition, or a substitute for the first "idha." On the first view, the meaning is: We seized their affluent ones at the time of their crying out, or at the moment of their sudden arrival, since "idha" may then be temporal or sudden. He did not permit making the aforementioned prohibition the response, because it lacks the obligatory fa' when it occurs in that manner. This view was criticized: it is not hidden that the primary purpose of the conditional clause is the response, so that their sudden crying out would become not a primary purpose.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you from Us will not be helped﴾ is a justification for the prohibition of crying out, by showing that it does not benefit, and "min" is for the beginning [of the limit], i.e., no help from Us will reach you that would save you from what you are in. It is permissible that "min" be connected to "nasr" (help), implying the meaning of prevention, or used figuratively for it, i.e., you will not be protected from Us. This was criticized: the context of the noble composition does not support it, because their crying out was not directed to other than Him, the Exalted, so that it would be refuted by their not being helped from Him, nor does its context [support it], since His statement, exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, My verses were recited to you﴾ up to its end is explicit that this is a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the non-arrival of help from God's side, due to their disbelief in the verses. Even if the help being denied were imagined to come from someone else, the reasons would be His inability or God's might and power. You know that these were the polytheists whose partners were before their eyes, and the verse did not restrict the crying out (al-ju'ar) to being directed to God. The matter of the causal explanation is easy. It may be said that the meaning on this view is a claim of shouting: "He does not protect you from Us, nor does He benefit you with Us. You have committed a great matter and a grave sin, which that does not remove." Then, what is in the words of the one who objects afterward is not hidden. The intended meaning is: "My verses were recited to you before your affluent ones were seized by the punishment," ﴿and you used to turn back on your heels﴾ at their recitation, that is, you turned away from their hearing in the strongest way, let alone believing in them and acting upon them. The nukūs (turning back) is returning, and al-a'qāb is the plural of 'aqb, which is the back part of a man's foot. A person's returning on his heel is his returning along the path he came by first, as one says: "He returned, his return upon his beginning." Some have considered the restriction by "heels" to be for emphasis (ta'kid), as in "I saw it with my own eye," on the basis that nukūs means going back backwards, and "on the heels" fits that. Whatever the case, it is used metaphorically for turning away.

And 'Ali, may God honour his face, read «تَنْكُصُونَ» with a ḍammah on the kāf (tankusūna), whereas the common reading is «تَنْكِصُونَ» with a kasrah on the kāf (tankiṣūna).

﴿Mustakbirin bihi﴾ (arrogant about it), that is, about the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Haram). The preposition *bi* (ب) indicates causation (al-sababiyyah). This omission of a referent is permitted even though there has been no prior mention of it, because their arrogance and boasting were well known: they claimed to be the servants and custodians of the House. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun). Close to it is the view that the pronoun refers to the Sacred Sanctuary (al-Haram). Al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) says: the pronoun refers to the verbal noun implied by "*tankusun*" (you turn back). This was criticised on the grounds that it adds little meaning, since that is already understood from making "*mustakbirin*" a circumstantial clause (hal). Another objection was raised to it, which is open to discussion. Mundhir ibn Sa'id mentioned that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). What supports this is that in the words of the Exalted, ﴿Verily, My verses were recited to you﴾, there is an indication of him (peace be upon him). The *bi* may be transitive, with "arrogance" implicitly carrying the sense of "denial" (al-tadmin), or it may be used metaphorically for it. Or it may indicate causation, because their arrogance appeared with his (ﷺ) mission. It is also permitted that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, understood from the verses, or to the verses themselves, by considering their interpretation as the Qur'an. The status of the *bi* is as you have just heard. It is also permitted that the phrase be connected to the words of the Exalted, ﴿samiran﴾ (conversing nightly), meaning: you converse about the mention of the Qur'an and about criticising it. This is because they used to gather around the House at night and converse, and most of their night-talk was about the Qur'an, calling it sorcery and poetry. On that reading the meaning holds, even if "*bihi*" is not connected to it. It is also permitted, if it is connected to "*samiran*", for the pronoun to refer to the Prophet (peace be upon him), and likewise the meaning may be upon him even if it is not connected to it. It has also been said that it is connected to "*tahjurun*", but this is far-fetched.

"*Samiran*" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). It is a collective noun (ism jam'), like *al-hajj* (pilgrims), *al-hadir* (those present), *al-jamil* (camel-drivers) and *al-baqir* (cattle-herders). It has also been said that it is a verbal noun (masdar) functioning as a circumstantial clause according to the well-known interpretation, so it includes both the few and the many, given its root. It is not hidden that a verbal noun on the pattern *fa'il* is rare, as in *al-'afiyah* (well-being) and *al-'aqibah* (outcome).

Al-samar (السَّمَر) originally means the shade of the moon. According to *al-Matla'*, it was so named for its darkness (sumrah). In *al-Bahr* it is the light of the moon that falls on trees. Al-Raghib said it is the darkness of the night, and then it was applied to conversation at night. Some interpreters explained *al-samir* as the dark night. Taking it to mean that here, and making it accusative by what follows it through the omission of the preposition, is not valid.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Haywa, Ibn Muhaysin, 'Ikrima, al-Za'faraniyy and Mahbub (from Abu 'Amr) read *samran* with a *damma* on the *sin* and a doubled *mim* with a *fatha*, as the plural of *samir*. Ibn 'Abbas also (read it so), as did Zayd ibn 'Ali, Abu Raja' and Abu Nahik, reading *simaran* with an *alif* added after the *mim*, which is also the plural of *samir*. Both are regular plural patterns for such words.

﴿Tahjurun﴾ is from *al-hajr* with a *fatha* and then a sukun, meaning cutting off and abandoning. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: abandoning the truth, or the Qur'an, or the Prophet (ﷺ). From Ibn 'Abbas: you abandon the House and do not honour it with the worship befitting it. *Al-hajr* also comes in the sense of raving (al-hadhayan), as in *al-Sihah*: "He *hajara* the sick man," i.e. he raved when he became delirious. It is also permitted that the meaning here is this: you rave concerning the Qur'an, or the Prophet (peace be upon him), or his Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), or all of these together.

In *Ad-Durr al-Masun* it is said that what carries the meaning of raving is *al-hajr* with two *fathas*.

It is also permitted that it derives from *al-hujr* with a *damma* and then a sukun, which is foul speech. Al-Raghib said: *al-hujr* is abusive speech, so called because it is abandoned on account of its ugliness. One says *hajara fulan* when he utters foul speech deliberately, and *ahjara al-mariḍ* when a sick person does so without intent. In *al-Misbah* it is said: "*Hajara al-mariḍ* in his speech" means he raved. *Al-hujr* with a *damma* is a verbal noun meaning obscenity, from *hujr* like *qatl*. There is another dialect in which it is *ihjur* with an *alif*. In accordance with this dialect is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Muhaysin, Nafi' and Hamid: *tuhjurun* with a *damma* on the *ta'*, a *kasra* on the *jim*. This makes it unlikely that *tahjurun* in the reading of the majority is from *al-hajr* meaning cutting off.

Ibn Abi 'Asim read it with a *ya'* as a shift of person (iltifat). Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas also, Zayd ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them), 'Ikrima, Abu Nahik, Ibn Muhaysin also, and Abu Haywa read *tuhajjarun* with a *damma* on the *ta'*, a *fatha* on the *ha'*, a *kasra* on the *jim* and a doubled *jim*, as a doubled form of *hajara*, from *al-hajr* with a *fatha* or a *damma*. The meaning is then: you cut off, or you rave, or you utter obscenities much.

[Page 50]

The interrogative particle (hamzah) here is for denying and censuring what has occurred, and the fa' is for coordination with an implied clause that the sentence carries along. The meaning is: "Do what they did of recoil (nukus), arrogance, and turning away, and so they did not ponder the Qur'an, so that they might know, through its aspects of inimitability (wujuh al-i'jaz), that it is the truth from their Lord, and thus believe in it." As for "am" (or) in His saying, ﴿Or has there come to them that which did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾, it is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and what it carries of the sense of "bal" (rather) is for idrab (turning away) and for moving from one rebuke to another rebuke. The hamzah is for denying the occurrence, not the thing occurring. The meaning is: "Rather, has there come to them from the Book what did not come to their forefathers of old, so that they found it strange and therefore fell into the disbelief and misguidance they fell into?" The sense is that the sending of Books from Him, the Exalted, to the messengers, peace be upon them, so that they might warn people with them, is an ancient custom of His, the Exalted, which one can hardly deny, and that the coming of the Qur'an in accordance with this way is therefore not something they should deny.

It was also said: the meaning is, "Have they not pondered the Qur'an, so that they would fear, upon pondering its signs and narratives, like what befell those who denied before them? Or has there come to them of security what did not come to their forefathers of old, when they feared God, the Exalted, and so believed in Him, His Books, and His messengers, and obeyed Him?" According to this reading, "their forefathers" refers to the believers, such as Isma'il, peace be upon him, Adnan, and Qahtan. It seems that describing them as "the earliest" (al-awwalin) on this reading is by way of approximation (al-aqrabin).

Page 51

In a report: "Do not revile Mudar and Rabi'ah, for they were both Muslims. Do not revile Qass, for he was a Muslim. Do not revile al-Harith ibn Ka'b, nor Asad ibn Khuzaymah, nor Tamim ibn Murr, for they were upon Islam. And if you have doubted anything, do not doubt that Tubba' was a Muslim."

It is also related that Dabbah ibn Udd was a Muslim and was in the shurtah (guard/police unit) of Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both.

In al-Kashshaf: making the benefit of pondering to be the consequence of knowledge means that the hamzah in the disjunctive clause is for affirmation (taqrir) and establishing that they persist in blind imitation (taqlid), which is why they did not ponder and did not know. If you take the purpose to be consideration (i'tibar) and fear, then the hamzah in it is for denial or affirmation in a mocking manner (tahakkum). End quote. So reflect upon this. Furthermore, it is not hidden that attributing the coming to security is not as evident as attributing it to the Book, and by this the rank of this interpretation falls below the first one.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 69:

﴿Or did they not recognize their Messenger?﴾ This is a transition (idrab) and a shift from rebuke for what was mentioned to rebuke on another ground. The hamza (interrogative particle) here also serves to express denial of occurrence; that is, "Rather, did they not know him, peace be upon him, for his trustworthiness, truthfulness, good character, and other perfections fitting for prophets, peace be upon them?"

It is authentically related that Abu Talib, on the day of the Prophet's ﷺ marriage, gave a speech in the presence of the chiefs of Mudar and Quraysh, saying: "I praise God who made us of the offspring of Abraham, the seed of Ishmael, the stock of Ma'add, and the origin of Mudar; who made us the custodians of His House, the guardians of His sanctuary; who gave us a house to be visited and a safe sanctuary, and made us the rulers over the people. Then, this nephew of mine, Muhammad son of Abdullah, cannot be weighed against any man but that he outweighs him. If he is lacking in wealth, then wealth is a passing shade and a transient matter. Muhammad is one whose kinship you know well. He has proposed to Khadija daughter of Khuwaylid, and he has offered her a dowry of such-and-such from my own property, both prompt and deferred. By God, after this he will have a great report and a noble destiny."

In this there is clear evidence that they knew him ﷺ to the utmost degree of perfection; otherwise they would have denied what Abu Talib said about him, peace be upon him.

﴿So they are deniers of him.﴾ The fa' is causal, indicating that denial results from non-recognition. Thus the sentence falls within the scope of denial, and the meaning is: "They knew him with the perfection fitting for prophets, peace be upon them, so how could they deny him?" The lam is for emphasis, and the fronting of the object (lahu) is for restriction or for the sake of the verse-ending (fasila). The statement is understood with an elided noun, meaning "deniers of his claim" or "deniers of his messengership, peace be upon him."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 70:

﴿Or do they say, "He has madness"?﴾ This is a transition to another rebuke, and the hamza (interrogative particle) is for denying the reality, as in the first one. That is: "Rather, do they say he has madness (junnah), that is, insanity, when in fact he, upon whom be prayers and peace, is the most intelligent of people, the most penetrating in judgment, and the most dignified in gravity?" In these four rebukes, two of which relate to the Qur'an and the other two to him, upon whom be prayers and peace, the progression from the lower to the higher has been observed, as Shaykh al-Islam (Shaykh al-Islam, a title for a leading jurist) explains. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, He has brought them the truth﴾ is a turning away from what the preceding indicates. That is: the matter is not as they claimed concerning the Qur'an and the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace; rather, He has brought them the truth, that is, the sincere reality that cannot be deviated from. What is meant by it is the Oneness of God and the religion of Islam which the Qur'an contains. It is also permissible that what is meant by it is the Qur'an.

﴿And most of them are averse to the truth﴾ because of the complete deviation and divergence in their natures. The apparent reading is that the pronouns refer to the Quraysh. The restriction of the judgment to "most of them" is because among them are those who refused Islam and following the truth out of fear of reproach from their people or the like, not out of aversion to the truth as such. Therefore, what has been said is not refuted: that whoever loves something hates its opposite, so whoever loves to remain in disbelief has necessarily hated the move to faith.
Page 52
Ibn al-Munir said: It is possible to take "most" to mean all, just as he took the "few" to mean negation, but this is far-fetched. Likewise is what he chose, that the pronoun in "most of them" refers to all people and not to the Quraysh, so that the statement is like the saying of Him, exalted is He: ﴿And most people, even if you were eager, are not believers﴾ [Yusuf: 103]. It may be said: since the intent is to affirm aversion to the truth in a continuous manner, and God, exalted is He, knew that among them are those who would believe and follow the truth, there was no alternative to restricting the judgment to "most." The apparent reading, based on the general rule of the majority in repeating a definite noun, is that the second "truth" is the same as the first "truth." The noun is made explicit rather than pronominalized because the explicit form is more apparent in censure, and a pronoun might be mistakenly taken to refer back to the Messenger, upon whom be prayers and peace. It has also been said: the article in the first is for prior reference, and in the second it is for totality or for genus, meaning: "and most of them are averse to the truth," that is, any truth whatsoever, not this truth alone, as the explicit mention indicates: "averse." The restriction of most of them with this attribute only requires that some of them are not averse to every truth among the truths, and that does not contradict their aversion to this truth. However, there is a discussion in this, for it is hardly granted that most of them are averse to every truth. Likewise, the apparent reading is that what is meant by "the truth" in the saying of Him, exalted is He:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 71:**

﴿Had the Truth followed their desires﴾. The Truth here is the truth that the Prophet (ﷺ) brought, with the "following" taken literally and the attribution taken figuratively. It was also said that the meaning is: had the Prophet (ﷺ) followed their desires and brought them polytheism instead of what he was sent with, ﴿the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted﴾. That is, God Most High would have laid waste the world and the Resurrection would have come about because of His extreme anger, glory be to Him. This is an impossible supposition, that he (peace be upon him) would alter what he was sent with from Him. It is also permissible that the Truth means the matter that corresponds to reality concerning divinity, and "following" is a metaphor for agreement. That is: if the matter corresponding to reality agreed with their desires, by polytheism being true, the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted, as established in His words: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22]. Perhaps the statement about it is a parenthetical remark, to indicate that they disliked something that is impossible to oppose in any way, so there is no benefit for them in this dislike. It has been objected that this does not suit the context, and there is discussion about that. Likewise is what was said: that what agrees with their desires is polytheism in divinity, because the Quraysh were idolaters, and that does not necessarily entail corruption. What entails it is polytheism in lordship, as the Dualists (al-thanawiyyah) claim, and they were not like that, as His words indicate: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [Luqman: 25; al-Zumar: 38].

It is also permissible that the meaning is: if the Truth in general agreed with their desires, the heavens and the earth would have gone entirely out of order and soundness. The statement is a digression to magnify the status of the Truth in general, that the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them stand only by it, and this is not devoid of beauty. It was also said: the Truth here is Allah Most High.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted it from Abu Salih, and some of them related it from Ibn Jurayj, and al-Zamakhshari from Qatadah. Its meaning on this reading is: if Allah Most High were to follow their desires and do what they wish, so that He legislated polytheism for them and commanded them to it, He, glory be to Him, would not be God, and the heavens and the earth would be corrupted. This is based on the principle that legislating polytheism is a deficiency from which Allah Most High must be exalted. al-Khafaji mentioned this and said that the rational proof has been established for it and that there is no disagreement about it. Perhaps the statement about it is also a parenthetical remark, to indicate the impossibility of the Prophet (peace be upon him) being sent to them in a way that would be acceptable to them, unlike what he brought, which they do not dislike. Their dislike of what the Prophet (peace be upon him) brought therefore benefits them nothing. So the claim that it is remote from what the context requires is not in its proper place. It was also said: the meaning on this reading is: if Allah Most High did what agrees with their desires, the order of the world would be disrupted, because their opinions are contradictory. This contains an indication of the corruption of their minds, and that for this reason they disliked what they disliked of the Truth which the Prophet (peace be upon him) brought, and this, as you see, is far-fetched.

Ibn Wathhab recited ﴿wa-law ittaba'a﴾ with a ḍammah on the waw (i.e. the reading "wa-lawu ittaba'a" in the sense of the same consonants with a different vowel pattern). ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾. This is a transition from censuring them for disliking the Truth to censuring them for turning away from what every soul is inclined to desire, namely that in which lies its good. The "reminder" here is the Qur'an, which is their pride and honour, as His words indicate: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]. That is: rather, We have brought them their pride and honour, which it was incumbent upon them to turn to with the utmost attention and to receive with the utmost acceptance. ( So they ) by what they did of recoiling ﴿from their reminder﴾, that is, from their pride and honour specifically, ( are turning away ), not from anything else that does not require attention and concern. Placing the noun in the position of the pronoun adds further censure and rebuke against them. The particle "fa" (so) indicates that what follows, their turning away from their reminder, is consequent upon what precedes it, the bringing of their reminder. Whoever interprets "the Truth" in His words ﴿Rather, he has brought them the Truth﴾ as the noble Qur'an says here: attributing the bringing of the reminder to the royal "We" after attributing it to the Prophet's pronoun (peace be upon him) is an honouring of the Prophet (ﷺ) and an alerting to his having a great station from the Mighty and Majestic. In the mention of the noble Qur'an when it is attributed to the Prophet (ﷺ) under the title of truth, and when it is attributed to Allah Most High under the title of reminder, there is a secret subtlety and a brilliant wisdom that is not hidden. For declaring its truth, which entails the truth of the one who brought it, is what the context of relating what the falsifiers said about him requires. As for honouring, it is fitting only for Him Most High, especially since the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is one of the honoured. It was also said: the "reminder" here is what they wished for when they said: ﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples﴾, ﴿we would surely have been sincere servants of Allah﴾. So it is as if it was said: rather, We have brought them the Book which they wished for. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the reminder means admonition.

It was supported by the reading of Isa, "bi-dhikrāhum" with the feminine alif. The first two views were preferred because censure on them is more severe, for turning away from their admonition is not comparable to turning away from their honour and pride, or from their Book which they wished for, in terms of shamefulness and ugliness.

It was also said: admonition contains the explanation of what makes the condition of the one being admonished sound, so censuring the turning away from it is no less than censuring turning away from either of those two matters. And the obstinacy in this is not hidden. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Isa ibn Umar and Yunus from Abu Amr recited ﴿Bal ataytuhum﴾ with the first person "ta" (I have brought them). Ibn Abi Ishaq, Isa also, Abu Haywa, al-Jahdari, Ibn Qatib and Abu Rajaa recited ﴿Bal ataytuhum﴾ with the second person "ta" addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ). Abu Amr, and in one transmission, recited ﴿atayna-hum﴾ with a long vowel. On this reading there is no need to resort to a metaphor or to assume an omitted genitive, as in the reading of the majority, if the bi- is taken to mean accompaniment. Qatadah recited ﴿nadhkuruhum﴾ with the nun, as the present tense of dhakara (we remember them).

*[Page 53]*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 72:

﴿Or do you ask them for any payment?﴾ This is connected to His saying, ﴿Or do they say, "He has a madness"?﴾ So it is a shift to another rebuke, and the address was changed to suit what follows it. The meaning is: "Or do they claim that you ask them for payment for conveying the message," ﴿kharj﴾, that is, a wage. Therefore they do not believe in you because of it. His saying, ﴿But the payment of your Lord is better﴾, that is, His provision in this world and His reward in the Hereafter, is a reason for the negation of asking that is implied by the rebuke; that is, do not ask them that, for what Allah the Exalted has given you in this world and the next is better than that, because of its abundance, its permanence, and the absence of bearing any obligation to men in it. In the mention of the title of Lordship together with its attribution to his pronoun, peace be upon him, there is an explanation of the ruling and an honouring of him (ﷺ) that is not hidden.

"Al-kharj" is the counterpart of "al-dakhl" (income), and it is said of everything you bring out to another. "Al-kharaj" is predominantly used for the tax on land, so it implies
page 54
abundance and obligation, and thus it is more emphatic. For this reason it is used to express the bounty of Allah the Exalted. Likewise, according to what has been said, that "al-kharj" is what you give voluntarily while "al-kharaj" is what is obligatory upon you; and obligation, with respect to Him the Exalted, is only by the grace of His promise, glorified and majestic is He. It has also been said that "al-kharj" is more general than "al-kharaj," and some have equated the two.

ʿĀmir recited ﴿kharjan fa-kharaja﴾, and Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī recited ﴿kharājan fa-kharājun﴾ for the sake of harmony (mushākalah). Al-Ḥasan and ʿĪsā recited ﴿kharajan fa-kharaja﴾. It seems that the choice of ﴿kharjan﴾ in relation to him, upon him be prayer and peace, is to indicate a strength that enables them in disbelief, and the choice of "kharajan" in relation to Him, the Exalted, is for the sake of emphasis in belittling their tax, since the meaning is: a little from Him, glorified and majestic is He, is better than their much; so what is to be thought of His much, exalted is He. ﴿And He is the best of providers﴾ is an emphasis on the excellence of His payment, glorified and exalted is He, for whoever is the best of providers, his provision is better than the provision of others.

Al-Jubba'i used this to argue that no one equals Him, glorified is He, in bestowing favours upon His servants, and that servants may indeed provide for one another.

﴿And indeed you call them to a straight path.﴾ Sound minds bear witness to its straightness, with no trace of crookedness that would give rise to accusation. Al-Zamakhshari said: God, glorified and exalted, has indeed established the proof against them and removed their excuses in these verses, by showing that the one sent to them is a man whose affairs and condition are well known, whose secret and public conduct is tested, and who is fit to be chosen for prophethood from among them. He had not begun to claim such a great claim falsely, nor did he make it a means to gain from their worldly goods or to seek their wealth. He called them only to the religion of Islam, which is the straight path, while exposing what lay hidden in their ailments: their neglect of reflection and contemplation, their frivolous treatment of the religion of their forefathers, their error without proof, and their pretext that he is a madman after the truth had become manifest and the confirmation from God through miracles and clear signs was established, as well as their aversion to the truth and their turning away from what it contains that preserved them from remembrance. End of quotation. It is indeed of great excellence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 74:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ are the disbelievers of Quraysh mentioned about in what passed before. They were described with this to denounce them for their immersion in this world and their claim that there is no life after it, and as an indication of the cause of the ruling, for belief in the Hereafter and fear of the calamities therein are among the strongest motives to seeking the truth and following its path. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is those who include them and other disbelievers who deny the gathering (al-hashr), and they enter into this as a primary entry. ﴿Are deviating from the path﴾ — the straight path which they are called to — ﴿those who deviate﴾, i.e., those who swerve (la-'adilun). It was also said: the intended meaning of "the path" is its genus, i.e., they deviate from the very category of the path, let alone the straight path to which they are called. This was preferred on the grounds that it is more indicative of the completeness of their misguidance and the extreme of their error, since it reveals that what they have adopted is not something to which the name "path" applies, even if it were crooked. However, the argument that the causal reasoning by the content of the relative clause supports only the intention of the straight path is weak. I think that whoever claimed that the intended meaning here is the path stretched over the back of Hell (jahannam), which is the road to Paradise, has deviated from the path, meaning that on the Day of Resurrection they will be inclining away from the road to Paradise, to the right and to the left, toward the Fire.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 75:

﴿Even if We had mercy upon them and removed the harm that is upon them﴾, i.e., the bad condition. It was said: it is what befell them because of the punishment inflicted on their affluent ones (mutrafun) at the Battle of Badr, namely the grief over them, and that [removal] would be by bringing them back to life and returning them to the world after being killed. That is, even if We had mercy upon them and removed their harm by returning their affluent ones to them, ﴿they would persist﴾ (lalajju), i.e., they would continue, ﴿in their transgression﴾, i.e., their excess in disbelief, arrogance, and enmity toward the Messenger
[p. 55]
(ﷺ) and the believers, ﴿wandering blindly﴾ (ya'mahun), i.e., bewildered, hesitating in error. It is said: ʿamiha (like manaʿa and faraḥa), yaʿmahu ʿamahan and ʿamhanan, meaning he was bewildered. It was also said: it is what they were in of intense fear of being killed and taken captive, and of great turmoil because of that, when they saw what had befallen their affluent ones at Badr, and [the removal of that] would be by the Prophet's (ﷺ) command to refrain from fighting them and taking them captive afterward, or something similar. This is an opinion that is not far-fetched. It was also said: the intended harm is the punishment of the Hereafter, meaning that they are in such depravity and obstinacy that, if they were shown mercy, and the punishment of the Fire were removed from them, and they were returned to the world, they would revert, because of the intensity of their stubbornness in what they are upon. There is in this some remoteness.

Abu Hayyan preferred that the intended harm is the drought and hunger that befell them through the supplication of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He mentioned that this is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jurayj. The Prophet (ﷺ) supplicated against them with this in Mecca on the day when the polytheists threw [the entrails of] a slaughtered camel upon him while he was standing praying at the House. He said:

"O Allah, make Your grip heavy upon Mudar. O Allah, make it upon them as years like the years of Joseph."

He also supplicated with this in Medina. It is narrated that he (peace be upon him) persisted for a month, when he raised his head from the second rakʿah of the dawn prayer after saying "Allah hears those who praise Him," saying: "O Allah, deliver al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Salamah ibn Hisham, ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿah, and the oppressed believers in Mecca. O Allah, make Your grip heavy, etc." Perhaps he did this after raising his head from the last rakʿah of the ʿIsha prayer. Both narrations were mentioned by Burhan al-Din al-Halabi (al-Ḥalabī) in his Sirah.

Most [scholars] hold that it is the hunger that befell them because of Thumamah's withholding of grain from them. This is because Thumamah ibn Uthal al-Hanafi was brought to Medina by the expedition (sariyyah, a small military detachment) of Muhammad ibn Maslamah when the Prophet (ﷺ) sent it against the Banu Bakr ibn Kilab. He embraced Islam after having refused to embrace it for three days. Then he set out as a ʿumrah pilgrim. When he reached Mecca, he pronounced the talbiyah (the call "Labbayka", i.e., the formula of the pilgrim), and he was the first to enter it reciting the talbiyah. From this, the Hanafi (poet) said:

"And among us is the one who pronounced the talbiyah in Mecca openly, in defiance of Abu Sufyan, in the sacred months."

Then the Quraysh seized him and said: "You have dared against us, and you have become a apostate, O Thumamah!" He said: "I have embraced Islam and followed the best religion, the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ). By Allah, not a single grain will reach you from al-Yamamah, which was a fertile land for the people of Mecca, until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permits it." Then Thumamah went out to al-Yamamah and prevented them from bringing anything to Mecca, until hunger harmed them and the Quraysh ate al-ʿalhaz (a food made of blood mixed with hair or similar material).

So the Quraysh wrote to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do you not claim that you were sent as a mercy to the worlds? You have killed the fathers with the sword and the sons with hunger. You command the keeping of kinship ties, yet you have severed our ties of kinship!" So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to Thumamah, may Allah be pleased with him: "Let my people be free to obtain their grain," and he did so. In another narration, Abu Sufyan came to him (ﷺ) and said, "Do you not...," etc. The reconciliation between the two is evident. This was shortly before the Conquest. However, in my view, the particle (law, "if/even if") makes this opinion remote, as is not hidden. Yes, Ibn Jarir and a group [of narrators] transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas a text clearly stating that the story of Thumamah was the cause of the revelation of the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 76:

﴿And We had already seized them with punishment﴾ — to its end. Thus hunger is intended by the punishment mentioned therein, according to this view. And the statement of the Exalted, ﴿So they did not humble themselves﴾ — they did not submit thereby ﴿to their Lord﴾ — does not counter the one who holds this view, because he may say: what is meant by humbling oneself before Him, may He be glorified and exalted, is submission to His command, may He be glorified, and faith in Him, may He be exalted and high. What they did with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had none of that in it. The well-known view, however, is that the punishment intended is what befell them on the Day of Badr of killing and capture. And it is not countered against the one who interpreted the punishment in the words of the Glorified:

**Page 56**

﴿Until, when We seize their affluent ones with punishment﴾. Also, there is a contradiction between what is said there, ﴿Then they cry out for help﴾, and what is said here, the negation of humble submission (istikana) to their Lord and the negation of supplication (tadarru') that is understood from His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and they do not supplicate﴾. One may say: al-juʼar (crying out) is a general term for shouting, and it is other than humble submission to God, mighty and majestic is He, and other than supplication to Him, glorified is He. This is evident. The same applies if al-juʼar is taken to mean shouting for help, on the basis that what is meant by humble submission to Him, exalted is He, is what you have just learned: submission to His command, mighty and majestic is He. Supplication is that which comes from the core of the heart, while juʼar is that which does not come from it. It seems that the expression of juʼar there is to indicate that their cries for help were most like the sounds of animals. It has also been said: what came earlier explains the state of those who were killed, and what is here explains the state of those who remain. The verb for supplication is in the present tense to indicate continuity, but what is meant is the continuity of the negation, not the negation of continuity. That is, it is not their habit to supplicate to Him, exalted is He, at all. If this is taken as the negation of continuity, as is the apparent meaning, then there is no contradiction, as may be suspected, between His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they cry out for help﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and they do not supplicate﴾, either.

Istakana is of the form istaf'ala from al-kawn (being), and its original meaning is "to move from one state to another," like istahjara (to turn into stone). Then custom came to use it for moving from the state of arrogance to the state of humility, so there is no ambiguity in it by custom. Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Faris said: "I was asked about this in Baghdad when I entered it during the time of the Imam al-Nasir, and he gathered its scholars for me. I said, and he approved of what I said: it is derived from the saying of the Arabs, 'I was for you when I submitted (kuntu laka idha khada'tu),' and this is a Hudhali dialect, which Abu 'Ubayda transmitted in al-Gharibayn. According to this, it belongs to the category of qarra and istaqarra (to settle and to be settled). The form istaf'ala, used for intensification, like ista'sama and istahsara, does not apply, unless what is meant in the verse is then the intensification of the negation, not the negation of intensification." It has also been said that it comes from al-kayn, the flesh hidden within the private part, due to the humiliation of the one who is humbled. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that it may be ifta'ala from al-sukun (stillness), with the alif being an elongation, as in his saying:

*"And you, from calamities when you throw, and from the blame of men, are a shelter-seeker."*

And his saying:

*"I seek refuge in God from the scorpions, the raised-tailed ones with knotted tails."*

It has been objected that the elongation mentioned is specific to the necessity of poetry, and that it is not known to occur in all the inflections of the word; and istakana in all its inflections is not like this. This indicates that it is not one of the words that contain elongation.

﴿Until, when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment﴾, of the punishment of the Hereafter, as the awe conveyed by the opening of the gate and the description of it as severe indicates. This is the view of al-Jubba'i. "Hatta" (until), although it is an endpoint for the preceding negation, is the beginning of what follows it in the conditional sentence, as if it were said: they remain in this state until, when We open upon them on the Day of Resurrection a gate of severe punishment, ﴿they are then in it﴾, that is, in that gate, or in that punishment, or because of the opening; there are several views, ﴿despairing﴾, bewildered, despairing of every good, or grieved because of the severity of the calamity. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the day the Hour is established, the criminals will despair﴾ [al-Rum: 12], and ﴿It will not be lightened for them, and they will be in it, despairing﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 75]. It has also been said: this gate is the domination of the Prophet ﷺ and the believers over them on the Day of Conquest, when they despaired on that day of every good they had imagined. Ibn Jarir reported that it was the hunger in which they ate al-'ahlaz (a mixture of blood and hair). And from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, it was the killing at Badr. The Imamiyya (Twelver Shia) reported (they are the house of lies):

From Abu Ja'far, may God be pleased with him, that this is a punishment with which they will be punished in the return (al-raj'a). By my life, they have indeed fabricated lies against God, exalted is He, and have gone far astray. In my view, the correct interpretation of the verse is what has preceded. The apparent view is that these verses are Medinan, and some who say they are Meccan claim that they contain reports about the future in the past tense, to indicate the certainty of its occurrence.

﴿And it is He who brought into being for you hearing and sight﴾ so that you might perceive by them the revealed verses (al-ayat al-tanziliyya) and the created verses (al-ayat al-takwiniyya), ﴿and hearts﴾ so that you might reflect by them upon the signs and infer by them other benefits. He placed hearing first because of the abundance of its benefits, and used the singular for it because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar), and the eloquent Arabs mostly did not pluralize it. It has been said that it is used in the singular because it perceives one kind of perceptible thing, namely sounds, unlike sight, which perceives lights, colours, bodies and shapes, and unlike the heart (fu'ad), which perceives various kinds of conceptions and affirmations. The verse contains an indication of both the sensory and the rational proof. The mention first of what points to the former has already been made, so consider this. ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾, meaning: little thanks is what you give for those magnificent blessings, because the essence of thanksgiving lies in directing those faculties, which are in themselves manifest blessings, to the purposes for which they were created. Thus ﴿little﴾ is in the accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. The littleness is to be taken in its apparent sense, on the basis that the address is to people in general with the believers given precedence. It is permitted that it carry the sense of negation, on the basis that the address is to the polytheists by way of iltifat (a shift in address). It has been said that it is exclusively for the believers, but this is not correct. In my view, the more appropriate reading is that it is exclusively for the polytheists, while it is also permissible that the littleness is to be taken in its apparent sense, as will not be hidden from one who reflects. The added emphasis (ma 'ala sa'ir al-aqwal mazida li-l-ta'kid) is over all other opinions.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verses 79–80:

﴿And it is He who created you (dhara'akum) on the earth﴾, i.e., He brought you into being and scattered you upon it; ﴿and to Him you will be gathered﴾, i.e., you will be assembled on the Day of Resurrection after your dispersal, not to anyone other than Him, exalted is He. Or it means their differing (mukhalafa) in increase and decrease. It has also been said: the meaning is that their alternation is by His command and decree, glorified is He; so there is an elided genitive (mudaf muqaddar) in the speech, and the lam (la) before it may be a lam of causation (li-l-ta'lil). ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾, i.e., will you not reflect, so that you would not understand; or, will you reflect and then understand, by looking and contemplating, that the whole belongs to Us, and that Our power encompasses all possible things, of which the resurrection is one? Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 83:

﴿Indeed we and our fathers have been promised this﴾, [this resurrection] ﴿before﴾. The phrase ﴿before﴾ is connected (muta'allaq) to the verb in terms of its being attributed to the one conjoined to (ma'tuf 'alayh) and the conjoined (ma'tuf), which is the apparent meaning. This is valid with respect to them, because the prophets who informed of the resurrection used to inform of it with respect to everyone who dies. It is also permissible that it be connected to the verb in terms of its being attributed to their fathers and not to them, meaning: "and our fathers were promised before," or that it be connected to a deleted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (hal) from "our fathers," meaning: "being [those promised] from before." ﴿This is not﴾, i.e., this is not, ﴿except the fables of the ancients﴾, i.e., their falsehoods which they inscribed. ("Asatir" is) the plural of ustura, like uhduwtha and u'juwba. This is the view of al-Mubarrad and a group. It was said: it is the plural of asfar, the plural of satr, like faras and afras. The first, as al-Zamakhshari said, is more suitable, because the plural of a singular form is preferred and more regular, and because the pattern uf'ula comes for what involves amusement. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 84–85:

﴿Say: "To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it" of creatures?﴾ [Here "whoever" is used] by giving precedence to the rational beings over the others.

﴿If you know﴾ Its answer is omitted, relying on the indication of the interrogative (istifham) upon it. That is: if you are among the people of knowledge and among the rational, or know this, then inform me of it. In the verse there is an exaggeration in belittling them and affirming the extreme of their ignorance that is not hidden.

What strengthens this is that He, glory be to Him, reported the answer before they answered, saying: ﴿They will say, "To Allah."﴾ For the self-evidence of reason compels them to acknowledge that He, glory be to Him, created it, so the lam is for ownership in consideration of creation. ﴿Say﴾, i.e., when they acknowledge that, as a rebuke to them. ﴿Then will you not remember?﴾ i.e., do you know, or do you say that, yet not remember? That is, the One who originated the earth and whoever is in it is able to bring them back a second time, for originating is not easier than restoring; rather, the matter is the reverse according to the analogy of reason. It has also been read as "tatadhakkarun" according to the original form.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verses 86–87:

﴿Say, "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?"﴾ The word "Lord" (al-Rabb) is repeated to draw attention to the status of the Throne (al-'Arsh) and to elevate its station, lest it be considered a mere appendage to the heavens in existence or in mention. Ibn Muhaysin read "al-'Azim" (the Mighty) in the nominative (bi'l-raf'), as a qualifier (na't) of "the Lord."

﴿They will say, "To Allah."﴾ Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it without the lam (preposition "li"). As for what follows, it is not read without the lam, as was said regarding the previous one. The reading without the lam is according to the apparent wording, and the reading with the lam is according to the meaning. Both are permissible. For if it were said, "Who is the owner of this house?" and the answer was "Zayd," this would be a reply according to the wording of the question. But if it were said, "Li-Zayd," it would be a reply according to the meaning, since the meaning of "Who is the owner of this house?" is "To whom does this house belong?" Both usages occur in their speech. The author of al-Mut,la' recited:

When it is asked, "Who is the lord of the villages and the settlements, and the lord of the sleek, swift horses?" I say, "Khalid."

And al-Zajjaj recited:

"When the questioners asked, 'For whom did you dig?' the informants answered them, 'A vizier.'"

﴿Say﴾ as a rebuke and a reproach to them: ﴿Will you not then fear Allah?﴾ That is: do you know this and yet not fear for yourselves His punishment for not acting upon what knowledge requires? You disbelieve in Him, the Exalted, deny what He has informed of concerning the Resurrection, and ascribe to Him, glory be to Him, a partner.

﴿Say: "In whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of everything"﴾, of what He has mentioned and of what He has not mentioned. The form malakut is intensive from malik (king), so it means the all-encompassing, manifest sovereignty. It has also been said that it means ownership and governance (al-malikiyyah wa al-mudabbiriyyah), and it has been said that it means the treasuries.

﴿And He grants protection﴾, that is, He prevents whom He wills from whom He wills. ﴿And none can be given protection against Him﴾, that is, no one can prevent anyone from Him, exalted is He. ﴿If you know﴾ is a repetition, reflecting their contempt and their ignorance, as has already passed.

﴿They will say, "To Allah."﴾ The dominion of everything belongs to Allah, and the attribute that He is the One who grants protection and against whom no protection can be given.

﴿Say﴾: a rebuke and a reproach to them.

﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ That is, how or from where are you deceived and turned away from right guidance, although you know it, toward what you are upon of transgression? For whoever is not bewitched (maskhur) or deranged in mind does not act in this way.

These three verses, from ﴿Say: "To whom"﴾ up to here, according to what was established in al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari), are a confirmation of what precedes and a preparation for what follows. In the question within them the principle of ascent (al-tarraqqi) has been observed: He was asked about the one to whom the earth belongs and whoever is in it; it has been said that ﴿whose﴾ is used to give precedence to rational beings (taghlib lil-ʿuqala') and because it follows that the earth belongs to Him, and whoever is in it, by way of priority. Then He was asked about the one to whom the seven heavens and the Mighty Throne belong, and the earth, which in relation to Him is nothing. Then He was asked about the one in whose hand is the dominion of everything, so He used the most general of generals and the word of comprehensiveness, and He preferred malakut, which is the vast sovereignty. It has been said that ﴿in His hand﴾ is a depiction and an imaginative representation. This same subtlety has been observed in the verse endings (fawasil): first they were reproached for not taking heed, since the simplest reflection suffices to unravel their knot; then for not being wary, and in this there is a warning; then with amazement at the deceptions of their intellects, for they imagined falsehood to be truth and truth to be falsehood, and how could they then remember or fear?

﴿Nay, We have brought them the truth.﴾ This is a turning away (idrab) from their saying: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients.﴾ By "the truth" is meant the promise of resurrection.
