Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 91:

﴿God has not taken any offspring﴾, for He is exalted, Mighty and Majestic, above need, and holy, Exalted, above being like anyone.

﴿Nor was there any god with Him﴾ who would share with Him, glory be to Him, in divinity, ﴿for then each god would have taken away what he created﴾, meaning he would have been independent with what he created, self-sufficient in its management, and his dominion would have been distinguished from the dominion of the other, ﴿and some of them would have prevailed over others﴾, and there would have occurred mutual warfare and domination among them, as is the case among kings. The consequent is false, because it entails the negation of the divinity of all of them, or the divinity of all but one of them, and this contradicts the supposition. Or, because it entails that the dominion of all things would not be in His hand alone, and this is false in itself, as has been demonstrated in theology and according to the opponent, since he holds that the dominion of all things belongs exclusively to Him, as the preceding question and answer just above indicate. Thus it is said. It should not be overlooked that the implication in the conditional understood from the verse is customary (ʿādī), not rational (ʿaqlī). For this reason it has been said: the verse is an allusion to a persuasive (iqnāʿī), not a certain (qaṭʿī), proof of Tawhid (divine unity). In al-Kashf: "It has become clear to us, by the subtle grace and support of God Most High, that the verse is a luminous proof of His unity, glory be to Him. Its formulation is that the one who gives preponderance to the possible (mumakkanāt) is the Necessary Existent, Exalted in His rank, transcendent above every plurality. As for plurality of constituents or quantitative parts, its negation is evident, since they entail contingency. As for multiplicity together with unity in quiddity, it is likewise (negated), because of the need for a distinguisher (mumayyiz), and the quiddity does not require their unity in it, so contingency is entailed. Then the criterion in both sides is attributes of perfection, because attributing what has no perfection is deficiency. So both are deficient, contingent, and in need in existence of an external perfecter, which is the Necessary in truth. Likewise, need in the perfection of what pertains to existence entails contingency, because it entails that there be in it something actual and something potential, and it requires composition and contingency.

From here the scholars said: the Necessary Existent in Himself is necessary in all His attributes; there is nothing in Him awaiting. With difference in quiddity it follows that the one who gives preponderance is not a preponderator, i.e., the god is not a god. For each one of the possibles, if each were independent in giving preponderance to it, it would entail the concurrence of two complete causes upon one individual effect, which is evidently impossible. So his being a preponderating god entails need of him, and the other's being independent in preponderance entails independence from him, so he would be a preponderated non-preponderator in one state. And if they cooperate, it is like the parable, since neither of them is a preponderator, yet supposing both to be preponderators, together with the incapacity to bring into existence and the need of the other. And if each is specialized with some part, while need of both is equal, it entails that the preponderator be specialized by a specifier that specializes it with that part, necessarily; and that specifier is not the essence, because need of both is equal, so there is no priority of preponderance from the standpoint of essence, nor is it an effect of the essence, because it would then be possible, and the discussion regarding it recurs. Thus the two first impossibilities follow: need of a distinguisher other than the essence and its requirement, and the entailment of deficiency for each, because this distinguisher is an attribute of perfection. Then the specifier of each by that distinction is the external Necessary, not the two of them. To the first impossibility, the verse refers: ﴿for then each god would have taken away what he created﴾, which is necessary on the supposition of difference in quiddity and the specialization of each with a part. It singled out this division because the other is more evidently impossible. And to the second, His words refer: ﴿and some of them would have prevailed over others﴾, i.e., either absolutely or in some respect, so that the superior would be the god, or there would be no god at all. This is necessary on the supposition of difference, unity, specialization, and otherwise. So it is a completion of the proof in one respect and a second proof from another. Thus it has become clear, as plain as the dawn, that He, Exalted, is the One, the Unique, whether His existence is made additional to the quiddity or not, whether He is an agent by choice or not. The proof of unity is not based on His being an agent by choice, as Imam al-Razi, may God sanctify his secret, supposed." End of quotation. This is a statement that shows the marks of verification, and perhaps some objections may be raised against it which are dispelled by sincere reflection.

What we have pointed to, the understanding of a conditional proposition from the verse, is very evident according to what al-Farra' held. He said: when ʾidhan ("then") is followed by lam (the lam of emphasis), there is an implied law (law) before it if it is not expressed, as in ﴿for then each god would have taken away what he created﴾; so it is as if it were said: "If there were with Him gods as you claim, then each god would have..."

Abu Hayyan said: ʾidhā is a particle of answer and conditional, and an oath is presumed, so that ﴿la-dhahaba﴾ is its answer; the estimate is "by God, if there were with Him a god, it would have gone away," and it is in the sense of la-yadhhabanna, as in His words: ﴿And if We sent a wind and they saw it yellowed, they would surely remain disbelieving﴾ [al-Rum: 51], i.e., la-yazallunna, because ʾidhā indicates the future, and this is as you see. It may be said that this ʾidhā is not the well-known word, but rather the conditional ʾidhā whose clause that it is attached to has been omitted and replaced by tanwin, as in yawma'idhin; and the original is ʾidhā kāna maʿahu min ilāhin la-dhahaba, etc. The use of ʾidhā is for the sake of accommodating the opponent. It was also said: ﴿each god﴾ because the negation is general and indicates the comprehensiveness of the genus. The "mā" in ﴿with what He created﴾ is a relative pronoun with an omitted return-pronoun, as we have indicated.

He permitted it to be a verbal (maṣdariyya) mā, but this requires a kind of strained construction that is not hidden. He did not argue for the negation of taking offspring, either because its corruption is extremely evident, or because he was content with the argument established for the negation of there being with Him, glory be to Him, any god, based on what has been said: that the son of a god must be a god, since the offspring is of the same kind as the parent and of its substance. There is discussion about this. ﴿Glory be to God above what they describe﴾: an intensification in declaring Him exalted above offspring and partner. Here "mā" is a relative pronoun, and he permitted it to be a verbal mā. It was read "taṣifūna" with the second-person "ta".

And ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾: that is, of every unseen thing and every witnessed thing. The word ﴿Knower﴾ is in the genitive case, either as a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for the Greatest Name or as an adjective (*sifah*, qualifier) of it, because what is intended is permanence and continuity, so it becomes definite through the construct (*idafah*).

A group of the seven canonical readers (*al-sab'a*, the seven readers) and others read it in the nominative, as the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*, subject), meaning: "He is the Knower." According to al-Akhfash, the genitive is more excellent, and according to Ibn 'Atiyya, the nominative is more eloquent. Whichever reading is adopted, it is, as has been said, a pointer to another proof for the negation of partners, based on the agreement of Muslims and polytheists that God, exalted is He, is alone in this. In the *Kashshaf*, it is stated that in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Knower﴾ and what follows, there is a pointer to another proof, which returns to establishing exaltedness, or to the necessity of ignorance, which is a deficiency and the opposite of exaltedness. This is because multiple beings have no way for each to know the reality of the other as the other knows itself, by necessity, and this is a kind of ignorance and deficiency. Furthermore, their knowledge of one another would be receptive, following the existence of the known, and thus it would be dependent in one of the attributes of perfection, namely knowledge, and this indicates deficiency and contingency.

﴿Exalted is God above what they associate﴾: this is a consequence of His being knowing of that, so it is like the conclusion of the proof to which He has pointed.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the *fa'* (fa, "so") is conjunctive, as if it were said: "He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, so exalted is He," just as you say, "Zayd is brave, so his rank has become great," in the sense of "he showed courage, so it became great." It is also possible that the meaning is "so I say, exalted is He," as a new independent statement.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verses 93–94:

﴿Say: "My Lord, if You should show me that which they are promised,﴾
page 61
That is: if it must be that You show me [it], because مَا (mā) and the nūn (nūn al-tawkīd) have been added for emphasis. ﴿that which they are promised﴾, that is, the worldly punishment that they are promised, which uproots [them]; as for the otherworldly punishment, it is not suited to the context. ﴿My Lord, do not place me among the wrongdoing people﴾, that is, do not make me a companion to them in the punishment they are in. The apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate that they deserve the punishment. The supplication has come before the condition and before the consequent, for the sake of intensifying supplication and humble entreaty. The word "Lord" (Rabb) has been chosen because it conveys that He, glory be to Him, is the Owner who looks after the interests of the servant and his affairs. That the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to supplicate with this, although he, peace and blessings be upon him, was in a great fortress against being made a companion to them, is an indication of the complete dreadfulness of the promised punishment and that it is of such a kind that one who can hardly imagine it befalling him must seek refuge from it. And it contains a rejection of their denial of the punishment and their urging of it, in the manner of mockery.

It has also been said that he ﷺ was commanded to say this out of humbling himself and showing the perfection of servanthood. It has also been said that the ill omen of the disbelievers may befall others besides them, as in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And guard yourselves against a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. It is related from al-Hasan that He, majestic is His glory, informed His Prophet ﷺ that there would be a vengeance upon his community, without informing him of its time, whether it would be during his life or after it; so He commanded him with this supplication.

Al-Dahhak and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni recited «تَرِئَنِي» with a hamza in place of the yā' (ya'), and it is, as in al-Bahr, a weak substitution.

and We are certainly able to show you [the punishment] that We promise them ﴿وإنّا عَلى أنْ نُرِيَكَ ما نَعِدُهُمْ﴾ of the torment ﴿لَقادِرُونَ﴾ — ﴿and indeed We are able to show you what We promise them﴾ — but We do not do so; rather We delay it from them, because of Our knowledge that some of them, or some of their descendants (a'qab), will believe, or because We do not punish them while you are among them. It has been said that Allah, glorified is He, had already shown him that, namely what befell them on the day of Badr or the conquest of Makkah. Shaykh al-Islam said: "Its remoteness is not hidden, for what is apparent is that what they deserve of the promised torment is a tremendous torment that uproots them entirely, one that does not manifest at his hands (ﷺ), because of the wisdom that calls for it."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 96:

﴿Repel [evil] with that which is best.﴾ That is: repel the evil deed with the good deed that is the best of good deeds by which one repels [evil], namely, that you be as kind as you can to the wrongdoer in return for it. Below this in goodness is that you be kind to him in general, and below that is that you merely pardon his wrong. In this there is an exhortation to him, ﷺ, toward what befits his noble station of good character, which is not hidden. And it is more eloquent than "Repel evil with good," because of the word ﴿best﴾, and the comparative in it is in its literal sense, as we have mentioned; this is a good interpretation of the verse. He also permitted that the comparison be considered between the good deed and the evil deed in the sense that the good deed, within the category of good deeds, is more excellent than the evil deed within the category of evil deeds. This applies to every comparison between two opposites, such as their saying: "Honey is sweeter than vinegar," for they mean that it is more distinguished among sweet things than vinegar is among sour things. Of this kind is what is related of Ash'ab the libertine, that he said: "Al-A'mash and I were raised in the lap of so-and-so, and he kept rising and falling until we became equal," for he meant their equality in each of them reaching the extreme: he reached the extreme of hanging low, and al-A'mash the extreme of rising high. On both interpretations, this "best" and likewise "evil" are not specifically determined.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya narrated from Anas that he said regarding the verse: A man says to his brother what is not in him, and he [the other] says: "If I am lying, then I ask Allah Most High to forgive you; and if you are truthful, then I ask Allah Most High to forgive me."

It has been said: "That which is best" is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and "the evil deed" is polytheism. ʿAtaʾ and al-Dahhak said: "That which is best" is peace (al-salam), and "the evil deed" is obscenity (al-fuhsh). It has been said: the first is admonition (al-mawʿiza) and the second is the reprehensible (al-munkar). Some chose generality, and that what is mentioned is before the illustration. It has been said that the verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword; and it has been said that it is muhkam (not abrogated), because the repelling mentioned is required so long as it does not lead to the undermining of the religion and the disgracing of manliness. ﴿We know best what they describe﴾, that is, with their description of you, or with that which they describe you by, of what you are not; and in this there is a warning to them of recompense and punishment, and consolation for the Messenger of Allah, ﷺ, and guidance for him, peace be upon him, to entrust his affair to Him, Mighty and Majestic. The apparent meaning from this is that the verse is a verse of conciliation (muwada'a), so understand.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verses 97–98:

﴿And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the goadings (hamazat) of the devils"﴾. That is, from their enticing whisperings (waswas) toward what You have not commanded. The word is the plural of hamzah, and al-hamz means to prod or push, with the hand or otherwise. From it comes mihmaz (a spur), the iron piece fastened to the back of a rider's heel, with which he prods the animal so that it speeds up or stands firm. Applying the term to whispering and inciting to sins is based on the apparent resemblance between them. The plural form refers either to the many occurrences, to the variety of whisperings, or to the multiplicity of devils.

﴿And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, from their presence (yahdurun) with me﴾. That is, from their presence around me in any state. Specifying the state of prayer and recitation of the Qur'an, as narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), and the state of the approach of death, as narrated from Ikrimah, is because these are the states most worthy of seeking refuge from, especially the last state. For this reason it has been said: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the struggle at the moment of the struggle (of death)." Ibn Zayd took the meaning to be general. The command to seek refuge from their presence after the command to seek refuge from their goadings serves to emphasize the warning against associating with them. Repeating the verb with the repeated address shows the complete care given to the thing commanded and expresses the utmost earnestness in the request.

It is recommended (yusann) to seek refuge from the goadings of the devils and from their presence when intending to sleep, for Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, reported from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to teach us words that we would say at sleep because of fright: 'In the name of Allah, I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah from His anger and His punishment, and from the evil of His servants, and from the goadings of the devils and that they should be present (with me).'"

﴿And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the goadings (hamazat) of the devils"﴾. That is, from their enticing whisperings (waswas) toward what You have not commanded. For this reason it has been said: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the struggle at the moment of the struggle (of death)." Ibn Zayd took the meaning to be general. ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them﴾. *Ḥattā* here is *ibtidā'iyya* (introducing a new clause, "until"/"even to the point that"), and it marks the end point (*ghāya*, limit) of an implied clause that the preceding words indicate. The sense is: "So I will not be like the disbelievers, whom the devils prick and who are present with them, until, when death comes to one of them, etc." Its parallel is the poet's line:

*fa-yā 'ajaban ḥattā Kulayb tasubbunī*
"How strange, even Kulayb reviles me!"

The implied sense is "all people revile me, even Kulayb," but the clause has been omitted here because of what follows *ḥattā*. It has also been said that this statement is connected to the second *yaṣifūn* (they describe), meaning that *ḥattā* is linked to an omitted element that the context indicates, as if it were said: "They continue in evil speech and slander in the presence of the Messenger, until, when, etc." The words of the Exalted, ﴿Say: My Lord, etc.﴾, form a parenthetical interjection (*i'tirāḍ*) that emphasizes the forbearance implied by His words, ﴿Repel evil with what is better﴾, etc., by seeking refuge with Him, Exalted is He, from the devils, lest they make him, peace and blessings be upon him, deviate from what he was commanded. It has also been said that it is connected to the first *yaṣifūn* (they describe) or to *yushrikūn* (they associate partners), but this is not valid.

Al-Zamakhsharī permitted that it be a continuation of His words, ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾, and that it extends from His words, Exalted is He, ﴿God has not taken any son﴾, up to this point, as a parenthetical interjection confirming their lying and their deserving of His punishment. But this is not the correct view. It is understood from the words of Ibn 'Aṭiyya that *ḥattā* here may be inceptive without being a limit for what precedes it. Abū Ḥayyān criticized this, saying that when it is inceptive it does not lose the sense of a limit. The apparent meaning, which should not be departed from, is that the pronoun in ﴿aḥadahum﴾ refers to the disbelievers, and the meaning of the arrival of death is the appearance of its signs, i.e., when the signs of death appear to any one of them, whoever he may be, and the conditions of the Hereafter become manifest to him.

﴿He says﴾, in regret over what he neglected regarding the right of God, Exalted is He, ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾, i.e., return me to the world. The *wāw* (in *ārji'ūnī*) is for honoring the one addressed, who is God, Exalted is He, as in the words of the poet:

*lā farḥamūnī yā ilāha Muḥammadin*
*fa-in lam akun ahlan fa-anta lahu ahl*
"Do not have mercy on me, O God of Muhammad;
if I am not worthy, You are worthy of it."

And the words of another:

*wa-in shi'ta ḥarramat al-nisā'u siwākum*
*wa-in shi'ta lam uṭ'im nuqāḥan wa-lā baradā*
"If You wish, the women other than you become forbidden [to me],
and if You wish, I shall not taste cool water or hail."

The truth is that honorific plural may be used with the first person, second person, and even the third person, and with a proper noun. To deny this is not acceptable. The ambiguity that Ibn Mālik claims here is not to be considered. It has also been said that the *wāw* is because the address is to the angels, peace be upon them, and the speech is in the sense of an elided noun: "O angels of my Lord, return me." It was also permitted that *rabbi* be an invocation to Him, Exalted is He, and *ārji'ūnī* be an address to the angels, peace be upon them. Perhaps support for this is found in what Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "They claim that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to 'Ā'isha, may God be pleased with her: 'When the believer sees the angels, they say: We will return you to the abode of the world?' He said: 'To the abode of worries and sorrows; rather, [it is] advancing to God, Exalted is He.' As for the disbeliever, they say to him: 'We will return you?' He says: 'My Lord, return me, return me.'" 

Al-Māzinī said: He used the plural pronoun to indicate repetition, as if he had said: "My Lord, return me, return me, return me." Similar to this is the dual pronoun in *qifā nabki* and the like.

Al-Khafājī raised an objection to this, saying: If the original form of *irji'ū* is, for example, *irji' irji' irji'*, then the plural pronoun would not be there; rather its structure in which there is a real meaning is what applies. If it is a metaphor, then which kind of metaphor is it, and how does it indicate the intended meaning, and what is its relation? Otherwise it is something for which there is no justification. Among his strange remarks is that its pronoun was a singular hidden pronoun that must be concealed, so it became a non-singular pronoun that must be made manifest. Then he said: This objection has been in my mind for a long time, and what occurred to me is that we have another metaphor besides what was mentioned in the discussions of meaning (*ma'ānī*). Because it has no relation to meaning, it was not mentioned. It is the metaphor of using one expression in place of another expression for a purpose, regardless of its meaning. This is common in pronouns, such as using the explicit genitive pronoun in place of the hidden nominative pronoun in *kafā bihi*, to the point that it moved from one attribute to another attribute and from one expression to another expression. What we are dealing with is of this kind, for it is other than the hidden pronouns, changed to an explicit plural pronoun. Thus it became necessary to suffice with one of the verb's forms, and the indication of the plural pronoun on the repetition of the action was made to stand in its place for emphasis, without any figurative use in it. Ibn Jinnī in *al-Khaṣā'iṣ* has a statement that indicates what we have mentioned, so reflect. End of his words.

By my life, he has gone very far astray. Perhaps the closer view is to say: al-Māzinī intended that he used the plural pronoun for honor, by treating the single addressee as a group of addressees. This entails that the verb issued from him is like the verb issued from a group, and this in turn entails that *ārji'ūnī*, for example, is like *ārji'nī ārji'nī ārji'nī*. But applying such a thing to *qifā nabki* is not possible unless it is said that the dual pronoun may also intend honor, just as the plural pronoun may intend that. This did not occur to me before, but I have now seen it; so let it be investigated, and let it be pondered.

[Page 63]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 100:

﴿That I may do righteousness in that which I have left behind.﴾ That is, in the faith which I have left behind. "La'alla" (perhaps) here expresses hope (tarajji). It may refer either to both the deed and the faith, since he knows that he will not return, or to the deed alone, in order to realize his faith should he return. It is then like your saying: "Perhaps (la'alli) I will profit from this wealth," or like your saying: "Perhaps (li'alli) I will build upon a foundation," meaning: "Let me lay the foundation first, then build." It has also been said: "in that which you have left behind" refers to wealth or worldly goods, the departure from them being made equivalent to leaving them. It is also permissible for la'alla to express causation (ta'lil).

صفحة 64
In al-Burhan, al-Baghawi reports from al-Waqidi that everything in the Qur'an containing la'alla is for causation, except the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Perhaps you will abide forever﴾, where it is for comparison (tashbih).

Ibn Abi Hatim related, through the chain of al-Suddi from Abu Malik, something similar. Furthermore, the request for a return is not exclusive to the disbelievers. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, it is reported that the withholder of zakat and the one who abandons Hajj while able both ask for a return at the time of death.

Al-Daylami related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When death comes to a person, everything that prevents him from the truth is gathered for him and placed between his eyes. At that moment he says: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ ﴿that I may do righteousness in that which I have left behind.﴾"

This report supports that what is meant by "that which he has left behind" is wealth and the like. ﴿No!﴾ is a rebuke against seeking the return and a declaring of it as remote. ﴿Indeed, it is a word he speaks﴾, that is, his saying: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ etc., ﴿it is a word he is saying,﴾ without doubt: he will not be left to it, nor will he be silent about it, because of the overwhelming regret and the domination of remorse upon him. The fronting of the predicate's subject here is for emphasis (taqwa). Or, ﴿he is its sole speaker﴾, so the fronting is for exclusivity (ikhtisas). The meaning of this is that he will not be answered in it and it will not be heard from him, treating its answer and consideration as if it were its utterance, so that the one who is considered is as a partner to its speaker. Such usage is common: one who is addressed by his companion with something of no benefit says: "Occupy yourself alone with this word, speak and listen," meaning that it is something from which you are not heard and which does not deserve an answer. The word here carries the meaning of speech, as in their saying "the word of testimony" (kalimat al-shahada). In this sense, according to the grammarians, it is a metaphor (majaz); but according to the lexicographers, it is said to be a literal usage, and it is said to be a well-known metaphor.

The apparent view is that ﴿No!﴾ and what follows it are from the speech of Allah the Exalted. Far removed is he who claims that ﴿No!﴾ is from the words of one who has witnessed death, saying it to himself by way of lament and remorse. ﴿And before them﴾, that is, in front of them, and its verification has already passed. The pronoun refers to one of them, and the plural is used according to meaning, since he is in the ruling of all of them, just as the singular in the earlier pronouns is according to wording. ﴿A barrier﴾ stands between them and the return ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ from their graves, which is the Day of Resurrection. This makes their return to the world conditional upon impossibility, like the conditioning of their entry into Paradise upon His saying: ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40]. It is reported from Ibn Zayd that what is meant by "before them" is a barrier between death and resurrection from graves on the Day of Resurrection, which remains until the day they are resurrected. It has also been said: it is a barrier between them and complete recompense, which remains until the Day of Resurrection; when that day comes, they will be recompensed in the most complete manner.

﴿Then when the Horn is blown﴾ for the arrival of the Hour. This is the second blast, at which resurrection and rising take place. It has also been said that the meaning is: when He blows into the bodies their spirits, taking ṣuwar (ṣuwar) to be the plural of ṣūrah (form), like busr and busrah, and not the horn (al-qarn). This is supported by the recitation of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan and Ibn ʿIyad, "fī al-ṣuwar" with a ḍammah on the ṣād and a fatḥah on the wāw, and by the recitation of Ibn Razin, "fī al-ṣiwar" with a kasrah on the ṣād and a fatḥah on the wāw. In these two recitations, what is mentioned is definitely the plural of ṣūrah and not in the sense of the horn, and the original principle is that the meanings of the recitations are consistent with one another. There is no contradiction between blowing into the Horn in the sense of the qarn, which is reported in the khabar and indicated by other verses, and blowing into the ṣuwar as the plural of ṣūrah, for it has been reported that this blowing takes place at that time. ﴿Then there will be no kinship among them that Day﴾, that is, on the Day when the Horn is blown, just as there is kinship among them today. The meaning is that kinship will not benefit them at all, so it is treated as though it did not exist, because of the greatness of the terror and because each person is preoccupied with himself, such that a man flees from his brother, his mother, his father, his spouse and his children.

Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nuʿaym in al-Hilyah, and Ibn ʿAsakir reported from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah, exalted is He, will gather the first and the last."

In another wording: "A servant or a female servant will be taken by the hand on the Day of Resurrection before the heads of the first and the last. Then a caller will call out: 'Behold, this is so-and-so, son of so-and-so. Whoever has a right against him, let him come to his right.'" And in another wording: "Whoever has a wrong done to him, let him come and take his right." By Allah, a man will rejoice that he has a right against his father, his son or his wife, even if the right is small.

The proof of this in the Book of Allah, exalted is He, is ﴿Then when the Horn is blown, there will be no kinship among them﴾. This report indicates that this ruling is not specific to the disbelievers, but includes them and others. It has also been said that it is specific to them, as the context of the verse requires. It has also been said that no lineage will benefit on that Day except the lineage of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi, Abu Nuʿaym, al-Hakim and al-Diya in al-Mukhtarah reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Every cause and every lineage will be cut off on the Day of Resurrection, except my cause and my lineage.'"

A group also reported something similar from Musawwar ibn Makhramah, may Allah be pleased with him, as a marfuʿ report (traced to the Prophet). Ibn ʿAsakir also reported something similar, likewise as a marfuʿ report, from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both.

This is an accepted report, which only someone with a trace of nasb (enmity toward the family of the Prophet) in his heart would reject. Yes, it should be said that the benefit of the lineage of the Prophet (ﷺ) applies only to the believers who were honoured by it. As for the disbeliever, may Allah protect us, there is no benefit to him from it at all. It may also be said that this report does not contradict the intended generality of the verse, by taking the meaning to be the negation of attention to lineages immediately after the second blast, without any interval, as the conditional fāʾ (fāʾ al-jazāʾiyyah) indicates, for it, according to the preferred view, indicates immediate sequence. The purpose is to magnify the greatness of that time by explaining that every person will be so distracted that he will not pay attention to anyone to whom he is related, nor will it occur to him, let alone whether it will benefit him or not. This does not indicate that no lineage at all will benefit, let alone that the lineage of the Prophet (ﷺ) will not benefit.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and it is related from al-Jubba'i that the meaning is that on that Day one will not boast of lineages as one boasts of them in this world, but will boast there only of deeds and of deliverance from terrors. Since he does not boast of them there, they are as though they did not exist. According to this, and likewise according to what has preceded, the words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿there will be no kinship﴾ are a case of majaz (metaphor).

It has also been permitted that there is an implied adjective, meaning: "no kinship that is beneficial, or to which attention is paid, or in which one boasts." But this is not the right view. The apparent view is that the governing element of ﴿that Day﴾ is the same as the governing element of ﴿among them﴾, not "kinship," for that is clear. ﴿Nor will they ask one another﴾, that is, they will not ask one another about his condition, or from whom he is, or the like, because each of them is preoccupied with himself and does not pay attention to the people of his kind. This is immediately after the second blast, also without interval. Thus it is restricted to ﴿that Day﴾, though it is not mentioned again after it, relying on what has come before. It seems that both rulings apply after the reality of that blast has become clear to them and they know why it occurred. In that case it may be said that their saying ﴿Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾ (Yasin: 52) occurs before the reality of that blast has become clear to them, so there is no difficulty. It is also possible that both rulings apply at the beginning, before the aforementioned saying, as though when they hear the cry they become distracted from everything, including lineages and other things, like a sleeper who is roused by a frightening shout, jumps up from his sleep in terror, and forgets those beside him for a time. When their panic has subsided to some extent, one of them says: ﴿Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾

It has also been said: we do not grant that their saying ﴿Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾ was in the manner of asking one another. On both possibilities, this does not raise a difficulty together with His saying, exalted is He, concerning the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿And some of them will turn toward others, asking one another﴾ (al-Saffat: 27; al-Tur: 25), and concerning the believers: ﴿So some of them will turn toward others, asking one another﴾ (al-Saffat: 50). The asking of the disbelievers that is negated in one place and the asking of them that is affirmed in another place are different: the affirmed asking may be at Hell, and that is long after the second blast. Likewise the asking of the believers is also long after it, for it takes place in Paradise, as a return to what precedes the verse indicates. It may be said that the negated asking here is the asking for recognition and the like, through which harm is averted or benefit is obtained. The affirmed asking for the people of the Fire is a different kind of asking, and He, glory be to Him, has explained it by His saying, mighty is the One who speaks: ﴿They will say: "You used to come to us from the right"﴾ (al-Saffat: 28), and so on. He, majestic and exalted, has also explained the asking of the people of Paradise by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿One of them will say: "I had a companion"﴾ (al-Saffat: 51), and so on. This too is another kind of asking, in which there is nothing more than seeking companionship, without averting harm from the one speaking to him or obtaining benefit for him.

It has also been said that what is negated is asking by means of lineages, so that it is as though it were said: there is no kinship among them, and they do not ask one another about them. The meaning is that they are not beneficial in themselves and in their estimation. The verse concerns the disbelievers, and their affirmed asking in another verse is not asking by lineages, which is clear, so there is no difficulty.

A group reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he was asked about how to reconcile the negation here with the affirmation in the words of Allah, glory be to Him: ﴿And some of them will turn toward others, asking one another﴾ (al-Saffat: 27). He said: the negation of asking is at the first blast, when there remains on the face of the earth nothing, and its affirmation is at the second blast. According to this, the meaning for him of the words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿Then when the Horn is blown﴾ is: when He blows the first blast. This is one of two reports from him, may Allah be pleased with him. The second report takes it to refer to the second blast. In that case, regarding how to reconcile them, he chooses one of the aspects we have indicated.

Ibn Masʿud recited (wa-la yassaʾalūn) with a shaddah on the sīn.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 102:

﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy﴾ — i.e., the things weighed of his good deeds, from beliefs and actions. It is also permissible that al-mawazin (the scales) is the plural of mizan (scale), and the reason for its plural form has already been mentioned.

The meaning according to this is: whoever's scales are heavy with good deeds, ﴿those are the successful ones﴾ — those who attain every sought-after goal and are saved from every feared thing.

﴿And whoever's scales are light﴾, meaning the scales of his good deeds, or his deeds which have no weight and no regard, namely his evil deeds. This is what has been said, and it is built upon their disagreement over whether the deeds of disbelievers are weighed. Whoever holds that they are weighed says the first, and whoever does not says the second. The discussion of the parallel of this verse was already presented in Surat al-A'raf, so recall it.

﴿those are the ones who have lost their souls﴾, meaning they wasted them by squandering the time of their perfection, and they nullified their readiness to attain their perfection. The demonstrative in both places is an expression for the relative pronoun, and its plural form is in view of its meaning, just as the singular form of the two pronouns in the two relative clauses is in view of its wording.

﴿in Hell they will abide eternally﴾. It is a second predicate for ﴿those﴾. It is also permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are abiding eternally in Hell. The sentence is either a resumptive sentence brought to explain their losing their souls, or it is a second predicate for ﴿those﴾ as well. It is also permitted that ﴿who﴾ be a qualifier (na't) of the demonstrative, with ﴿abiding eternally﴾ as the predicate. It has also been said that ﴿abiding eternally﴾ together with its complement is a substitute (badal) for the relative clause. Al-Khafaji said: that is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), because their eternal abiding in Hell includes their loss, and it is treated thus in view of its meaning, that they will abide eternally in Hell, and by this it is suitable to be a relative clause, as the substitution from the relative clause requires. The apparent practice of al-Zamakhshari requires preferring this view, but it is not, in my opinion, the correct view, as its reasoning is not hidden. Abu Hayyan criticized the statement that ﴿in Hell they will abide eternally﴾ is a substitute, saying: this is a strange substitute, and its reality would be that the substitute is what is related to ﴿in Hell﴾, meaning they settled, and it is as if he substituted one thing for another while they refer to one named entity by way of metaphor, because whoever loses his soul settles in Hell. You know that the apparent reading is that ﴿in Hell﴾ is related to ﴿abiding eternally﴾, and that relating it to an omitted element and making that omitted element a substitute, while leaving ﴿abiding eternally﴾ detached from what it should be connected with, is not something that should be considered, especially with the clear reading that involves no artificiality.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 104:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Fire burns their faces﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah) or a resumptive new sentence (mustaʾnafah). Al-lafḥ (scorching) is the touch of the fire's flame upon a thing, and it is, as al-Zajjaj said, more intense in effect than al-nafḥ (blowing). The meaning is: the Fire scorches their faces. The specification of the faces with this [punishment] is because they are the most noble of the organs, so describing their condition is more effective in deterring from the sins that lead to the Fire, and this is the secret of placing them before the agent (al-fāʿil).

﴿And they therein are grim-faced﴾: drawn back, their lips retracted from the teeth, because of the effect of that scorching.

It has been authentically related, through the narration of al-Tirmidhi and a group [of narrators], from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said concerning the verse: "The Fire will sear him, so his upper lip will contract until it reaches the middle of his head, and his lower lip will hang down until it strikes his navel."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya', in [his book] Sifat al-Nar, related from Abu al-Darda', who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Fire scorches﴾, etc.: 'It will scorch them with one blast, and their flesh will flow off their heels.'" And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that al-kulūḥ (grimness) is the contraction of the face's features and its frowning. Abu Ḥaywa, Abu Biḥurriyya and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read "kalḥūna" without an alif, the plural of kalaḥ, like ḥadhar.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 105:

﴿Were not My verses recited to you?﴾ This is by way of implying a statement: it is said to them, as rebuke, reproach, and reminder of the reason why they deserved the punishment with which they were afflicted: "Were not My verses recited to you in the world?" ﴿And you used to deny them﴾ at that time.

﴿They said, "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us"﴾. That is, our wretchedness (shiqwah) prevailed over us and took possession of us. This wretchedness was necessitated by the poor disposition (su' isti'dad) we had, as the attribution of it to themselves indicates. Shibl, in his own reading (ikhtiyar), read «shiqwatinā» with a fatḥah on the shīn. ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd), al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim, Abān, al-Zaʿfarānī and Ibn Muqsim read «shaqāwatinā» with a fatḥah on the shīn and an alif after the qāf. Qatādah also, and al-Ḥasan in the transmission of Khālid ibn Ḥawshab from him, read «shaqāwatanā» with an alif and a kasrah on the shīn. In all of these readings it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and its meaning is the opposite of happiness (saʿādah). A group of scholars explained it as the bad outcome which God, exalted is He, knew they deserved because of their evil deeds. This is attributed to the majority of the Muʿtazilah (a theological school that held human beings create their own acts). It is reported from the Ashʿariyyah (followers of al-Ashʿarī) that what is meant by it is what God, exalted is He, had written against them from eternity of disbelief and sins. al-Jubbāʾī said: what is meant by it is caprice (hawā) and the satisfaction of desires, as a metaphor of the kind where the effect is named for its cause (iṭlāq al-musabbab ʿalā al-sabab). Whatever the case, the attribution of overcoming to it is by considering it as likened to something from which such an act can proceed. Thus the expression contains a implicit (makniyyah) imaginative (takhyīliyyah) metaphor (istiʿārah). Perhaps the better view is that the statement should be taken in the manner of an illustration (tamthīl). Their intention by this, on all the views concerning wretchedness, is the acknowledgment that God's proof (ḥujjah) stands against them, because its source, on all views when examined closely, is what they are in themselves. So it is as if they said: "Our Lord, a matter prevailed over us whose source is our own selves," ﴿and we were﴾ because of that ﴿a people astray﴾ from the truth, denying the signs that were recited. Hence it cannot be called an injustice in our punishment. It is not permissible that this be an excuse based on what God knew about them and wrote for them of disbelief. That would mean: "what You wrote against us of wretchedness prevailed over us, and we were in Your knowledge a people astray," or "what You knew and wrote prevailed over us, and we were, because of that, a people astray." Then the disbelief that happened from us against Your signs is something we have no power to remove. The implication is that knowledge would turn into ignorance, and that is impossible, because that claim is itself false and cannot serve as an excuse. For He, glorified is He, wrote only what He knew, and He knew only what they are in the reality of the matter, namely the poor disposition that leads to poor choice. For knowledge, as has been established in its proper place, follows the known. The acknowledgment is supported by His saying, exalted is He, quoting them:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 107:

﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it; then if we return, we will indeed be wrongdoers.﴾ That is: "Our Lord, bring us out of the Fire and return us to the world. Then if we return after that to what we were upon in it of disbelief and disobedience, we will indeed be exceeding the limit in wrongdoing." Their boldness in this request is more fitting to their earlier words being an acknowledgment, for the sinner often mollifies the anger of the one he has wronged by this means. Apology, though it is of this kind, and even greater, is nonetheless most like an objection, which brings about intense anger, and with which it is not good to undertake a request such as this. This is in addition to the fact that, had they not believed that this was an acceptable excuse and that apologizing with it was beneficial, they would not have advanced upon it. And with this belief, they have no need to request the bringing out and the returning. Nor can it be said that such a thing [is an acknowledgment], on the assumption that it is an acknowledgment, because they only said it as a preface to the aforementioned request, since it is a likely means of calming the blaze of the fire of anger, as you have heard. Furthermore, the people perhaps thought that what they were upon of poor preparedness would change if they returned, because of what they witnessed of their own condition on that day; and for this reason they made the requests they made.

In their saying ﴿we return﴾ there is an indication that they were, at the time of the request, upon faith and obedience. So the promise, on the assumption of the return to the world, is steadfastness upon these two, so that they may benefit from them after they die and are gathered. So reflect.

﴿He said﴾ — God, glorified is He, [saying this] to despair them with the utmost despair — ﴿Be driven away therein﴾. That is: be humbled and rebuffed with the rebuff of dogs, like a dog that is chased away when you chase it, so it is driven off (*khasaʾa*), i.e., it withdraws. Or: be silent with the silence of contempt. In this there is an *istiʿarah makniyyah* (concealed metaphor), whose *qarinah tasrihiyyah* (explicit indicator) is [the verb] "be driven away." ﴿And do not speak to Me﴾ — [that is,] by asking to be brought out of the Fire and returned to the world. It is also said: "Do not speak to Me about lifting the punishment." The first is more suitable to what precedes it and to the reason given afterward. It is also said: "Do not speak to Me ever," and this is the last speech they will utter.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya related in *Sifat al-Nar* from Hudhayfah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When God, the Exalted, says to the people of the Fire, 'Be driven away therein and do not speak to Me,' their faces will return to a piece of flesh with no mouths or nostrils, and the breath will move back and forth in their bellies."

Al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Baʿth*, ʿAbdullah ibn Ahmad in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd*, and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, along with a group [of scholars], related from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs that he said: "The people of Hell will call out, 'Malik! Let your Lord put an end to us' (*Liyaqḍi ʿalayna rabbuka*). He will leave them forty years without answering them. Then he will answer them: 'Indeed you will remain [here]' (*Innakum mākithūn*). Then they will call out to their Lord: 'Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers' (*Rabbana akhrijna minha fa-in ʿudna fa-inna ẓālimūn*). He will leave them for double the length of the worldly life and will not answer them. Then He will answer them: ﴿Be driven away therein and do not speak to Me﴾." He said: "After that, the people will not utter a single word; there will only be the groaning and the sobbing."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others related from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb that he said: "The people of the Fire have five supplications; God answers them in four. When the fifth comes, they will never speak after it. They will say: ﴿Our Lord, You have made us die twice and given us life twice, so we have acknowledged our sins; is there any way out?﴾ [Ghafir: 11]. Then God answers them: ﴿That is because when God alone was invoked, you disbelieved, and when partners were associated with Him, you believed. So the judgment belongs to God, the Most High, the Great﴾ [Ghafir: 12]. Then they say: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us, and we will do righteousness; indeed we are certain﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12]. Then God answers them: ﴿So taste [the punishment] for having forgotten the meeting of this your Day﴾ — this — ﴿Indeed We have forgotten you, so taste the punishment of eternity for what you used to do﴾ [al-Sajdah: 14]. Then they say: ﴿Our Lord, delay us to a near term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]. Then God answers them: ﴿Did you not swear before that there would be for you no cessation?﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]. Then they say: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out; we will do righteousness, other than what we used to do﴾ [Fatir: 37]. Then God answers them: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough for whoever would take heed to take heed in it, and the warner came to you? So taste [it], for the wrongdoers have no helper﴾ [Fatir: 37]. Then they say: ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness has overcome us, and we were a misguided people﴾ ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers﴾. Then God answers them: ﴿Be driven away therein and do not speak to Me﴾, and they will never speak after that."

It is also mentioned in some reports: "They will cry out every supplication for a thousand years." These reports are problematic because of the apparent sense of the subsequent addresses, as is not hidden, and perhaps none of them is sound. Al-Hakim's authentication is subject to the judgment that it is not to be relied upon. And God, the Exalted, knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verses 109–110:

﴿Indeholdingly﴾... 

Let me correct and render the passage properly:

"Innahu" (indeed, verily) is an explanation (ta'lil) of what precedes it, namely the prohibition against supplication; that is, "indeed the matter is that..." And Ubayy and Harun al-'Ataki read "annahu" with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "because the matter..." ﴿Kana﴾ (there was) in the world to which you desire return, ﴿a group of My servants﴾, and they are the believers,

Page 69

and it is said: they are the Companions, and it is said: the people of the Suffah, may Allah be pleased with them all.

﴿They would say: "Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ ﴿But you took them in mockery﴾, meaning ridicule, that is: be silent from supplicating with your saying "Our Lord..." etc., because you used to mock those who called upon Him out of fear of this Day by their saying "Our Lord, we have believed..." etc. ﴿Until they caused you to forget My remembrance﴾ by your preoccupation with mocking them, ﴿My remembrance﴾, that is, the fear of My punishment on this Day.

﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾, and that is the utmost of mockery. It is also said: the explanation is in the sense of "We only pushed you away like a dog and did not regard you when you called, because you mocked, to the utmost degree, My friends when they called, and this continued from you until you wholly forgot My remembrance and did not fear My punishment, so this is your recompense." It is also said: the essence of the meaning of the verse is that there was a group of My servants who used to call, and you occupied yourselves with them scornfully, and your occupation with their mockery continued until it led you to abandon My remembrance regarding My friends, so you did not fear Me in mocking them. Then it is said: this appended clause is necessary so that His saying, exalted is He, "Indeed, he was..." etc. as an explanation is valid, the discourse is connected, and it harmonizes with His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾. If it were not meant so, the causing to forget of remembrance would be like something foreign in this context; and in it is great displeasure at their deed and an indication of the profound distinction of those servants who were mocked, as He drew attention to it first in His saying: "of My servants," and concluded it with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed I have rewarded them today for their patience; that they are the triumphant﴾ up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are the winners﴾, and He increased their humiliation by the honoring of their opposites. End. And it is not free of discussion.

Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "sikhriyyan" with a damma on the sin, and the rest of the seven with a kasra. The meaning in both is one, namely ridicule, according to al-Khalil, Abu Zayd al-Ansari and Sibawayh. Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the damma-ed sin means subjugation/employment without wage, and the kasra-ed means mockery. Yunus said: when subjugation is intended, the sin is damma only; when ridicule is intended, both damma and kasra are permissible. It is in both cases a verbal noun to which the ya' of relation has been added for intensity, as in "ahmariyy."

And His, exalted is He, saying:

﴿They would say: "Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ ﴿But you took them in mockery﴾, meaning ridicule, that is: be silent from supplicating with your saying "Our Lord..." etc., because you used to mock those who called upon Him out of fear of this Day by their saying "Our Lord, we have believed..." etc. ﴿Until they caused you to forget My remembrance﴾ by your preoccupation with mocking them, ﴿My remembrance﴾, that is, the fear of My punishment on this Day.

﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾, and that is the utmost of mockery. It is also said: the explanation is in the sense of "We only pushed you away like a dog and did not regard you when you called, because you mocked, to the utmost degree, My friends when they called, and this continued from you until you wholly forgot My remembrance and did not fear My punishment, so this is your recompense." It is also said: the essence of the meaning of the verse is that there was a group of My servants who used to call, and you occupied yourselves with them scornfully, and your occupation with their mockery continued until it led you to abandon My remembrance regarding My friends, so you did not fear Me in mocking them. Then it is said: this appended clause is necessary so that His saying, exalted is He, "Indeed, he was..." etc. as an explanation is valid, the discourse is connected, and it harmonizes with His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾. If it were not meant so, the causing to forget of remembrance would be like something foreign in this context; and in it is great displeasure at their deed and an indication of the profound distinction of those servants who were mocked, as He drew attention to it first in His saying: "of My servants," and concluded it with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed I have rewarded them today for their patience; that they are the triumphant﴾ up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are the winners﴾, and He increased their humiliation by the honoring of their opposites. End. And it is not free of discussion.

Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "sikhriyyan" with a damma on the sin, and the rest of the seven with a kasra. The meaning in both is one, namely ridicule, according to al-Khalil, Abu Zayd al-Ansari and Sibawayh. Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the damma-ed sin means subjugation/employment without wage, and the kasra-ed means mockery. Yunus said: when subjugation is intended, the sin is damma only; when ridicule is intended, both damma and kasra are permissible. It is in both cases a verbal noun to which the ya' of relation has been added for intensity, as in "ahmariyy."

And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 111:

﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for their patience﴾. That is, because of their patience in enduring your harm. This is a resumption (istinaf) explaining the excellence of their state and that they benefited from what they were made to suffer. Within it there is also an element of enraging them. As for the words of Him, glorified is He: ﴿that they are the triumphant ones﴾, it may be in the place of the second object of "jaza" (to reward), which takes its object directly and also with the preposition bi, as al-Raghib said; that is, I have rewarded them with their triumph, comprising all that they desired, as the object of the descriptive phrase indicates, while they are specially singled out for this, as the insertion of the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) indicates. It may also be in a place of genitive governed by an implied causal lam (li-ta'lil), meaning: because of their triumph through monotheism, which leads to every happiness. Nor does the causation of the reward by patience prevent this, because causes, since they are not complete causes, may be multiple.

Zayd ibn Ali, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Kharijah from Nafi' read ﴿innahum﴾ with a kasra, on the basis that the sentence is a resumption giving the reason for the reward. It has also been said that it explains its manner. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 112:

﴿Said﴾ Allah, exalted is His majesty. Or it is the angel (malak) who was commanded to say this, not some of the leaders of the people of the Fire, as has been said, as a reminder of how long they remained, concerning what they asked, namely returning to this world after the warning about its impossibility. In this there is also a rebuke for their denial of the Hereafter. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read "qul" (say) in the imperative, addressed to the angel (malik), not to some of the leaders, as has been said, nor to all the disbelievers, by making the singular stand for the plural, as al-Tha'alibi claimed. ﴿How many years did you remain on the earth﴾ which you wish to return to?

That is, how many years did you dwell there alive? ﴿In number of years﴾: a specification (tamyiz) for "you" (lakum), and it is an adverb of time for "labithtum" (you remained). Abu al-Baqa' said: "adadan" (in number) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿kam﴾ (how many). Al-A'mash and al-Mufaddal from Asim read "adadan" with tanwin. Abu al-Fadl al-Razzi said: "sinin" is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and "adadan" is a verbal noun (masdar) placed in the position of a noun, so it is a qualifying adjective (na't) placed before the qualified noun (manut). The suggestion that the meaning of "labithtum" is "you counted" is far-fetched. Abu al-Baqa' said: "sinin" in this reading is a substitute (badal) for "adadan".

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 113:

﴿They said: "We remained a day or part of a day."﴾ This is a belittling of the duration of their stay, in comparison with what they had come to know of the long duration of their abiding in the Fire. It was also said: they belittled it because it was the days of their happiness, compared with what they were in, and days of happiness are short. It was also said: because it was past, and what is past is not cared about, so its measure, whether long or short, is not known, and so one supposes it was short. ﴿So ask those who count﴾, i.e. those who are able to count, for we, with what we have suffered of punishment, are far removed from that; or it means the angels who count the lifespans and deeds of the servants, according to what a group related from Mujahid.

Al-Hasan and al-Kisa'i, in one transmission, read «al-'addin» (the ʿādd̲īn) with a light (unshadda) dal, i.e. the wrongdoers (al-ẓalama), for they say as we say: the followers used to call the leaders by this name because of their wronging them by misguiding them. And «al-'addiyyin» (﴿العادِّينَ﴾) was recited with a shaddah on the ya', the plural of ʿādiyy, a relative form derived from the people of ʿĀd; and what is meant by them is the long-lived, because the people of ʿĀd used to live very long, i.e. ask the ancient long-lived ones, for they too belittle the duration of their stay.

﴿He said﴾: that is, God Most High, or the angel. The Ikhwan (the Qur'anic readers Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i) read ﴿Qul﴾ ("Say") in the imperative, as they did in the earlier instance.

In ad-Durr al-Masun (a Qur'an commentary by al-Samin al-Halabi), it is said that in the codices (masahif) of Kufa the two verbs are written without an alif, while in the codices of Makkah, Madinah, Syria and Basra they are written with an alif. He transmits the same from Ibn 'Atiyya. In al-Kashshaf (by al-Zamakhshari), the reverse is reported. It seems that the orthography (rasm) without an alif allows for the alif being omitted from the past tense contrary to analogy. There are many peculiarities in the orthography of the codex (rasm al-mushaf) that are not hidden, so do not be heedless.

﴿If you remained﴾: that is, ﴿only a little﴾, is a confirmation of them in their statement, ﴿had you but known﴾: that is, you would know something, or had you been among the people of knowledge. (The word ﴿law﴾, "had", is conditional, and its answer is omitted, relying on the context to indicate it.) That is, had you known, you would have known on that Day the shortness of the days of the world, as you know it today, and you would have known the consequence of that, and nothing would have proceeded from you that necessitated your eternal abiding in the Fire. Our saying to you is ﴿Begone therein, and do not speak to Me﴾. It has also been said that the meaning is: had you known the brevity of your stay in the world in comparison with the Hereafter, you would not have been deceived by it and disobeyed. The negation of knowledge of that from them, on this view, is because they did not act upon its requirement, and whoever does not act upon his knowledge is equal to the ignorant.

Abu al-Baqa' estimated the answer to be: "Had you answered with this duration." Perhaps he makes the preceding speech a rebuttal of them and not a confirmation; otherwise this estimation is not valid. He also permitted that ﴿law﴾ be for wishing (tamanni), in which case it needs no answer. It should not be considered a connective (wasliyyah), because without the waw it is rare or non-existent.

Furthermore, many of the exegetes have said: the intention is their being asked about the duration of their stay in the graves, since they used to claim that after death they would become dust and would never rise from their graves.

Ibn 'Atiyya claimed that this is the most correct view, and that His later statement ﴿and that you will not be returned to Us﴾ requires it. But there is a clear objection to this. What supports what we have adopted is what has been related as a marfu' (traced back to the Prophet ﷺ) hadith: "When God Most High admits the people of Paradise into Paradise and the people of the Fire into the Fire, He says: 'O people of Paradise, how many years did you remain on the earth?' They say: 'We remained a day or part of a day.' He says: 'How excellent is what you achieved in a day or part of a day: My mercy, My good pleasure and My Garden. Abide therein forever, eternally.' Then He says: 'O people of the Fire, how many years did you remain on the earth?' They say: 'We remained a day or part of a day.' He says: 'How evil is what you achieved in a day or part of a day: My Fire and My wrath. Abide therein forever, eternally.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 115:

﴿Did you then suppose that We created you without purpose?﴾ That is: Did you not know anything, so that you supposed We created you without wisdom, such that you denied the Resurrection? "ʿAbathan" (without purpose) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the "nūn" of greatness (the royal "We"), meaning: playing/acting in vain (ʿābithīn). Or it is an accusative of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), meaning: Did you suppose that We created you for vain play (al-ʿabath), which is that which is devoid of benefit absolutely, or devoid of a benefit that is considered, or that which opposes the act, as the usūliyyūn (scholars of legal theory) mentioned.

Al-Khafajī preferred the first meaning here, and some of the investigating scholars (muḥaqqiqīn) chose the second. ﴿And that you to Us will not be returned?﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿that We created you﴾, meaning: Did you suppose that, and did you suppose that you will not be resurrected?

It is permitted that it be coordinated upon ﴿ʿabathan﴾, and the meaning would be: Did you suppose that We created you for vain play, and for your being left without being returned, or acting in vain and presuming that you will not return to Us? In the verse there is a rebuke of them for their heedlessness, and an indication that wisdom requires their being obligated and resurrected for recompense. Al-Akhawān (Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī) read "turjaʿūn" with an opening "t" (tā'), from the root "return" (ruj‑ūʿ).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 116:**

﴿So exalted is Allah﴾: this is a declaration of His majesty, exalted be He, and of His affairs, glory be to Him, by which He directs His servants, majestic and high is He, in origination, return, reward and punishment, in accordance with the far-reaching wisdom. That is, He, glory be to Him, is elevated in His essence and is far above resembling created beings in His essence, His attributes and His acts, and far above His acts being devoid of judgment and praiseworthy interests.

﴿The King, the Truth﴾: that is, the One deserving of absolute dominion, in bringing into existence and annihilating, in beginning and returning, in giving life and causing death, in punishment and reward. Everything other than Him is owned by Him, subdued under His dominion. It has been said that "the Truth" means the Established, who does not cease to exist and whose dominion does not cease. Although this is the more well-known view, the first is more suitable to the context. ﴿There is no god but He﴾, for everything other than Him is His servant, exalted be He. ﴿Lord of the Noble Throne﴾: it is a great body beyond the world of bodies and masses, and it is the greatest of them. Descriptions of its greatness that dazzle the intellects have been reported. It follows from His being its Lord, exalted be He, that He is the Lord of all bodies and masses, glory be to Him. It is described as "noble" because of its honour, and everything that is honoured within its category is described with nobility, as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And crops and a noble station﴾ [Surah al-Dukhan: 26], and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And say to them a noble word﴾ [Surah al-Isra': 23], and so on.

It has been honoured by the secrets that Allah, exalted be He, has deposited in it, and its greatest honour is His specifying it by His settling upon it, glory be to Him. It has been said that ascribing nobility to it is figurative (majaz, a word used in a non-literal sense), and what is meant is that its Lord is noble; or that this is meant by way of metonymy (kinaya, an expression in which the intended meaning is implied rather than stated). It has also been said that it is by way of comparing the Throne, because of the descent of mercy and blessing from it, to a noble person. What we have mentioned is probably the most apparent.

Aban ibn Taghlib, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Ja'far and Isma'il, from Ibn Kathir, read ﴿al-Karimu﴾ with a *raf'* (nominative ending, *al-Karīmu*), on the basis that it is an attribute of the Lord. It is permissible that it be an attribute of the Throne by way of *al-qat'* (the grammatical shift of a qualifier from the genitive to the nominative or accusative, to indicate a separate emphasis), written as القَطْع. It may be preferred on the grounds that it is more consistent with the reading of the majority.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 117:

﴿And whoever calls﴾ i.e., worships ﴿with Allah﴾ i.e., alongside His existence, exalted be He, and His reality, glorified be He ﴿another god﴾, singly or as a associate; or [it means] whoever worships another god alongside the worship of Allah, exalted be He, in the same manner. This is realized in the disbeliever when he singles out his false object of worship for worship at times and associates it with Allah, exalted be He, at other times. He may also restrict it to the intention of association in both cases, and the state of one who worships other than Allah, glorified be He, singly is known by the first.

As for the mention of ﴿another﴾, it has been said that it is for explicit declaration of His divinity, exalted be He, and to indicate a partner in it, and this is the intended purpose. So its mention is not an emphasis of what the "with" (ma'iyyah) indicates, though that is permissible; so reflect.

Indeed, the saying of the Exalted: ﴿for which he has no proof therein﴾ is a necessary attribute of ﴿another god﴾, not a restrictive one; it is brought for emphasis. And the building of the ruling derived from the conditional's answer, of the threat of requital in proportion to what he deserves, is a warning that adhering to religion without any evidence is forbidden, let alone that for which the evidence points to the contrary.

It is also permissible that it be a parenthetical clause between the condition and its answer, brought for emphasis, as in your saying: "Whoever does good to Zayd, there is no one more deserving of goodness from him, so Allah, exalted be He, will reward him."

Some people have claimed that it is the answer of the condition, apart from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿then indeed his account is with his Lord﴾, and have made it a consequence of the whole sentence. This is not correct, because it would necessitate omitting the fa' in the answer of the condition, and that is not permissible, as Abu Hayyan said, except in poetry.

And "account" is a metonymy for recompense, as if it were said: whoever worships a god alongside Allah, exalted be He, then Allah, glorified be He, will recompense him in proportion to what he deserves. ﴿Indeed, He does not prosper, the disbelievers﴾ i.e., indeed the matter is that the disbelievers do not prosper, etc.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah read "annahu" with a fathah, as causative, or they made what results from the composition the predicate of ﴿his account﴾, i.e., his account is non-prosperity. This, according to what al-Khafaji said, is from the category of "greeting among them is a painful striking." With this, and with the absence of the need for a supposition, he preferred this aspect over the preceding one, and the two readings agree upon it in the resulting meaning. He preferred the first on the basis that agreement upon it is more complete. The original form of the speech is in the informative mode: "then indeed his account is with his Lord, that he does not prosper," that is, he; so he placed ﴿the disbelievers﴾ in place of the pronoun, because "whoever calls" carries the sense of the plural, and likewise "his account, that he does not prosper" carries the sense of "their account, that they do not prosper."

Al-Hasan read "yuflah" with a fathah on the ya' and the lam. How elegant is the opening of this surah with the prosperity of the believers, and the mention of the non-prosperity of the disbelievers at its close. And there is no hiding what these sentences contain of consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is as if Allah, glorified be He, after consoling him by mentioning the end of one whose supplication does not avail, commanded him with what signals the abandonment of his opponents, so He, exalted and high, said:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 23, verse 118:**

﴿Say: "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, for You are the best of the merciful."﴾ Ibn Muhayṣin read "Rabb" with a ḍammah (Rabbu). The apparent meaning is that the request for both forgiveness and mercy is general, for him (ﷺ) and for those who follow him. It is also more general than a request for the act itself and for persistence in it, so there is no difficulty. It may be answered otherwise. The singling out of this supplication for mention indicates the importance of what it contains. The Prophet (ﷺ) taught Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) to say something similar in his prayer.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban and a group [of scholars] narrated from Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, teach me a supplication to recite in my prayer." He said: "Say: 'O Allah, I have wronged myself greatly, and none forgives sins but You. So forgive me with a forgiveness from You, and have mercy on me; indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful.'" Reciting these verses, meaning His saying: ﴿Did you then think﴾ to the end of the surah, has great benefit for the afflicted, and likewise persistence in reciting some of it while travelling.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) that he recited ﴿Did you then think﴾ into the ear of an afflicted person until he finished the surah, and he was cured. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, if a certain believer recited it upon a mountain, it would move."

Ibn al-Sunni, Ibn Mandah, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Ma'rifa narrated with a good chain, through Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Harith al-Taymi, from his father, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent us on a expedition and commanded us to say, when we evening and morning: ﴿Did you then think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ We recited it, and we gained booty and were safe."

This, and Allah the Exalted is the One asked for all good.
